title: Fast Competitive I/O & Stream Synchronization
coreConcept: Disabling C stdio sync buffers and untying cin from cout
timeComplexity: O(1) amortized per token (~4x faster than standard cin)
spaceComplexity: O(1) stream buffer allocation
theory:
#### Problem Definition & Motivation
By default in C++, standard input (`std::cin`) and standard output (`std::cout`) synchronize their internal stream buffers with the underlying C library standard I/O functions (`scanf`, `printf`). This synchronization ensures that interleaving C and C++ I/O statements produces deterministic, in-order output.

However, this compatibility layer comes at a severe performance cost:
* Every `std::cin` read flushes and syncs with C's `stdio` buffers.
* `std::cin` is tied to `std::cout` by default, meaning every read automatically triggers an explicit flush of the output buffer:
$$\text{Buffer Flush Overhead} = O(K) \text{ system call interrupts per interactive line}$$
In competitive programming or high-throughput batch processing with $N = 10^5$ to $10^6$ integer tokens, default `std::cin` frequently causes **Time Limit Exceeded (TLE)** purely due to buffer synchronization latency.

#### Invariants & The Fast I/O Blueprint
To achieve equivalent throughput to raw C `fread` and `scanf`, two essential stream transformations are applied at program initialization:

1. **`std::ios_base::sync_with_stdio(false);`**:
   * Disables synchronization between C++ iostreams and C standard streams.
   * Allows `std::cin` and `std::cout` to manage their own contiguous block memory buffers without making costly POSIX system calls per token.

2. **`std::cin.tie(nullptr);`**:
   * Unties `std::cin` from `std::cout`.
   * Eliminates the automatic flushing of `std::cout` before every `std::cin` extraction operation.

3. **`'\n'` over `std::endl`**:
   * `std::endl` writes a newline character and forces a physical buffer flush:
   $$\text{std::endl} \equiv \text{'\n'} + \text{std::flush}$$
   * Using `'\n'` allows output to accumulate in userspace buffers, flushing only when the buffer is full ($4\text{KB}$ to $64\text{KB}$ chunks).

#### ASCII Stream Architecture
```text
DEFAULT MODE (High Latency):
std::cin --------> [Sync Guard] -------> C stdio (stdin) ------> POSIX read()
                      | (Tied)
std::cout -------> [Sync Guard] -------> C stdio (stdout) -----> POSIX write() [Flushed on every read]

FAST I/O MODE (Zero Overhead):
std::cin --------> [Independent 4KB C++ Stream Buffer] --------> Direct OS Read
std::cout -------> [Independent 4KB C++ Stream Buffer] --------> Direct OS Write [Batch Flushed]
```

#### Complexity Analysis
* **Time Complexity**: $O(1)$ amortized per token processed. Throughput increases from ~300,000 ints/sec to over 2,000,000 ints/sec.
* **Space Complexity**: $O(1)$ auxiliary memory (uses built-in stream buffers).
description: Disabling C stdio synchronization and untying stream buffers for sub-millisecond competitive I/O throughput.

title: Multi-Word String Streaming & Getline Mechanics
coreConcept: Buffer cleansing with cin.ignore and in-memory tokenization via stringstream
timeComplexity: O(L) linear in characters read per line
spaceComplexity: O(L) contiguous string memory
theory:
#### Problem Definition & The Newline Trap
In C++, reading mixed data types (integers followed by multi-word text sentences) introduces a classic input trap:
* `cin >> num` reads up to the whitespace preceding the newline character `'\n'`, leaving the `'\n'` unconsumed in the input buffer.
* A subsequent call to `std::getline(cin, text)` immediately terminates upon encountering that lingering `'\n'`, returning an empty string:
$$\text{Buffer State: } [\text{42}] \xrightarrow{\text{cin >> n}} \text{Buffer: } [\text{'\n'}, \text{"Hello World"}] \xrightarrow{\text{getline}} \text{Result: } ""$$

#### The Invariant & The Proper Cleanse
To read line-based multi-word text following token extraction:
1. **`std::cin.ignore(numeric_limits<streamsize>::max(), '\n');`**:
   Discards all remaining characters in the input stream buffer up to and including the next newline delimiter.
2. **`std::stringstream` Tokenization**:
   Loads the extracted line into an in-memory stream buffer, allowing space-delimited or comma-delimited parsing of heterogeneous data.

#### ASCII Execution Trace
```text
Step 1: cin >> count
[ Buffer: "3\nAlice Wonderland\nBob Builder\n" ]
  --> count = 3
  --> Remaining buffer: "\nAlice Wonderland\nBob Builder\n"

Step 2: cin.ignore()
  --> Discards '\n'
  --> Buffer: "Alice Wonderland\nBob Builder\n"

Step 3: getline(cin, line)
  --> line = "Alice Wonderland"
  --> Processed via stringstream into ["Alice", "Wonderland"]
```

#### Complexity Analysis
* **Time Complexity**: $O(L)$ where $L$ is the number of characters in the line.
* **Space Complexity**: $O(L)$ memory for buffer and token vector.
description: Mastering std::getline, clearing lingering newline delimiters with cin.ignore, and tokenizing with stringstream.

title: Modern Iteration Loops & Range-Based Traversals
coreConcept: Reference-based range traversal avoiding deep copies and stride bounds
timeComplexity: O(N) single-pass linear traversal
spaceComplexity: O(1) auxiliary loop pointer state
theory:
#### Problem Definition & Motivation
Iteration is the fundamental building block of algorithmic manipulation. In older C++ paradigms, loops were written exclusively with index arithmetic:
`for (size_t i = 0; i < vec.size(); ++i)`
While useful when indices are strictly required, index loops have notable pitfalls:
* Risk of off-by-one errors and signed/unsigned comparison warnings (`int` vs `size_t`).
* Redundant index-to-address calculation: `vec[i]` computes `*(vec.data() + i)` on every access.

#### Modern C++ Range-Based Iteration
C++11 and C++20 introduced range-based `for` loops that operate directly on iterators `begin()` and `end()`:
1. **By Value (`for (auto x : vec)`)**: Copies each element. Fast for primitive types (`int`, `char`), but catastrophic $O(N \times M)$ performance penalty if elements are large strings or nested containers.
2. **By Mutable Reference (`for (auto& x : vec)`)**: Directly mutates elements in-place with zero copying.
3. **By Const Reference (`for (const auto& x : vec)`)**: The golden standard for read-only inspection. Zero copying, compiler-enforced const safety.
4. **Structured Bindings Iteration (`for (const auto& [k, v] : map)`)**: Directly destructures pairs and tuples during loop header initialization.

#### Complexity Analysis
* **Time Complexity**: $O(N)$ single linear pass through $N$ contiguous elements.
* **Space Complexity**: $O(1)$ auxiliary overhead when using reference iteration.
description: Modern C++20 iteration paradigms: index-based, reference range-for, structured bindings, and reverse iteration.

title: Function Semantics: Pass-by-Reference & Return Invariants
paradigm: Aliased In-Place Modification vs Copy Prevention
coreConcept: Preventing O(N) copy overhead with const references and in-place reference mutation
timeComplexity: O(1) parameter passing overhead
spaceComplexity: O(1) pointer-sized frame reference
theory:
#### Value Semantics vs. Reference Semantics
In C++, function arguments default to **Pass-by-Value**:
* When passing an argument `void solve(vector<int> arr)`, C++ allocates a brand-new memory buffer and copies all $N$ elements into the function frame.
* If `solve` is called inside a loop $K$ times, the time complexity balloons from $O(K)$ to $O(K \cdot N)$ purely due to hidden deep copies!

#### The Reference Paradigm
A reference (`T&`) is not a new object; it is an **alias** (direct pointer under the hood) to the existing variable in the caller's frame:
* **`T&` (Mutable Reference)**: Allows the function to mutate the caller's argument directly without pointer indirection syntax.
* **`const T&` (Const Reference)**: Prevents copying while guaranteeing that the function cannot accidentally modify the source data.
$$\text{Cost of Pass-by-Value: } O(N) \text{ allocation} \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad \text{Cost of Pass-by-Ref: } O(1) \text{ alias}$$

#### Return Value Optimization (RVO)
Modern C++ (C++17/20) mandates Return Value Optimization (Guaranteed Copy Elision). When a function constructs and returns a vector by value, the compiler constructs the object directly in the destination memory address of the caller, incurring zero copy overhead.

#### Complexity Analysis
* **Time Complexity**: $O(1)$ overhead to pass arguments by reference.
* **Space Complexity**: $O(1)$ stack allocation (8-byte address reference on 64-bit systems).
description: Mastering pass-by-value, pass-by-reference (&), const-references (const &), and multi-return tuples.

title: Object Encapsulation: Structs & Member Initializer Lists
coreConcept: Member initialization lists preventing double initialization overhead
timeComplexity: O(1) object instantiation
spaceComplexity: Contiguous member byte alignment with struct padding
theory:
#### Structs vs. Classes in C++
In C++, the difference between `struct` and `class` is strictly default visibility:
* In a `struct`, members are `public` by default.
* In a `class`, members are `private` by default.
In competitive programming and performance engineering, `struct` is widely preferred for aggregate data models, while `class` is used when maintaining complex internal state invariants.

#### Member Initializer Lists
When an object constructor executes:
* Body assignment (`this->x = x;`) first default-constructs the member, then calls the assignment operator.
* A **Member Initializer List** (`: x(x), y(y)`) initializes the member variables directly in-place during memory allocation:
$$\text{Direct Construction: } \text{Field}(val) \quad \text{vs} \quad \text{Field}() \to \text{Field} = val$$
Initializer lists are mandatory for `const` members and reference members, which cannot be default-initialized and assigned later.

#### Const Member Methods
A member method marked `const` at the end of its signature (e.g. `double norm() const`) guarantees that it will not modify any member variables of the calling instance, allowing it to be safely invoked on `const` references.

#### Complexity Analysis
* **Time Complexity**: $O(1)$ initialization and method execution.
* **Space Complexity**: Total size of members aligned to word boundaries (typically 8 bytes alignment on 64-bit platforms).
description: Designing C++ structs and classes with member initializer lists, const methods, and encapsulated invariants.

title: Operator Overloading & Custom Strict Weak Ordering
coreConcept: Implementing operator< with irreflexivity and transitivity for STL algorithms
timeComplexity: O(1) comparison operator
spaceComplexity: O(1) auxiliary
theory:
#### The Need for Custom Comparators
When storing custom objects in sorted containers like `std::set`, `std::map`, or sorting arrays via `std::sort`, C++ requires a relational operator to determine relative ordering.
By convention, the STL relies exclusively on **`operator<`** (less-than).

#### Strict Weak Ordering Axioms
To prevent undefined behavior, infinite loops, or segmentation faults inside `std::sort` (which uses introsort/quicksort), `operator<` must satisfy **Strict Weak Ordering**:
1. **Irreflexivity**: `a < a` is always `false`.
2. **Asymmetry**: If `a < b` is `true`, then `b < a` must be `false`.
3. **Transitivity**: If `a < b` and `b < c`, then `a < c`.
4. **Transitivity of Incomparability**: If `a` and `b` are incomparable, and `b` and `c` are incomparable, then `a` and `c` must be incomparable.

$$\text{CRITICAL BUG: Using } \le \text{ instead of } < \text{ violates Irreflexivity: } (a \le a = \text{true}) \implies \text{Heap Corruption!}$$

#### Tie-Breaking Patterns
When sorting records with multiple fields (e.g. interval start ascending, then interval end descending):
```cpp
if (start != other.start) return start < other.start;
return end > other.end; // Tie-breaker
```
Or via modern `std::tie`:
`return std::tie(start, other.end) < std::tie(other.start, end);`

#### Complexity Analysis
* **Time Complexity**: $O(1)$ per comparison check.
* **Space Complexity**: $O(1)$ auxiliary overhead.
description: Implementing operator< adhering to Strict Weak Ordering for automatic compatibility with std::sort and std::set.

title: Pointers, References & Dynamic Memory Architecture
coreConcept: Understanding stack vs heap allocations, pointer arithmetic, and null safety
timeComplexity: O(1) memory address resolution
spaceComplexity: 8 bytes per pointer on 64-bit systems
theory:
#### Memory Hierarchy: Stack vs. Heap
Every C++ program executes across two distinct memory regions:
* **The Stack**:
  * Ultra-fast LIFO memory managed automatically by the CPU call frames.
  * Local variables (`int x = 10;`) live on the stack and are freed automatically when the function scope exits.
* **The Heap (Free Store)**:
  * Dynamic memory requested via `new` or containers like `std::vector`.
  * Persists until explicitly deallocated via `delete` or container destruction.

#### Pointer Fundamentals
A pointer (`T*`) is an integer variable whose value is the **memory address** of another variable:
* **Address-Of Operator (`&`)**: Returns the hexadecimal memory address of a variable.
* **Dereference Operator (`*`)**: Reads or writes the value stored at the address pointed to.
* **`nullptr`**: A type-safe null pointer literal (introduced in C++11) replacing unsafe `0` or `NULL` macros.

#### Pointer Arithmetic & Array Decay
In C++, an array name decays to a pointer to its first element:
$$\text{arr}[i] \equiv *(\text{arr} + i)$$
Incrementing a pointer (`ptr++`) advances the address by `sizeof(T)` bytes, not by 1 byte.

#### Complexity Analysis
* **Time Complexity**: $O(1)$ constant time for direct dereference and address offset operations.
* **Space Complexity**: Strictly 8 bytes per pointer variable on 64-bit operating systems.
description: Navigating raw memory: address-of (&), dereferencing (*), nullptr guards, and pointer arithmetic.

title: Modern Lambda Closures & Inline Predicates
coreConcept: Capturing lexical scopes by reference or value for localized algorithm customization
timeComplexity: O(1) closure instantiation overhead
spaceComplexity: O(1) captured frame state
theory:
#### Motivation: The Power of Inline Closures
Prior to C++11, passing custom logic to algorithms like `std::sort` or `std::count_if` required writing a separate standalone function or a verbose functor `struct`.
**Lambdas** provide anonymous, localized function objects that can capture variables from their enclosing lexical scope.

#### Anatomy of a Modern C++ Lambda
```cpp
[captures] (parameters) mutable -> return_type { body }
```

1. **Capture Clauses `[...]`**:
   * `[]`: Captures nothing. Can decay to a raw C function pointer.
   * `[&]`: Captures all variables in outer scope by **reference** (zero copy, highly efficient in competitive programming).
   * `[=]`: Captures all variables by **value** (creates copies of outer variables).
   * `[x, &y]`: Explicit captures: `x` by value, `y` by reference.
2. **Parameters `(...)`**:
   * Same as standard function parameters. C++14+ allows `auto` for generic lambdas.
3. **Recursive Lambdas**:
   * To implement recursion (like DFS) inside a lambda, pass `auto&& self` or use `std::function`:
   `auto dfs = [&](auto&& self, int u) -> void { self(self, v); };`

#### Complexity Analysis
* **Time Complexity**: $O(1)$ closure creation. The compiler inlines lambdas directly at call sites, making them often faster than function pointers!
* **Space Complexity**: Memory proportional to captured variables.
description: Creating inline closures with capture lists ([&], [=]), parameter lists, and trailing return types.

title: std::array<T, N>: Fixed-Size Sequential Stack Container
coreConcept: Fixed-size contiguous sequential memory allocated directly on the stack with complete standard container interface
timeComplexity: O(1) Random Access [i] & at(), O(1) size(), O(N) fill() / swap()
spaceComplexity: O(N) on stack (0 heap allocations, sizeof(T) * N)
theory:
#### Container Specification & Header Definition (<array>)
The `std::array<T, N>` container class template represents a sequence of $N$ elements of type $T$ stored in strict contiguous memory. Unlike built-in C-style arrays (`T arr[N]`), `std::array` is a first-class sequence container:
* It does not implicitly decay to a raw pointer (`T*`) when passed to functions.
* It supports standard copy construction, copy assignment (`arr1 = arr2;` in $O(N)$), and move semantics.
* It provides random-access iterators compatible with all standard algorithms in `<algorithm>`.
* The size $N$ is fixed at compile-time and forms an integral part of the type signature (`array<int, 5>` and `array<int, 10>` are entirely distinct types).

#### Internal Memory Model & ASCII Architecture
`std::array<T, N>` is implemented as an aggregate struct containing a single member array `T _M_elements[N]`.
* **Zero Overhead**: There is no heap pointer, no stored size integer, and no virtual table.
* **Exact Size**: Total memory footprint is strictly $N \times \text{sizeof}(T)$ bytes on the execution stack frame.

```text
Stack Frame: std::array<int, 4> arr = {10, 20, 30, 40};
+---------------+---------------+---------------+---------------+
| Index 0: 10   | Index 1: 20   | Index 2: 30   | Index 3: 40   |
+---------------+---------------+---------------+---------------+
0x7ffd00        0x7ffd04        0x7ffd08        0x7ffd0C
^
arr.data() -> Direct pointer to first contiguous element (int*)
```

#### Exhaustive Member Function Reference Table
| Category | Function (Example) | Use Case (Code Snippet) | Time Complexity | Description & Behavior |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Iterators** | `arr.begin()`, `arr.end()` | `sort(arr.begin(), arr.end());` | $O(1)$ | Random-access iterator to first element / past-the-end. |
| | `arr.cbegin()`, `arr.cend()` | `for (auto it = arr.cbegin(); it != arr.cend(); ++it)` | $O(1)$ | Read-only const iterator preventing element mutation. |
| | `arr.rbegin()`, `arr.rend()` | `for (auto it = arr.rbegin(); it != arr.rend(); ++it)` | $O(1)$ | Reverse iterator traversal from terminal element. |
| **Capacity** | `arr.size()` | `for (size_t i = 0; i < arr.size(); ++i)` | $O(1)$ | Returns compile-time constant $N$. |
| | `arr.empty()` | `if (arr.empty()) return 0;` | $O(1)$ | Returns `true` if compile-time template parameter $N == 0$. |
| | `arr.max_size()` | `static_assert(arr.max_size() == 5);` | $O(1)$ | Maximum potential elements supported (always $N$). |
| **Element Access** | `arr[0]` / `arr[i]` | `sum += arr[i]; // fast unchecked inner loop` | $O(1)$ | Direct pointer offset calculation without bounds checking. |
| | `arr.at(2)` | `int val = arr.at(user_idx); // bounds safety` | $O(1)$ | Checked access; throws `std::out_of_range` if $i \ge N$. |
| | `arr.front()` | `int first = arr.front();` | $O(1)$ | Returns reference to the element at index 0. |
| | `arr.back()` | `int last = arr.back();` | $O(1)$ | Returns reference to the element at index $N - 1$. |
| | `arr.data()` | `memcpy(buf, arr.data(), arr.size() * sizeof(int));` | $O(1)$ | Returns direct pointer `T*` to contiguous stack buffer. |
| **Modifiers** | `arr.fill(0)` | `arr.fill(0); // zero-initialize entire buffer` | $O(N)$ | Assigns specified value to all elements in the array. |
| | `arr.swap(other)` | `arr.swap(backup_arr);` | $O(N)$ | Swaps elements pairwise with another array of same size $N$. |
| **Non-Member** | `std::get<0>(arr)` | `auto [x, y, z] = arr; // structured bindings` | $O(1)$ | Extracts reference to $I$-th element at compile-time. |

#### Iterator Invalidation Guarantees
* Iterators and references to elements are **never invalidated** during the entire lifetime of the array object.
* The buffer is destroyed strictly when the containing stack frame unwinds.

#### Common Pitfalls & Best Practices
1. **Large Stack Arrays**: Declaring a large array (e.g. `array<int, 1000000>`) inside a local function scope will cause an immediate **stack overflow** (Linux stack limits are typically 8MB). Use `std::vector` or declare the array globally/static for large buffers.
2. **Bounds Safety**: Use `.at(i)` when indexing is driven by untrusted external inputs or during debugging, and `[i]` inside hot computational loops after bounds are verified.
description: Standard C++ fixed-size contiguous sequence container encapsulating static stack arrays without pointer decay or heap allocation overhead.

title: std::vector<T>: Dynamic Contiguous Array & Capacity Growth
coreConcept: Contiguous heap buffer with geometric capacity doubling, reserve vs resize semantics, and in-place emplace_back
timeComplexity: O(1) amortized push_back / emplace_back, O(1) random access [i], O(N) insert / erase
spaceComplexity: Contiguous heap buffer with geometric doubling factor (2x / 1.5x)
theory:
#### Container Specification & Header Definition (<vector>)
`std::vector<T>` is a sequential container representing a dynamically sized contiguous array. It is the default sequence container recommended by the C++ Core Guidelines due to its unmatched cache locality, zero pointer indirection per element, and amortized constant-time append operations.

#### Internal 3-Pointer Memory Model & Reallocation Mechanics
Standard implementations of `std::vector` hold exactly three 64-bit pointers on the stack frame (occupying 24 bytes total):
* `_M_start`: Pointer to the first element of the allocated heap block.
* `_M_finish`: Pointer to one past the last initialized element (`size() = _M_finish - _M_start`).
* `_M_end_of_storage`: Pointer to the end of the reserved memory buffer (`capacity() = _M_end_of_storage - _M_start`).

```text
Stack Object (24 Bytes):
+--------------------+--------------------+--------------------+
| _M_start           | _M_finish          | _M_end_of_storage  |
+---------+----------+---------+----------+---------+----------+
          |                    |                    |
          v                    v                    v
Heap:   [ 10 | 20 | 30 | 40 ] [ uninitialized slots ]
        |<--- size() = 4 --->|
        |<--------------- capacity() = 8 --------------------->|
```

#### Exhaustive Member Function Reference Table
| Category | Function (Example) | Use Case (Code Snippet) | Time Complexity | Description & Behavior |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Iterators** | `vec.begin()`, `vec.end()` | `sort(vec.begin(), vec.end());` | $O(1)$ | Random-access iterators to contiguous buffer. |
| | `vec.rbegin()`, `vec.rend()` | `int last = *vec.rbegin();` | $O(1)$ | Scanning backwards from most recently pushed element. |
| **Capacity** | `vec.size()` | `for (int i = 0; i < (int)vec.size(); ++i)` | $O(1)$ | Checking current number of active initialized elements. |
| | `vec.capacity()` | `if (vec.size() == vec.capacity()) ...` | $O(1)$ | Monitoring allocated headroom before the next geometric reallocation. |
| | `vec.empty()` | `if (vec.empty()) return;` | $O(1)$ | Safety guard checking whether vector contains zero elements. |
| | `vec.reserve(100000)` | `vec.reserve(n); // avoids repeated reallocations` | $O(N)$ (if $n > C$) | Pre-allocates heap memory without changing `size()`. |
| | `vec.resize(50, 0)` | `vec.resize(n, 0); // resets size and default values` | $O(\Delta N)$ | Changes `size()` to $n$, default-constructing or trimming elements. |
| | `vec.shrink_to_fit()`| `vec.shrink_to_fit(); // frees unused headroom` | $O(N)$ | Requests deallocation of excess capacity (`capacity() -> size()`). |
| **Element Access** | `vec[0]` / `vec[i]` | `sum += vec[i];` | $O(1)$ | Unchecked fast array indexing in performance-critical code. |
| | `vec.at(3)` | `int x = vec.at(query_idx); // bounds-checked` | $O(1)$ | Defensive indexing throwing `std::out_of_range` on breach. |
| | `vec.front()`, `vec.back()` | `int head = vec.front(), tail = vec.back();` | $O(1)$ | References to first and last elements. |
| | `vec.data()` | `memcpy(dest, vec.data(), vec.size() * sizeof(int));` | $O(1)$ | Direct pointer to contiguous heap array for C APIs. |
| **Modifiers** | `vec.push_back(10)` | `vec.push_back(val);` | $O(1)$ amortized | Appends element to end; copies or moves. |
| | `vec.emplace_back(x, y)` | `vec.emplace_back(row, col); // in-place construction` | $O(1)$ amortized | Constructs element in-place via placement new. |
| | `vec.pop_back()` | `vec.pop_back(); // drop last element` | $O(1)$ | Destroys last element and decrements `_M_finish`. |
| | `vec.insert(pos, val)` | `vec.insert(vec.begin() + i, 42);` | $O(N)$ | Inserts element at position, shifting rightward elements. |
| | `vec.erase(pos)` | `vec.erase(vec.begin() + idx);` | $O(N)$ | Erases element at position, shifting following elements left. |
| | `vec.clear()` | `vec.clear(); // resets size to 0` | $O(N)$ | Destroys all elements; `size()` becomes 0, capacity unchanged. |
| | `vec.swap(other)` | `vec.swap(temp); // O(1) buffer swap` | $O(1)$ | Swaps 3 internal pointers in constant time. |

#### Iterator Invalidation Rules
1. **Reallocation**: If insertion causes `size() > capacity()`, **every iterator, pointer, and reference** to vector elements is invalidated!
2. **No Reallocation**: If no reallocation occurs:
   * Insertions invalidate iterators and references at and after the insertion position.
   * Deletions invalidate iterators and references at and after the erasure position.
   * `pop_back()` invalidates only `end()` and the erased element.
description: The primary C++ dynamic contiguous sequence container with amortized O(1) growth, memory reserve controls, and iterator invalidation safety.

title: std::deque<T>: Double-Ended Queue with Chunked Paged Buffers
coreConcept: Non-contiguous paged array buffers providing O(1) insertion and removal at both front and back without full reallocation
timeComplexity: O(1) push_front / push_back, O(1) pop_front / pop_back, O(1) random access [i]
spaceComplexity: O(N) across multiple fixed-size pages + map pointer directory
theory:
#### Container Specification & Header Definition (<deque>)
`std::deque<T>` (double-ended queue) is an indexed sequence container that allows fast $O(1)$ insertions and deletions at **both its beginning and its end**. Unlike `std::vector`, elements of a deque are **not** stored in a single contiguous memory block.

#### Internal Architecture: The Central Map & Paged Buffers
`std::deque` is structured around a two-level indexing hierarchy:
1. **Central Map Table**: A dynamically sized array of pointers to fixed-size memory chunks (pages, typically 512 bytes each).
2. **Fixed-Size Data Pages**: Contiguous blocks of memory that hold the actual elements.

```text
Central Map Directory (Array of Pointers):
+---------+---------+---------+---------+
| Chunk 0 | Chunk 1 | Chunk 2 | Chunk 3 |
+----+----+----+----+----+----+----+----+
     |         |         |         |
     v         v         v         v
   [Page]    [Page]    [Page]    [Page]
   [a | b]   [c | d]   [e | f]   [g | h]
    ^                             ^
    Front Element                 Back Element
```

#### Exhaustive Member Function Reference Table
| Category | Function (Example) | Use Case (Code Snippet) | Time Complexity | Description & Behavior |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Iterators** | `dq.begin()`, `dq.end()` | `for (int x : dq) sum += x;` | $O(1)$ | Random-access iterators across paged chunks. |
| **Capacity** | `dq.size()` | `int count = dq.size();` | $O(1)$ | Total number of elements across all pages. |
| | `dq.empty()` | `if (dq.empty()) return -1;` | $O(1)$ | Checks if deque contains 0 elements. |
| | `dq.resize(20, 0)` | `dq.resize(k, 0);` | $O(\Delta N)$ | Truncates or extends deque with default value. |
| | `dq.shrink_to_fit()`| `dq.shrink_to_fit(); // drops unused boundary chunks` | $O(N)$ | Requests deallocation of unused boundary chunks. |
| **Element Access** | `dq[2]` | `int mid = dq[dq.size() / 2];` | $O(1)$ | Random indexing via 2-level pointer arithmetic. |

title: std::forward_list<T>: Minimalist Singly-Linked List
coreConcept: Singly-linked nodes maintaining only a forward next-pointer with zero size tracking overhead and after-node insertion semantics
timeComplexity: O(1) push_front, O(1) insert_after, O(1) erase_after, O(N) search / linear traversal

theory:
#### Container Specification & Header Definition (<forward_list>)
`std::forward_list<T>` is a sequential container implemented as a **singly-linked list**. It is designed with the C++ zero-overhead principle in mind: when compared to a raw hand-written C singly-linked list, `std::forward_list` has **zero space or time penalty**.

#### The Zero-Overhead Design & Omission of `size()`
Unlike all other standard containers, `std::forward_list` deliberately provides **no `.size()` member function**:
* Maintaining a size counter would add 8 bytes of storage per list instance and would require $O(N)$ updates during operations like `splice_after`.
* Each node stores exclusively the element value and one pointer:
$$\text{Node Size} = \text{sizeof}(T) + \text{sizeof}(\text{pointer})$$

```text
before_begin()      head
      [ * ] ------> [ 10 | * ] ------> [ 20 | * ] ------> [ 30 | nullptr ]
                        ^
                        insert_after(it, 15) splices node right here!
```

title: std::list<T>: Doubly-Linked List & Constant-Time Splicing

theory:
#### Container Specification & Header Definition (<list>)
`std::list<T>` is a sequential container implemented as a **circular doubly-linked list** with a dummy sentinel node. It provides bidirectional iterators (`it++`, `it--`) and constant-time insertion and erasure at any point in the container once an iterator is known.

#### Complete Iterator Invariance: The Ultimate Guarantee
`std::list` offers the most robust iterator stability guarantees in the C++ Standard Library:
* **Insertion**: Inserting elements anywhere in the list **never invalidates any iterators, pointers, or references** to other elements.
* **Deletion**: Erasing an element invalidates **only** iterators pointing to the specific deleted element; all other iterators remain perfectly valid.

```text
Sentinel Dummy Node <-----------------+
   | (prev)             (next)        |
   v                      v           |
[ Node: 10 ] <=======> [ Node: 20 ] <=+
  prev | next            prev | next
```

title: std::stack<T>: LIFO Container Adaptor Architecture
coreConcept: Wrapping underlying sequential containers into a strict LIFO interface with exception-safe push, pop, and top operations
timeComplexity: O(1) push / emplace, O(1) pop, O(1) top, O(1) empty, O(1) size
spaceComplexity: O(N) determined by the underlying sequential container
theory:
#### Container Specification & Header Definition (<stack>)
`std::stack<T, Container>` is not a first-class memory container; it is a **container adaptor**. It encapsulates an underlying sequential container and exposes exclusively a strict Last-In, First-Out (LIFO) interface:
```cpp
template <class T, class Container = std::deque<T>>
class stack;
```

#### Why `std::deque` is the Default Container
* `std::vector` must reallocate memory when full, causing latency spikes and copying elements.
* `std::list` allocates individual nodes on the heap, incurring 16 bytes of pointer overhead per element.
* `std::deque` allocates memory in chunks without relocating existing elements, balancing $O(1)$ push/pop performance with superior cache locality.

```text
push(10) -> push(20) -> push(30)
+-----------------------+
| Top Element: 30       |  <--- stk.top()
+-----------------------+
| Element: 20           |
+-----------------------+
| Bottom Element: 10    |
+-----------------------+
stk.pop() discards 30 in O(1) -> 20 becomes the new top!
```

#### Exhaustive Member Function Reference Table
| Category | Function (Example) | Use Case (Code Snippet) | Time Complexity | Description & Behavior |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Capacity** | `stk.empty()` | `while (!stk.empty()) { ... }` | $O(1)$ | Returns `c.empty()`; true if stack has 0 elements. |
| | `stk.size()` | `int depth = stk.size();` | $O(1)$ | Returns `c.size()`; total elements on stack. |
| **Element Access** | `stk.top()` | `int curr = stk.top();` | $O(1)$ | Returns `c.back()`; reference to topmost element. |
| **Modifiers** | `stk.push(0)` | `stk.push(node_id); // push state onto LIFO frame` | $O(1)$ | Calls `c.push_back(val)`; appends element onto stack. |
| | `stk.emplace(x, y)` | `stk.emplace(row, col); // in-place construction` | $O(1)$ | Calls `c.emplace_back(args...)`. |
| | `stk.pop()` | `if (!stk.empty()) stk.pop();` | $O(1)$ | Calls `c.pop_back()`; removes top element. Returns `void`! |
| | `stk.swap(other)` | `stk.swap(backup_stk);` | $O(1)$ | Exchanges underlying container contents. |

#### Exception Safety: Why `pop()` Returns `void`
If `pop()` returned the element by value, it would invoke a copy/move constructor while returning. If that constructor threw an exception, the element would already have been removed from the stack and permanently lost! By separating `top()` (inspection) from `pop()` (removal), the strong exception guarantee is preserved.
description: Standard LIFO container adaptor restricting access to the top element, templated over sequential backings with deque as default.

title: std::queue<T> & std::priority_queue<T>: FIFO & Binary Heap Adaptors

title: std::set<T> & std::multiset<T>: Ordered Red-Black Trees
coreConcept: Strict weak ordering with logarithmic search, insertion, and deletion, range queries via lower_bound and upper_bound, and multiset single-element erasure
timeComplexity: O(log N) insert, O(log N) erase, O(log N) find, O(log N) lower_bound / upper_bound
spaceComplexity: O(N) node allocations (each node has parent, left, right pointers + color bit: ~32-40 bytes per node)
theory:
#### Container Specification & Header Definition (<set>)
The `<set>` header provides ordered associative containers:
1. **`std::set<Key, Compare = std::less<Key>>`**: Unique keys sorted by strict weak ordering.
2. **`std::multiset<Key, Compare = std::less<Key>>`**: Allows duplicate keys.

#### Red-Black Tree Invariant & Memory Structure
Elements are stored inside a self-balancing Red-Black binary search tree:
* Every node stores the element $T$, pointers to `parent`, `left`, and `right`, and a color flag (Red or Black).
* The tree height is strictly bounded by $h \le 2 \log_2(N + 1)$, guaranteeing **$O(\log N)$ worst-case** lookups, insertions, and deletions.

```text
                 [ 20 (Black) ]
                /              \
         [ 10 (Red) ]       [ 30 (Red) ]
         /          \
    [ 5 (Black) ] [ 15 (Black) ]
```

#### Exhaustive Member Function Reference Table
| Category | Function (Example) | Use Case (Code Snippet) | Time Complexity | Description & Behavior |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Iterators** | `s.begin()`, `s.end()` | `for (int x : s) cout << x << " ";` | $O(1)$ | In-order traversal yielding keys in sorted order. |
| **Capacity** | `s.size()` | `int unique_count = s.size();` | $O(1)$ | Number of active elements. |
| | `s.empty()` | `if (s.empty()) return 0;` | $O(1)$ | Checks if set contains 0 elements. |
| **Modifiers** | `s.insert(42)` | `auto [it, inserted] = s.insert(val);` | $O(\log N)$ | Inserts element; in `set`, returns false if duplicate. |
| | `s.emplace(42)` | `s.emplace(coord);` | $O(\log N)$ | Constructs element directly in tree node. |
| | `s.erase(it)` | `auto it = s.find(val); if (it != s.end()) s.erase(it);` | Amortized $O(1)$ | Erases node at `pos`; returns following iterator. |
| | `s.erase(42)` | `s.erase(val); // deletes ALL copies in multiset` | $O(\log N + K)$ | Erases matching keys. In `multiset`, wipes ALL copies! |
| | `s.extract(42)` | `auto node = s.extract(val); node.value() = 99; s.insert(move(node));` | $O(1)$ amortized | Extracts node handle without destroying memory! |
| | `s.clear()` | `s.clear(); // destroys all tree nodes` | $O(N)$ | Destroys all nodes. |
| **Lookup** | `s.find(42)` | `if (s.find(val) != s.end()) { ... }` | $O(\log N)$ | Returns iterator to key, or `end()` if absent. |
| | `s.count(42)` | `int copies = ms.count(val);` | $O(\log N + K)$ | In `set`: returns 0 or 1. In `multiset`: returns frequency. |
| | `s.contains(42)` | `if (s.contains(val)) { ... } // C++20` | $O(\log N)$ | Returns `true` if key exists. |
| | `s.lower_bound(10)` | `auto it = s.lower_bound(k); // first element >= k` | $O(\log N)$ | First element that is **greater than or equal to** $k$. |
| | `s.upper_bound(10)` | `auto it = s.upper_bound(k); // first element > k` | $O(\log N)$ | First element that is **strictly greater than** $k$. |
| | `s.equal_range(10)` | `auto [low, high] = ms.equal_range(k);` | $O(\log N)$ | Returns `{lower_bound(k), upper_bound(k)}`. |

#### Multiset Erase Pitfall & Safe Idiom
* Calling `ms.erase(val)` erases **ALL** occurrences of `val` in $O(\log N + K)$.
* To erase only **one single instance**, pass the iterator:
```cpp
auto it = ms.find(val);
if (it != ms.end()) ms.erase(it); // Erases strictly ONE instance!
```

title: std::unordered_set<T>: Chained Hash Table with Custom Hasher

theory:
#### Container Specification & Header Definition (<unordered_set>)
`std::unordered_set<Key, Hash, KeyEqual>` is an unordered associative container implemented as a **chained hash table**:
* Elements are organized into buckets according to their hash codes: `bucket_index = hash(key) % bucket_count`.
* Collisions are handled via separate chaining (a singly-linked list of nodes per bucket).
* Average time complexity for search, insert, and erase is strictly **$O(1)$**.

```text
Buckets Array (Pointers):
[ 0 ] ----> [ Node: 16 | * ] ----> [ Node: 32 | nullptr ]  (Collision Chain)
[ 1 ] ----> nullptr
[ 2 ] ----> [ Node: 42 | nullptr ]
[ 3 ] ----> nullptr
```

title: std::bitset<N>: Fixed-Size Bit Array & Bit-Parallelism
coreConcept: Packing 64 boolean flags into each 64-bit machine word, enabling 64x bit-parallel logical operations and O(N/64) subset sum transitions

theory:
#### Container Specification & Header Definition (<bitset>)
`std::bitset<N>` is a specialized sequence container holding a fixed sequence of $N$ bits:
* In standard C++, a `bool` occupies 1 full byte (8 bits) because memory is byte-addressable.
* `std::bitset<N>` packs bits into native 64-bit machine words (`uint64_t`), consuming strictly:
$$\text{Total Memory} = \left\lceil \frac{N}{64} \right\rceil \times 8 \text{ bytes}$$

#### The 64x Bit-Parallel Speedup
Modern 64-bit CPUs execute bitwise instructions (`&`, `|`, `^`, `~`, `<<`, `>>`) across an entire 64-bit register in a **single clock cycle**.
* By packing booleans into bits, algorithms operating on bitsets process 64 states simultaneously per instruction, reducing time complexity by an enormous factor of 64:
$$\text{Complexity} = O\left(\frac{N}{64}\right)$$

```text
64-Bit CPU Word:
Bit:   63 62 61 60 ... ... ... 4  3  2  1  0
Val: [ 0  0  1  0  ... ... ... 1  1  0  1  0 ]
       ^                                    ^
       bitset[63]                           bitset[0]
A single CPU instruction computes AND/OR across all 64 bits simultaneously!
```

# Module 02: Language Basics — Data Types, Arrays & Operators > **Source Track:** Oracle Java Tutorials — *Learning the Java Language* > **Source Lessons:** `nutsandbolts/variables.html`, `datatypes.html`, `arrays.html`, `variablesummary.html`, `operators.html`, `op1.html`, `op2.html`, `op3.html`, `opsummary.html`, `expressions.html` > **Scope:** The 8 Primitive Types, Two's Complement Encoding, IEEE 754 Floating-Point, JVM Stack Frame Slots, Literal Bases, 1D & Multi-Dimensional Jagged Arrays, Operator Precedence, Signed (`>>`) and Unsigned (`>>>`) Bit Shifts. --- ## 1. Architectural Overview & Memory Representation Java is a statically-typed, strongly-typed programming language. Every variable must have a declared type before compilation. In the JVM architecture, data is categorized into two distinct memory topologies: 1. **Primitive Types:** Store raw binary values directly within the thread's local execution stack frame (in 32-bit stack operand slots) or packed inline within an object's heap layout. 2. **Reference Types:** Store 32-bit or 64-bit addresses (Compressed OOPs) pointing to dynamically allocated Heap objects. ```mermaid flowchart TD subgraph StackFrame ["JVM Thread Call Stack Frame (Local Variable Array)"] Slot0["Slot 0: this pointer (Reference: 4B)"] Slot1["Slot 1: int count = 42 (Raw 32-bit Two's Complement: 4B)"] Slot2["Slot 2 & 3: long timestamp (64-bit signed: 8B / 2 slots)"] Slot4["Slot 4: boolean flag = true (Stored as 1 in int slot)"] Slot5["Slot 5: int[] arrayRef = 0x10A0 (Compressed Reference: 4B)"] end subgraph HeapLayout ["JVM Heap Allocation (Contiguous Array)"] ArrObj["int[] Object at 0x10A0
- Mark Word: 64 bits (8 bytes)
- Klass Pointer: 32 bits (4 bytes)
- Array Length: 4 bytes (value = 4)
- arr[0]: 10 (4B)
- arr[1]: 20 (4B)
- arr[2]: 30 (4B)
- arr[3]: 40 (4B)
- Padding: 0 bytes (Aligned to 8B boundary)"] end Slot5 --> ArrObj ``` --- ## 2. The Eight Primitive Data Types: Binary Layout & Specifications All numeric primitives in Java are **signed two's complement** numbers (with the single exception of `char`, which is an unsigned 16-bit integer). There are no `unsigned int` or `unsigned long` primitive types in Java. | Primitive Type | Size (Bits / Bytes) | Stack Slots | Binary Representation & Formula | Value Range (Inclusive) | Default Value (Fields) | Wrapper Class | | :--- | :--- | :---: | :--- | :--- | :---: | :--- | | **`byte`** | 8 bits (1 B) | 1 slot | 8-bit Two's Complement: $-2^7 \text{ to } 2^7 - 1$ | `-128` to `127` | `0` | `Byte` | | **`short`** | 16 bits (2 B) | 1 slot | 16-bit Two's Complement: $-2^{15} \text{ to } 2^{15} - 1$ | `-32,768` to `32,767` | `0` | `Short` | | **`int`** | 32 bits (4 B) | 1 slot | 32-bit Two's Complement: $-2^{31} \text{ to } 2^{31} - 1$ | `-2,147,483,648` to `2,147,483,647` | `0` | `Integer` | | **`long`** | 64 bits (8 B) | 2 slots | 64-bit Two's Complement: $-2^{63} \text{ to } 2^{63} - 1$ | `$-9.22 \times 10^{18}$` to `$9.22 \times 10^{18}$` | `0L` | `Long` | | **`float`** | 32 bits (4 B) | 1 slot | IEEE 754: 1 sign bit + 8 exponent + 23 mantissa | $\approx \pm 1.4 \times 10^{-45}$ to $\pm 3.4 \times 10^{38}$ | `0.0f` | `Float` | | **`double`** | 64 bits (8 B) | 2 slots | IEEE 754: 1 sign bit + 11 exponent + 52 mantissa | $\approx \pm 4.9 \times 10^{-324}$ to $\pm 1.8 \times 10^{308}$ | `0.0d` | `Double` | | **`boolean`** | 1 bit (abstract) | 1 slot | Stored as 1 byte in memory; 4-byte int in stack bytecode | `true` or `false` | `false` | `Boolean` | | **`char`** | 16 bits (2 B) | 1 slot | Unsigned 16-bit Unicode (UTF-16 BMP) | `'\u0000'` (`0`) to `'\uffff'` (`65,535`) | `'\u0000'` | `Character` | > [!NOTE] > **Definite Assignment Invariant:** Local variables residing in method stack frames are **never assigned default values**. The compiler enforces compile-time definite assignment analysis, failing with *"variable might not have been initialized"* upon any read prior to assignment. ### Literal Notations & Underscore Formatting - **Integral Literals:** Decimal (`100`), Hexadecimal (`0x64`), Binary (`0b01100100`), Octal (`0144`). Suffix `L` denotes 64-bit `long` (e.g. `5_000_000_000L`). - **Floating Literals:** Suffix `F` or `f` specifies single-precision `float` (`3.14159F`); default without suffix is double-precision `double` (`3.14159`). Scientific notation: `6.022e23`. - **Underscores in Literals:** Permitted anywhere between digits to improve visual legibility (e.g., `long creditCard = 4000_1234_5678_9010L; double fine = 0.000_001;`). Cannot appear adjacent to decimal points, prefixes (`0x`, `0b`), or suffixes (`L`, `F`). --- ## 3. Arrays: 1D, Multi-Dimensional & Jagged Heap Topologies In Java, **arrays are full first-class Heap objects**. - An array declaration (`int[] arr`) allocates a reference pointer on the stack. - The instantiation (`new int[10]`) allocates a single contiguous block of memory on the Heap with a specialized 16-byte object header containing the array length. - Array length is immutable and stored in a public final field: `arr.length`. - Accessing an invalid index throws `java.lang.ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException` at runtime. ### Jagged Multi-Dimensional Arrays Multi-dimensional arrays in Java are **arrays of arrays**. Rows do not share a single rectangular memory block; instead, the root array stores references to independent row arrays allocated at arbitrary locations on the Heap: ```mermaid flowchart TD subgraph JaggedMatrix ["Jagged Array: int[][] jagged = new int[3][]"] Root["jagged ref -> Array of 3 Reference Pointers"] R0["Row 0: new int[2] -> [10, 20]"] R1["Row 1: new int[4] -> [30, 40, 50, 60]"] R2["Row 2: new int[1] -> [70]"] end Root -->|index 0| R0 Root -->|index 1| R1 Root -->|index 2| R2 ``` --- ## 4. Operator Precedence, Short-Circuiting & Bit-Shift Mechanics ### Operator Precedence Hierarchy (Highest to Lowest) 1. **Postfix:** `expr++`, `expr--` 2. **Unary:** `++expr`, `--expr`, `+expr`, `-expr`, `~` (bitwise complement), `!` (logical NOT) 3. **Multiplicative:** `*`, `/` (truncating integer vs float), `%` (modulus sign follows dividend: `(-7) % 3 == -1`) 4. **Additive:** `+`, `-`, string concatenation `+` 5. **Shift:** `<<` (signed left), `>>` (signed right), `>>>` (unsigned right) 6. **Relational:** `<`, `>`, `<=`, `>=`, `instanceof` 7. **Equality:** `==`, `!=` 8. **Bitwise AND:** `&` 9. **Bitwise Exclusive OR:** `^` 10. **Bitwise Inclusive OR:** `|` 11. **Logical AND (Short-Circuit):** `&&` 12. **Logical OR (Short-Circuit):** `||` 13. **Ternary Operator:** `booleanExpr ? trueVal : falseVal` 14. **Assignment:** `=`, `+=`, `-=`, `*=`, `/=`, `%=`, `&=`, `^=`, `|=`, `<<=`, `>>=`, `>>>=` ### Bitwise vs. Bit-Shift Operations - **Signed Right Shift (`>>`):** Performs arithmetic shift. High-order bits are filled with copies of the **Sign Bit (MSB)**, preserving the algebraic sign: ```text -8 in binary (32-bit): 11111111 11111111 11111111 11111000 -8 >> 1: 11111111 11111111 11111111 11111100 (-4) ``` - **Unsigned Right Shift (`>>>`):** Performs logical shift. High-order bits are **always filled with zeros**, regardless of the sign bit: ```text -8 in binary (32-bit): 11111111 11111111 11111111 11111000 -8 >>> 1: 01111111 11111111 11111111 11111100 (2,147,483,644) ``` - *Key Application:* In binary search algorithms, `(low + high) >>> 1` prevents positive 32-bit integer overflow when `low + high > Integer.MAX_VALUE`. --- ## 5. Exhaustive Member Function & Operator Reference | Category | Operator / Syntax (Example) | Use Case (Code Snippet) | Specification | Description & Behavioral Invariant | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | **Array Allocation** | `new int[N]` | `int[] buffer = new int[1024];` | $O(N)$ zeroed heap | Allocates contiguous heap block initialized to zero values. | | **Array Length Read** | `arr.length` | `for (int i = 0; i < arr.length; i++)`| $O(1)$ header read | Constant-time read of the immutable 32-bit length field in the array header. | | **Native Array Copy** | `System.arraycopy(s, sp, d, dp, l)` | `System.arraycopy(src, 0, dest, 0, 10);`| $O(N)$ native C++ | Hardware-accelerated memory block copy; handles overlapping regions. | | **Array Clone** | `arr.clone()` | `int[] copy = original.clone();` | $O(N)$ shallow copy | Instantiates a fresh Heap array with duplicated scalar values or reference addresses. | | **Short-Circuit AND** | `a && b` | `if (user != null && user.isActive())`| $O(1)$ short-circuit | Evaluates second operand only if first is true. Critical for null-safety. | | **Bitwise AND** | `a & b` | `boolean isEven = (num & 1) == 0;` | $O(1)$ ALU bitwise | Computes bitwise conjunction; also acts as non-short-circuit logical AND. | | **Signed Right Shift**| `val >> n` | `int divByTwo = val >> 1;` | $O(1)$ arithmetic shift | Shifts right while filling high bits with the sign bit; preserves negative signs. | | **Unsigned Shift** | `val >>> n` | `int mid = (low + high) >>> 1;` | $O(1)$ logical shift | Shifts right while filling high bits with zero; prevents binary search overflow. | | **Signed Left Shift** | `val << n` | `int mulByFour = val << 2;` | $O(1)$ logical shift | Shifts left while filling low bits with zero; equivalent to multiplying by $2^n$. | | **Ternary Operator** | `c ? t : f` | `int abs = (val < 0) ? -val : val;` | $O(1)$ conditional | In-line conditional evaluation returning either true-expression or false-expression. | --- ## 6. Modern Idiomatic Java Code Implementation ```java // Comprehensive demonstration of primitives, jagged arrays, and bit-shift arithmetic in Java 21 package devtype.engine.basics; import java.util.Arrays; public final class DataBasicsLab { // Binary search demonstrating unsigned bit-shift overflow protection public static int binarySearch(int[] arr, int target) { int low = 0; int high = arr.length - 1; while (low <= high) { // Unsigned shift >>> prevents positive overflow bug when (low + high) > Integer.MAX_VALUE int mid = (low + high) >>> 1; int midVal = arr[mid]; if (midVal < target) { low = mid + 1; } else if (midVal > target) { high = mid - 1; } else { return mid; // Target found } } return -(low + 1); // Target absent } // Multi-dimensional jagged array allocation and dynamic computation public static int[][] createPascalsTriangle(int numRows) { if (numRows <= 0) return new int[0][]; int[][] triangle = new int[numRows][]; for (int i = 0; i < numRows; i++) { triangle[i] = new int[i + 1]; // Variable row width triangle[i][0] = 1; triangle[i][i] = 1; for (int j = 1; j < i; j++) { triangle[i][j] = triangle[i - 1][j - 1] + triangle[i - 1][j]; } } return triangle; } } ``` --- ## 7. Common Traps, Anti-Patterns & Best Practices 1. **Integer Overflow in Midpoint Computations:** - *Trap:* `(low + high) / 2` silently overflows to a negative integer if `low + high > 2,147,483,647`, triggering an `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException`. - *Remedy:* Always use unsigned shift: `(low + high) >>> 1` or `low + ((high - low) / 2)`. 2. **Floating-Point Equality Checks (`==`):** - *Trap:* `(0.1 + 0.2) == 0.3` evaluates to `false` because binary floating-point fractions cannot represent decimals like `0.1` precisely in IEEE 754. - *Remedy:* Use `Math.abs(a - b) < EPSILON` or `java.math.BigDecimal` for financial calculations. 3. **Bitwise Shift Narrowing Promotion Trap:** - *Trap:* Applying a shift to `byte` or `short` (e.g. `b = b << 1`) causes automatic **numeric promotion to `int`**, causing a compilation failure without an explicit narrowing cast. - *Remedy:* Use compound shift operators (`b <<= 1`), which automatically inject the narrowing cast.

# Module 03: Control Flow Mechanics & Branching Invariants > **Source Track:** Oracle Java Tutorials — *Learning the Java Language* > **Source Lessons:** `nutsandbolts/flow.html`, `if.html`, `switch.html`, `while.html`, `for.html`, `branch.html`, `flowsummary.html`, `QandE/questions_flow.html` > **Scope:** Conditional Branching, Modern Switch Expressions (Java 14+), Bytecode Jump Tables (`tableswitch` vs `lookupswitch`), Iteration Loops, Loop Desugaring, Labeled `break` and `continue`, Definite Assignment. --- ## 1. Architectural Overview & Bytecode Execution Java executes instructions sequentially within a thread's frame unless diverted by a control flow statement. These instructions compile down to conditional jump bytecodes (`ifeq`, `ifne`, `if_icmpgt`, `goto`). Control structures are divided into three broad categories: 1. **Decision-Making:** `if-then`, `if-then-else`, and `switch`. 2. **Looping / Repetition:** `for`, enhanced `for`, `while`, and `do-while`. 3. **Branching / Jump:** `break`, `continue`, and `return`. ```mermaid flowchart TD Start([Input Value]) --> Decision{Branching Invariant} Decision -->|Dense Integers| TableSwitch["tableswitch
(O(1) Direct Offset Jump)"] Decision -->|Sparse Integers / Strings| LookupSwitch["lookupswitch
(O(log N) Binary Search)"] TableSwitch --> Action1[Execute Branch Body] LookupSwitch --> Action2[Execute Branch Body] Action1 --> Exit([Break / Return]) Action2 --> Exit ``` --- ## 2. Decision Statements: If-Else & Modern Switch Expressions ### Dangling-Else Ambiguity When nested `if` statements are used without braces, Java resolves the "dangling else" ambiguity by **always binding the `else` to the innermost preceding `if` statement**: ```java if (a > 0) if (b > 0) doSomething(); else doOther(); // Binds to (b > 0), NOT (a > 0)! ``` *Best Practice:* Always enclose conditional blocks in explicit `{}` braces to prevent semantic drift. ### The Evolution of the `switch` Statement 1. **Java 1.0 to 6:** Integral primitives (`byte`, `short`, `char`, `int`) and `enum`. 2. **Java 7+:** Added `String` support. The compiler generates a `lookupswitch` on `String.hashCode()`, followed by an `equals()` check inside each branch to handle hash collisions. 3. **Java 14+:** Introduced **Switch Expressions**: - Arrow labels (`case VAL -> expr;`) completely eliminate accidental fall-through. - Multiple comma-delimited labels per case: `case 1, 2, 3 -> doAction();`. - Returns a value directly, acting as an expression. Multi-statement code blocks return a value using the **`yield`** keyword. - **Exhaustiveness Invariant:** A switch expression must cover all possible input values (or include a `default` branch), verified at compile time. ### Bytecode Jump Tables: `tableswitch` vs. `lookupswitch` The JVM compiles switch constructs into one of two specialized bytecode instructions based on the density of the case constants: - **`tableswitch`:** Used when case constants are dense and contiguous (e.g. `case 1, case 2, case 3`). It builds a direct jump table in bytecode. Target instructions are fetched in **$O(1)$ constant time** by calculating `offset = index - low_bound`. - **`lookupswitch`:** Used when case constants are sparse (e.g. `case 10, case 5000, case 999999`) or based on `String` hash codes. It stores a sorted table of keys and target offsets, resolving branches via a **$O(\log N)$ binary search**. --- ## 3. Looping Statements & Iterator Desugaring ```mermaid flowchart LR subgraph EnhancedForDesugaring ["Enhanced For-Each Desugaring at Compile Time"] SourceCode["for (User u : userList) {
u.notifyUser();
}"] DesugaredBytecode["Iterator<User> it = userList.iterator();
while (it.hasNext()) {
User u = it.next();
u.notifyUser();
}"] end SourceCode -->|Compiler Transformation| DesugaredBytecode ``` 1. **`while` Statement:** Evaluates condition before entering the body. Executes zero or more times. 2. **`do-while` Statement:** Evaluates condition after the body executes. **Guaranteed to execute at least once**. 3. **Classical `for` Statement:** Compiles to standard loop header: `for (init; termination_condition; step_update)`. 4. **Enhanced `for-each` Statement:** For arrays, compiles to standard index traversal (`for (int i = 0; i < len; i++)`); for `Iterable`, compiles to iterator traversal. --- ## 4. Branching Statements: Unlabeled vs. Labeled Jumps Java does not provide a raw `goto` statement. Instead, it provides **Labeled `break` and `continue`** statements to escape or advance nested loop hierarchies safely: - **Unlabeled `break`:** Immediately terminates the innermost `switch`, `for`, `while`, or `do-while`. - **Labeled `break`:** Terminates the outer labeled statement block immediately, transferring execution to the statement directly following the labeled block. - **Unlabeled `continue`:** Skips the remainder of the current iteration of the innermost loop and advances to the next step expression / condition. - **Labeled `continue`:** Skips the current iteration of the specified outer labeled loop. ```mermaid flowchart TD subgraph OuterLoop ["searchMatrix: for (int r = 0; r < rows; r++)"] subgraph InnerLoop ["for (int c = 0; c < cols; c++)"] Check{"matrix[r][c] == target?"} Check -->|Yes| LBreak["break searchMatrix;"] Check -->|No| NextCol[Continue Inner] end end LBreak --> TargetFound[Found Target: Outside Both Loops] ``` --- ## 5. Exhaustive Member Function & Syntax Reference | Category | Syntax / Construct (Example) | Use Case (Code Snippet) | Complexity | Description & Behavioral Invariant | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | **If-Then-Else** | `if (c) { ... } else { ... }` | `if (count > 0) return true; else return false;` | $O(1)$ branch | Evaluates boolean expression; branches execution to true or false block. | | **Switch Statement** | `switch (x) { case 1: ... break; }` | `switch (status) { case 200: handleOk(); break; }` | $O(1)$ to $O(\log N)$ | Classic multi-way branch with explicit `break` to prevent fall-through. | | **Switch Expression** | `switch (x) { case 1 -> expr; }` | `int days = switch (month) { case 2 -> 28; default -> 30; };` | $O(1)$ to $O(\log N)$ | Modern expression returning a value with no fall-through and arrow syntax. | | **Switch Yield** | `yield value;` | `case 2 -> { boolean leap = isLeap(); yield leap ? 29 : 28; }` | $O(1)$ return | Produces the result value of a multi-statement switch expression block. | | **While Loop** | `while (cond) { ... }` | `while (!queue.isEmpty()) { process(queue.poll()); }` | Variable | Pre-tested loop; condition evaluated before entering loop body. | | **Do-While Loop** | `do { ... } while (cond);` | `do { token = read(); } while (token != DELIM);` | Variable (min 1) | Post-tested loop; guaranteed to execute body at least once. | | **Enhanced For** | `for (T item : collection)` | `for (User u : userList) { u.notify(); }` | $O(N)$ traversal | Syntactic sugar over `Iterable.iterator()`; throws `ConcurrentModificationException` on structural mutation. | | **Labeled Break** | `break labelName;` | `if (val == target) { found = true; break searchLoop; }` | $O(1)$ jump | Transfers control out of the enclosing labeled block or outer loop. | | **Labeled Continue**| `continue labelName;` | `if (skipRow) { continue rowLoop; }` | $O(1)$ jump | Skips current iteration of the outer labeled loop and advances its counter. | --- ## 6. Modern Idiomatic Java Code Implementation ```java // Comprehensive demonstration of control flow and modern switch expressions in Java 21 package devtype.engine.flow; public final class FlowControlLab { public enum Priority { LOW, MEDIUM, HIGH, CRITICAL } // Modern switch expression returning SLA hours based on priority public static int getSlaHours(Priority priority, boolean isWeekend) { return switch (priority) { case LOW -> isWeekend ? 72 : 48; case MEDIUM -> isWeekend ? 36 : 24; case HIGH -> 8; case CRITICAL -> { notifyOnCallEngineer(); yield isWeekend ? 2 : 1; } }; } // 2D Matrix search utilizing labeled break to escape nested loops public static boolean searchMatrix(int[][] matrix, int target) { if (matrix == null || matrix.length == 0) return false; boolean found = false; searchGrid: for (int r = 0; r < matrix.length; r++) { for (int c = 0; c < matrix[r].length; c++) { if (matrix[r][c] == target) { found = true; break searchGrid; // Escapes both loops immediately } } } return found; } private static void notifyOnCallEngineer() {} } ``` --- ## 7. Common Traps, Anti-Patterns & Best Practices 1. **Accidental Fall-Through in Classic Switch:** - *Trap:* Omitting `break;` in a classic `switch` causes execution to fall through into subsequent case blocks, leading to subtle logic defects. - *Remedy:* Always use modern Java 14+ switch expressions with arrow syntax (`case ->`), which enforce non-fallthrough semantics by design. 2. **Concurrent Modification During Enhanced For-Each Loop:** - *Trap:* Calling `collection.remove(item)` inside an enhanced `for (Item item : collection)` loop corrupts the internal `modCount` of the underlying iterator, throwing `java.util.ConcurrentModificationException`. - *Remedy:* Use explicit `Iterator.remove()`, `Collection.removeIf()`, or collect elements into a separate removal list. 3. **Floating-Point Counters in Loop Headers:** - *Trap:* Writing `for (double d = 0.0; d != 1.0; d += 0.1)` results in an **infinite loop** because `0.1` cannot be represented exactly in binary floating-point. - *Remedy:* Always use integer loop counters: `for (int i = 0; i < 10; i++) { double d = i * 0.1; }`.
description: Mastering Java control statements: modern arrow switch expressions, yield returns, bytecode jump tables, and multi-tier labeled branching.

# Module 04: Classes, Objects & Lifecycle Mechanics > **Source Track:** Oracle Java Tutorials — *Learning the Java Language* > **Source Lessons:** `javaOO/classes.html`, `classdecl.html`, `variables.html`, `methods.html`, `constructors.html`, `arguments.html`, `objects.html`, `objectcreation.html`, `usingobject.html` > **Scope:** Class Declarations, Method Signatures, Varargs, Constructor Chaining, Strict Pass-by-Value Semantics, Heap Object Memory Layout (Mark Word, Klass Pointer, Padding), Garbage Collection Lifecycle. --- ## 1. Architectural Overview & The Lifecycle Pipeline In Java, every running program operates by loading compiled classes into **Metaspace** and dynamically instantiating objects on the **JVM Heap**. An object undergoes three discrete phases during creation: 1. **Declaration:** Associating a variable identifier with a reference type in the local stack frame (`Point origin;`). Value is initially unassigned or `null`. 2. **Instantiation:** The `new` keyword dynamically allocates memory on the Heap and zeroes the field memory. 3. **Initialization:** Invoking the constructor (`new Point(10, 20)`), executing field initializers and instance initializer blocks. ```mermaid flowchart LR A["1. Declaration
Point p; (Stack ref allocated)"] --> B["2. Instantiation
new Point (Heap memory allocated & zeroed)"] B --> C["3. Initialization
Point(...) constructor runs
Fields populated"] C --> D["4. Active Usage
Methods invoked via vtable"] D --> E["5. Unreachability
Root-set references severed"] E --> F["6. Garbage Collection
Memory reclaimed by GC"] ``` --- ## 2. JVM Object Memory Footprint (HotSpot 64-bit) Every standard Java object allocated on a 64-bit HotSpot JVM occupies memory formatted with strict header and alignment rules: ```mermaid flowchart TD subgraph HotSpotObjectLayout ["Standard Java Object Layout (64-bit JVM with Compressed OOPs)"] direction TB MW["Mark Word (64 bits / 8 bytes)
- Identity HashCode (31 bits)
- GC Age (4 bits: 0 to 15)
- Biased Lock / Lock Bits (00 = Thin, 10 = Heavy Monitor)"] KP["Klass Pointer (32 bits / 4 bytes via Compressed OOPs)
Pointer to Class Metadata in Metaspace"] Fields["Instance Fields Payload
- Primitive fields (int: 4B, double: 8B, boolean: 1B)
- Reference fields (4B each via Compressed OOPs)"] Pad["Padding (0 to 7 bytes)
Aligns total object size to a multiple of 8 bytes"] MW --- KP KP --- Fields Fields --- Pad end ``` ### Memory Header Breakdown - **Mark Word (8 bytes):** Stores runtime metadata: - Identity hashcode (computed once upon invocation of `System.identityHashCode()`). - Generational GC age (4 bits: max tenure threshold of 15 before promotion from Survivor to Tenured/Old Gen). - Lock state markers (unlocked, lightweight thin lock, heavyweight inflated monitor lock). - **Klass Word (4 bytes with Compressed OOPs, 8 bytes without):** Direct reference pointing to the class metadata in Metaspace. - **Array Length (4 bytes, arrays only):** Stores the 32-bit element count of the array. - **8-Byte Alignment Padding:** Modern CPUs fetch cache lines aligned to 64-bit word boundaries; objects are padded with trailing bytes to ensure total byte size is divisible by 8. --- ## 3. Parameter Passing Semantics: Strict Pass-by-Value > [!IMPORTANT] > **Java is strictly 100% Pass-by-Value at all times.** > There is **no pass-by-reference** in the Java language. - When passing a **primitive**, a copy of the primitive value is pushed onto the callee's stack frame. Modifying the parameter inside the method has zero effect on the caller's variable. - When passing an **object reference**, a **copy of the reference address** is passed by value. - The caller and callee hold two distinct reference variables that happen to point to the *same* underlying Heap object. - Mutating the internal fields of the object affects both (state mutation). - **Reassigning the parameter variable (`param = new Object()`) rebinds only the local copy**; the caller's original reference remains completely unchanged! ```mermaid flowchart LR subgraph CallerFrame ["Caller Stack Frame: modify(p)"] OrigRef["Point p = 0x5000"] end subgraph CalleeFrame ["Callee Stack Frame: void modify(Point target)"] CopyRef["Point target = 0x5000 (Copied Value)"] ReboundRef["target = new Point(0, 0) -> 0x9000 (Rebinds local copy only!)"] end subgraph HeapObj ["Heap Object at 0x5000"] PointData["x: 100, y: 200"] end OrigRef --> HeapObj CopyRef --> HeapObj ``` --- ## 4. Constructors, Overloading & Chaining - **Default Constructor:** If no constructors are explicitly declared, the Java compiler automatically synthesizes a `public` no-argument constructor that invokes `super()`. If *any* constructor is declared, no default constructor is generated. - **Constructor Overloading:** Defining multiple constructors with distinct parameter signatures. - **Constructor Chaining (`this(...)`):** Calling another constructor within the same class using `this(...)`. **Must be the first statement in the constructor body**. --- ## 5. Exhaustive Member Function & Lifecycle Reference | Category | Syntax / Construct (Example) | Use Case (Code Snippet) | Specification | Description & Behavioral Invariant | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | **Object Instantiation**| `new ClassName(args)` | `Point p = new Point(10, 20);` | Heap allocation | Allocates zeroed heap memory, initializes headers, and runs constructor. | | **Constructor Chaining** | `this(args);` | `public Point() { this(0, 0); }` | First statement | Delegates instantiation to an overloaded constructor within the same class. | | **Super Constructor** | `super(args);` | `public Child() { super("init"); }` | First statement | Invokes the superclass constructor to initialize inherited state. | | **Varargs Parameter** | `void log(String... msgs)` | `public void print(int... nums)` | Syntactic array sugar | Desugars into `int[] nums` at compile time; allows zero or more arguments. | | **Field Shadowing** | `this.field = field;` | `public void setX(int x) { this.x = x; }` | O(1) assignment | Resolves ambiguity between a method parameter and an instance variable. | | **Garbage Collection** | `p = null;` | `p = null; // Sever root reference` | O(1) reference reset | Removes reachability link, qualifying object for next GC collection cycle. | | **Identity HashCode** | `System.identityHashCode(o)`| `int id = System.identityHashCode(obj);` | Native HotSpot lookup | Returns original default memory-based hash code, even if `hashCode()` is overridden. | --- ## 6. Modern Idiomatic Java Code Implementation ```java // Comprehensive demonstration of class architecture, constructor chaining, and pass-by-value package devtype.engine.lifecycle; public final class LifecycleLab { public static class Node { private int value; private Node next; // Overloaded constructor 1: default values public Node(int value) { this(value, null); // Constructor chaining } // Overloaded constructor 2: full initialization public Node(int value, Node next) { this.value = value; this.next = next; } public int getValue() { return value; } public void setValue(int value) { this.value = value; } public Node getNext() { return next; } public void setNext(Node next) { this.next = next; } } // Demonstrates pass-by-value with state mutation vs reference reassignment public static void demonstratePassByValue(Node node, int primitiveVal) { // Primitive copy mutated: Caller's primitive remains unchanged primitiveVal = 999; // Object internal state mutated: Visible to caller! node.setValue(500); // Reference reassignment: Local copy rebound; caller remains pointing to original node! node = new Node(1000); } // Varargs demonstration: desugars into int[] public static int sumAll(int initialMultiplier, int... values) { int sum = 0; for (int v : values) { sum += v; } return sum * initialMultiplier; } } ``` --- ## 7. Common Traps, Anti-Patterns & Best Practices 1. **Assuming Reassigning a Method Parameter Rebinds Caller's Reference:** - *Trap:* Thinking `void swap(Point a, Point b) { Point t = a; a = b; b = t; }` swaps the caller's objects. In Java, this only swaps the local stack frame copies of references. - *Remedy:* Pass a container object, array, or return a new composed object pair. 2. **Forgetting to Provide a No-Arg Constructor When Declaring Overloads:** - *Trap:* Adding `public User(String id)` causes the compiler to stop generating the default `public User()`. Frameworks requiring default reflection instantiation (JPA, Jackson) crash at runtime. - *Remedy:* Explicitly declare a parameterless constructor whenever custom constructors are added. 3. **Leaking Memory via Hidden Strong References (GC Leaks):** - *Trap:* Adding objects to static collections (caches, listeners) without eviction prevents the Garbage Collector from freeing them, leading to `OutOfMemoryError`. - *Remedy:* Explicitly remove unused entries, or utilize `WeakHashMap` / `WeakReference`.

# Module 08: Numbers, Formatting, Characters & Strings

> **Source Track:** Oracle Java Tutorials — *Learning the Java Language*  
> **Source Lessons:** `data/numbers.html`, `numberclasses.html`, `numberformat.html`, `beyondmath.html`, `numbersummary.html`, `characters.html`, `strings.html`, `converting.html`, `manipstrings.html`, `comparestrings.html`, `buffers.html`, `stringsummary.html`, `autoboxing.html`  
> **Scope:** Primitive Wrappers, Autoboxing Cache Pool (-128 to 127), `Math` & Exact Arithmetic, Unicode & Character Code Points, String Immutability, String Constant Pool, Compact Strings (`byte[]` + coder), `StringBuilder` vs `StringBuffer`.

---

## 1. Architectural Overview & Memory Mechanics

Java bridges primitive performance with object abstraction through **Wrapper Classes** (`Integer`, `Double`, etc.) and provides high-performance text processing through immutable `String` objects and mutable `StringBuilder` buffers.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph ConstantPool ["JVM String Constant Pool (Heap Space)"]
        S1["'hello' (Deduped Shared Object at 0x10)"]
    end

    subgraph HeapObjs ["Standard JVM Heap Objects"]
        S2["new String('hello') (Distinct Heap Object at 0x20)"]
        S3["new String('hello') (Distinct Heap Object at 0x30)"]
    end

    subgraph StackRefs ["Stack Reference Variables"]
        RefA["String a = 'hello'"]
        RefB["String b = 'hello'"]
        RefC["String c = new String('hello')"]
    end

    RefA --> S1
    RefB --> S1
    RefC --> S2
    S2 -.->|"intern()"| S1
```

---

## 2. Autoboxing, Unboxing & The Cache Pool Trap

- **Autoboxing:** The automatic conversion that the Java compiler makes between primitive types and their corresponding object wrapper classes (e.g., `int` to `Integer`).
- **Unboxing:** The reverse process, converting an object of a wrapper type to its corresponding primitive (e.g., `Integer` to `int`).

### The Integer Cache Pool (-128 to 127)
The JVM maintains an internal cache of pre-allocated `Integer` instances for values between **`-128` and `127`** (configurable via `-XX:AutoBoxCacheMax`).
- Invoking `Integer.valueOf(100)` returns a cached object reference.
- Values outside this range allocate fresh Heap objects.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["Integer x = 100; Integer y = 100;"] -->|Both point to cached 0x40| Cache["x == y is TRUE"]
    B["Integer p = 200; Integer q = 200;"] -->|Allocate separate objects| Heap["p == q is FALSE!"]
```

> [!CAUTION]
> **Never compare wrapper objects using `==`.**  
> Always use `.equals()` or unbox to primitives before comparing values.

---

## 3. String Architecture: Immutability & Compact Strings

`java.lang.String` objects are **completely immutable**. Once created on the Heap, their contents can never be modified.
1. **Thread-Safety:** Multiple threads can share strings without synchronization.
2. **Security:** Strings used for network connections, filenames, and database URLs cannot be maliciously mutated after validation.
3. **HashCode Caching:** Because the string is immutable, its 32-bit hash code is calculated once and cached in an internal field (`hash`), making strings ideal `HashMap` keys.

### Modern Java 9+ Compact Strings
Prior to Java 9, strings internally stored characters in a `char[]` array (16 bits / 2 bytes per character), wasting half of memory for standard Latin-1 ASCII text.
Modern Java uses **Compact Strings**:
- Internal storage is a **`byte[]`** array accompanied by a 1-byte encoding **`coder` flag** (`LATIN1` = 0, `UTF16` = 1).
- If all characters fit into ISO-8859-1 (1 byte each), memory usage is reduced by **50%**.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph CompactStringLayout ["String Object Layout (Java 9+)"]
        H["Header (Mark Word + Klass Pointer: 12B)"]
        C["byte coder (1 byte: 0 for LATIN-1, 1 for UTF-16)"]
        Hash["int hash (4 bytes cached hash code)"]
        Ref["byte[] value (Heap array containing raw 8-bit or 16-bit bytes)"]
    end
```

---

## 4. `StringBuilder` vs. `StringBuffer`

| Dimension | `StringBuilder` (Recommended) | `StringBuffer` (Legacy) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Synchronization** | Unsynchronized (Not thread-safe) | Synchronized methods (Thread-safe) |
| **Performance** | Extremely fast, zero lock overhead | Slow due to thread lock contention |
| **Buffer Growth** | Geometric capacity expansion (typically $2 \times \text{capacity} + 2$) | Identical geometric expansion |
| **Use Case** | Local string construction, loops, single-threaded processing | Rare legacy environments requiring shared mutable buffers |

---

## 5. Exhaustive Member Function & Syntax Reference

| Category | Method / Syntax (Example) | Use Case (Code Snippet) | Complexity | Description & Behavioral Invariant |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Numeric Parsing** | `Integer.parseInt(str)` | `int port = Integer.parseInt("8080");` | O(N) string parse | Parses string into signed 32-bit primitive int; throws `NumberFormatException`. |
| **Safe Arithmetic** | `Math.addExact(a, b)` | `long sum = Math.addExact(val1, val2);` | O(1) CPU flag check| Adds values, throwing `ArithmeticException` on integer overflow. |
| **String Intern** | `str.intern()` | `String canonical = raw.intern();` | O(1) hash pool lookup| Returns canonical string reference from the JVM String Constant Pool. |
| **String Formatting**| `String.format(fmt, ...)`| `String msg = String.format("%04d-%s", id, code);` | O(N) format build | Creates formatted string using printf-style placeholders. |
| **Character Check** | `Character.isDigit(c)` | `if (Character.isWhitespace(ch)) { ... }` | O(1) table lookup | Inspects Unicode character category properties. |
| **String Strip** | `str.strip()` | `String clean = rawInput.strip();` | O(N) Unicode scan | Strips leading and trailing Unicode-aware whitespace (superior to legacy `trim()`). |
| **String Join** | `String.join(delim, items)`| `String csv = String.join(",", tokens);` | O(N) buffer join | Combines elements with delimiter into a single compact string. |
| **Buffer Append** | `sb.append(str)` | `sb.append("id=").append(100);` | O(1) amortized | Appends characters to mutable buffer with geometric capacity expansion. |

---

## 6. Modern Idiomatic Java Code Implementation

```java
// Comprehensive demonstration of number parsing, string manipulation, and StringBuilder
package devtype.engine.text;

import java.util.List;

public final class TextNumbersLab {

    // Demonstrates safe exact math preventing silent rollover
    public static long calculateSafeCapacity(int users, int quotaPerUser) {
        try {
            return Math.multiplyExact((long) users, (long) quotaPerUser);
        } catch (ArithmeticException e) {
            System.err.println("Capacity overflow detected: capping at Long.MAX_VALUE");
            return Long.MAX_VALUE;
        }
    }

    // High-performance string construction using pre-sized StringBuilder
    public static String buildCsvReport(List<String> headers, List<List<String>> rows) {
        // Pre-estimate capacity to minimize internal buffer array resizing
        StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder(1024);

        // Append headers
        sb.append(String.join(",", headers)).append("\n");

        // Append rows
        for (List<String> row : rows) {
            for (int i = 0; i < row.size(); i++) {
                String cell = row.get(i);
                // Sanitize and escape commas
                if (cell != null && cell.contains(",")) {
                    sb.append('"').append(cell).append('"');
                } else {
                    sb.append(cell != null ? cell.strip() : "");
                }

                if (i < row.size() - 1) {
                    sb.append(',');
                }
            }
            sb.append("\n");
        }

        return sb.toString();
    }
}
```

---

## 7. Common Traps, Anti-Patterns & Best Practices

1. **Comparing Wrapper Objects with `==` Outside Cache Range:**
   - *Trap:* `Integer a = 128; Integer b = 128; a == b` evaluates to `false` because values $\ge 128$ allocate distinct heap instances.
   - *Remedy:* Always use `.equals()`: `a.equals(b)`.

2. **String Concatenation in Tight Loops (`s += str`):**
   - *Trap:* Concatenating strings with `+` inside a loop creates a new `StringBuilder` and a new `String` object on every iteration, causing $O(N^2)$ time complexity and catastrophic GC allocation churn.
   - *Remedy:* Create a single `StringBuilder` outside the loop and call `sb.append()`.

3. **Ignoring Nulls During Unboxing (`NullPointerException`):**
   - *Trap:* Attempting to unbox a `null` wrapper object (`Integer count = null; int c = count;`) throws an immediate runtime `NullPointerException`.
   - *Remedy:* Check for `null` before unboxing or use `Objects.requireNonNullElse(count, 0)`.
