# Module 10: Packages, Annotations & Compilation Architecture > **Source Track:** Oracle Java Tutorials — *Learning the Java Language* > **Source Lessons:** `package/index.html`, `packages.html`, `createpkgs.html`, `namingpkgs.html`, `usepkgs.html`, `managingfiles.html`, `summary-package.html`, `annotations/index.html`, `basics.html`, `declaring.html`, `predefined.html`, `type_annotations.html`, `repeating.html`, `environment/paths.html` > **Scope:** Package Namespaces, Compilation Units, Import Directives, ClassLoader Hierarchy (Delegation Model), Annotation System, Meta-Annotations, Retention Policies, Reflection Access. --- ## 1. Architectural Overview & Namespaces A **Package** is a namespace mechanism that groups related types (classes, interfaces, enums, annotations), providing access protection and preventing global namespace pollution. - Java enforces a 1:1 mapping between package declarations and the physical directory hierarchy on disk. - Package naming follows the **reverse Internet domain name** convention (`com.company.subsystem.module`). ```mermaid flowchart TD subgraph FileSystem ["Physical Directory on CLASSPATH"] D1["/project/src/main/java"] --> D2["/devtype"] D2 --> D3["/engine"] D3 --> D4["/core"] D4 --> F["AppEngine.java"] end subgraph BytecodeMetadata ["Compiled Bytecode (.class)"] F --> C["package devtype.engine.core;
public class AppEngine { ... }"] end ``` --- ## 2. Compilation Units & The ClassLoader Delegation Model When a Java program executes, the JVM dynamically locates and loads `.class` bytecode files through a hierarchical **ClassLoader Delegation Chain**: ```mermaid flowchart TD Req["Load Class Request"] --> AppLoader["Application / System ClassLoader
(Loads user classes on CLASSPATH)"] AppLoader -->|Delegates to Parent| PlatLoader["Platform / Extension ClassLoader
(Loads extended platform modules)"] PlatLoader -->|Delegates to Parent| BootLoader["Bootstrap ClassLoader
(Native JVM C++ Core: java.base, java.lang.*)"] BootLoader -->|Found?| Ret1["Return Class Instance"] BootLoader -->|Not Found| PlatSearch["Platform Loader Searches"] PlatSearch -->|Found?| Ret2["Return Class Instance"] PlatSearch -->|Not Found| AppSearch["Application Loader Searches CLASSPATH"] AppSearch -->|Not Found| CNF["Throw ClassNotFoundException"] ``` ### Delegation Invariant A ClassLoader always delegates the request to its parent before attempting to load the class itself. This guarantees that fundamental core classes (`java.lang.Object`, `java.lang.String`) cannot be spoofed by rogue user classes on the CLASSPATH. --- ## 3. The Annotation Architecture Annotations are a structured form of **metadata** that provide information about a program without having direct operational semantics at runtime. ### Anatomy of an Annotation Type (`@interface`) ```mermaid flowchart TD subgraph MetaAnnotations ["Meta-Annotations Governing Scope"] R["@Retention (SOURCE, CLASS, or RUNTIME)"] T["@Target (TYPE, METHOD, FIELD, PARAMETER, etc.)"] D["@Documented (Included in Javadoc)"] I["@Inherited (Inherited by subclasses)"] end subgraph CustomAnnotation ["Custom Annotation Definition"] A["@interface ServiceDescriptor {
String name();
int version() default 1;
boolean enabled() default true;
String[] tags() default {};
};"] end MetaAnnotations --> CustomAnnotation ``` ### Retention Policies (`java.lang.annotation.RetentionPolicy`) 1. **`SOURCE`:** Discarded by the compiler; exists only in source code (e.g., `@Override`, `@SuppressWarnings`). 2. **`CLASS` (Default):** Recorded in the `.class` file by the compiler, but **NOT** loaded into memory by the VM at runtime. Used by bytecode analysis tools. 3. **`RUNTIME`:** Recorded in the `.class` file and retained by the JVM in Metaspace. Accessible at runtime via **Reflection** (`Class.getAnnotation()`). --- ## 4. Predefined & Modern Type Annotations - **Predefined Annotations:** - `@Override`: Asserts that a method overrides a superclass or interface method. - `@Deprecated`: Marks an element as obsolete and hazardous to use. - `@SuppressWarnings`: Instructs the compiler to suppress specified compiler warnings. - `@SafeVarargs`: Asserts that the code does not perform unsafe operations on its varargs parameter. - `@FunctionalInterface`: Enforces the Single Abstract Method (SAM) invariant on interfaces. - **Type Annotations (JSR 308 - Java 8+):** Applied to the *use* of types anywhere (e.g., `@NonNull String`, `List<@Valid User>`), enabling third-party pluggable type-checkers (Checker Framework) to catch null pointers and buffer overflows at compile time. - **Repeating Annotations (`@Repeatable`):** Allows applying the same annotation multiple times to a single declaration. --- ## 5. Exhaustive Member Function & Annotation Reference | Category | Syntax / Construct (Example) | Use Case (Code Snippet) | Specification | Description & Behavioral Invariant | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | **Package Declaration** | `package com.app.core;` | First non-comment statement in file | Namespace scope | Binds the compilation unit to the logical and physical package namespace. | | **Static Import** | `import static Math.PI;` | `import static java.util.Collections.*;`| Direct member import| Imports static members into namespace, eliminating class qualification. | | **Annotation Declaration**| `@interface Config` | `public @interface Endpoint { String url(); }` | Metadata type | Declares an annotation interface; elements cannot take parameters or throw exceptions. | | **Retention Meta** | `@Retention(RUNTIME)` | `@Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)` | Meta-annotation | Directs compiler to preserve annotation metadata for runtime reflection. | | **Target Meta** | `@Target(ElementType.METHOD)`| `@Target({ElementType.TYPE, ElementType.METHOD})`| Meta-annotation | Restricts language constructs to which the annotation may be attached. | | **Reflection Check** | `isAnnotationPresent()` | `if (cls.isAnnotationPresent(Endpoint.class))`| O(1) Metaspace query| Inspects if a class, method, or field possesses the runtime annotation. | | **Reflection Read** | `getAnnotation(Class)`| `Endpoint ep = cls.getAnnotation(Endpoint.class);`| O(1) reflection read | Retrieves the annotation proxy instance to read its configured attributes. | --- ## 6. Modern Idiomatic Java Code Implementation ```java // Comprehensive demonstration of custom runtime annotations and reflection parsing package devtype.engine.meta; import java.lang.annotation.*; import java.lang.reflect.Method; public final class AnnotationLab { // 1. Declare custom runtime annotation with meta-annotations @Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME) @Target(ElementType.METHOD) @Documented public @interface TimedOperation { String name(); int warningThresholdMs() default 100; boolean critical() default false; } // 2. Class applying the annotation to internal routines public static class DatabaseService { @TimedOperation(name = "UserFetchQuery", warningThresholdMs = 50, critical = true) public void executeQuery() { try { Thread.sleep(20); // Simulated database latency } catch (InterruptedException ignored) {} } public void untimedMethod() { // Standard method without annotation } } // 3. Annotation Processor / Interceptor inspecting metadata via reflection public static void runDiagnosticScan(Class targetClass) { for (Method method : targetClass.getDeclaredMethods()) { if (method.isAnnotationPresent(TimedOperation.class)) { TimedOperation annotation = method.getAnnotation(TimedOperation.class); System.out.printf("Discovered Monitored Method: '%s' | Threshold: %dms | Critical: %b%n", annotation.name(), annotation.warningThresholdMs(), annotation.critical()); } } } } ``` --- ## 7. Common Traps, Anti-Patterns & Best Practices 1. **Forgetting `@Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)`:** - *Trap:* Declaring a custom annotation without `@Retention` causes it to default to `RetentionPolicy.CLASS`. At runtime, calling `method.getAnnotation()` returns `null`, silently breaking reflection logic! - *Remedy:* Always explicitly declare `@Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)` if reflection inspection is needed. 2. **Accidental Static Import Shadowing:** - *Trap:* Importing `static org.junit.Assert.*;` and `static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.*;` leads to ambiguous method errors on overlapping methods like `assertEquals()`. - *Remedy:* Explicitly import only specific static methods or qualify ambiguous calls with the class name. 3. **Treating Annotations as Active Code Instead of Passive Metadata:** - *Trap:* Expecting an annotation to execute logic automatically without an underlying annotation processor or reflection agent. - *Remedy:* Ensure an execution framework (Spring, Jackson, custom interceptor) is wired to read and act upon the annotation metadata.

# Module 12: Exceptions II — Try-with-Resources, AutoCloseable & Suppressed Exceptions > **Source Track:** Oracle Java Tutorials — *Essential Java Classes* > **Source Lessons:** `exceptions/tryResourceClose.html`, `putItTogether.html` > **Scope:** Try-with-Resources Statement (Java 7+), `java.lang.AutoCloseable` vs `java.io.Closeable`, Reverse Resource Closure Order, Suppressed Exception Chains (`addSuppressed()`, `getSuppressed()`), Bytecode Desugaring. --- ## 1. Architectural Overview & The Legacy Resource Leak Problem Prior to Java 7, releasing system resources (file handles, database connections, sockets) required verbose nested `try-finally` blocks. If an exception was thrown in the `try` block AND another exception occurred in `finally` during `close()`, the `finally` exception **overwrote and completely erased** the original exception from the stack trace. Java 7 introduced the **Try-with-Resources** statement: - Manages any resource implementing `java.lang.AutoCloseable`. - Closes all opened resources automatically upon block exit (whether normal or exceptional). - Enforces **Reverse Declaration Closure Order**. - Implements **Suppressed Exceptions**, preserving the root cause in the stack trace while attaching closure exceptions. ```mermaid flowchart TD subgraph TryWithResourcesExecution ["Try-with-Resources Execution Lifecycle"] Init["1. Initialize Resource A
2. Initialize Resource B"] --> TryBody["Execute Try Body Block"] TryBody -->|"Exception Thrown in Body!"| CloseB["Auto-Close Resource B (Reverse Order)"] CloseB -->|"B.close() Throws Exception!"| CloseA["Auto-Close Resource A"] CloseA --> Suppress["Primary exception propagated.
Secondary B.close() exception ATTACHED via addSuppressed()!"] end ``` --- ## 2. `AutoCloseable` vs. `Closeable` | Dimension | `java.lang.AutoCloseable` (Java 7+) | `java.io.Closeable` (Java 5) | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | **Package** | `java.lang` (Implicitly imported) | `java.io` | | **Method Signature**| `void close() throws Exception;` | `void close() throws IOException;` | | **Idempotency** | Recommended, but not strictly required. | **Strictly required**; subsequent calls must have no effect. | | **Scope** | General system resources (transactions, locks, sessions). | I/O byte and character streams. | --- ## 3. Suppressed Exceptions Invariants When multiple exceptions occur within a try-with-resources statement: 1. The exception thrown from the `try` block is the **Primary Exception**. 2. Exceptions thrown by `close()` methods are **Suppressed** and attached to the primary exception using `primary.addSuppressed(closeException)`. 3. Callers can retrieve all suppressed exceptions using `Throwable[] suppressed = primary.getSuppressed()`. --- ## 4. Exhaustive Member Function & Syntax Reference | Category | Method / Syntax (Example) | Use Case (Code Snippet) | Complexity | Description & Behavioral Invariant | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | **Try-with-Resources**| `try (Res r = open())` | `try (BufferedReader br = Files.newBufferedReader(p))` | $O(1)$ auto-close | Automatically calls `r.close()` in reverse order upon exiting block. | | **Multiple Resources**| `try (A a = ..; B b = ..)`| `try (InputStream in = ..; OutputStream out = ..)` | Reverse closure | Closes `b` first, then closes `a`. | | **AutoCloseable** | `void close() throws Ex` | `public void close() throws IOException { ... }` | Idempotent close | Interface contract required for try-with-resources management. | | **Add Suppressed** | `ex.addSuppressed(supp)` | `primary.addSuppressed(closeEx);` | $O(1)$ list append | Attaches a secondary exception to the primary exception's suppressed chain. | | **Get Suppressed** | `ex.getSuppressed()` | `for (Throwable t : ex.getSuppressed()) { ... }` | $O(K)$ array return | Returns an array containing all exceptions suppressed by this exception. | --- ## 5. Modern Idiomatic Java Code Implementation ```java // Comprehensive demonstration of try-with-resources, custom AutoCloseable, and suppressed exceptions package devtype.engine.exceptions; import java.io.*; import java.nio.file.Files; import java.nio.file.Path; public final class TryWithResourcesLab { public static class TransactionSession implements AutoCloseable { private final String txId; public TransactionSession(String id) { this.txId = id; } @Override public void close() throws Exception { // Emulates resource release System.out.println("Closed transaction session: " + txId); } } public static String readFirstLine(Path path) throws Exception { // Both resources closed automatically; session closed first, then reader try (TransactionSession tx = new TransactionSession("TX-101"); BufferedReader reader = Files.newBufferedReader(path)) { return reader.readLine(); } } } ``` --- ## 6. Common Traps, Anti-Patterns & Best Practices 1. **Reassigning Resource Variables Inside Try Body:** - *Trap:* Attempting to reassign a resource variable declared in the `try (...)` header fails compilation because resource variables are **implicitly final**. - *Remedy:* Declare a separate local variable inside the block body if mutation is needed. 2. **Throwing Checked `Exception` from `AutoCloseable.close()`:** - *Trap:* Implementing `AutoCloseable` without narrowing the `throws Exception` signature forces callers to catch generic `Exception`. - *Remedy:* Narrow the `close()` signature to specific exceptions (e.g. `throws IOException`) or omit `throws` if closure cannot fail.

# Module 17: Concurrency I — Thread Lifecycle, JMM, Volatile & Intrinsic Monitors

> **Source Track:** Oracle Java Tutorials — *Essential Java Classes*  
> **Source Lessons:** `concurrency/procthread.html`, `threads.html`, `runthread.html`, `sleep.html`, `interrupt.html`, `join.html`, `sync.html`, `interfere.html`, `memconsist.html`, `syncmeth.html`, `locksync.html`  
> **Scope:** Processes vs Threads, Thread States & Lifecycle, Java Memory Model (JMM) Happens-Before Invariants, `volatile` Memory Barriers, Intrinsic Monitor Locks (`synchronized`).

---

## 1. Architectural Overview: Processes, Threads & JMM

In modern computing, **Processes** are isolated execution environments with dedicated memory spaces, while **Threads** exist within a process and share access to the **JVM Heap**.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph MultiCoreCPU ["Multi-Core CPU Cache Coherence"]
        subgraph Core1 ["CPU Core 1"]
            L1["L1/L2 Cache (Registers)"]
            T1["Thread 1"]
        end
        subgraph Core2 ["CPU Core 2"]
            L2["L1/L2 Cache (Registers)"]
            T2["Thread 2"]
        end
        MainMem["Main Memory (Shared JVM Heap Space)"]
        L1 <-->|Hardware Cache Sync| MainMem
        L2 <-->|Hardware Cache Sync| MainMem
    end
```

### The Two Fundamental Hazards
1. **Thread Interference:** Simultaneous unsynchronized execution on shared mutable state corrupts data.
2. **Memory Consistency Errors:** Changes written by one thread remain stuck in local CPU caches and are invisible to other threads.

---

## 2. The Java Memory Model & `volatile`

The **Happens-Before Relationship** defines when memory writes by Thread A are guaranteed to be visible to Thread B:
- **Volatile Field Rules:** A write to a `volatile` variable happens-before every subsequent read of that same variable.
- **Intrinsic Monitor Rules:** An unlock (exit `synchronized`) on a monitor happens-before every subsequent lock acquisition on the same monitor.
- **Thread Lifecycle Rules:** `Thread.start()` happens-before any action in the started thread; completion of a thread happens-before `join()` returns.

> [!NOTE]
> `volatile` guarantees **visibility and ordering**, but does **NOT** guarantee mutual exclusion or atomicity for compound operations (e.g., `count++` is read-modify-write and NOT thread-safe with volatile alone).

---

## 3. Exhaustive Member Function & Concurrency Reference

| Category | Method / Syntax (Example) | Use Case (Code Snippet) | Complexity | Description & Behavioral Invariant |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Start Thread** | `thread.start()` | `new Thread(task).start();` | Native OS thread spawn | Allocates native OS thread executing the task's `run()` method. |
| **Sleep Thread** | `Thread.sleep(millis)`| `Thread.sleep(100);` | O(1) OS timer | Suspends execution without releasing any acquired monitor locks. |
| **Join Thread** | `thread.join()` | `worker.join();` | OS synchronization | Blocks calling thread until the target thread completely terminates. |
| **Interrupt** | `thread.interrupt()` | `worker.interrupt();` | O(1) flag set | Sets the thread's interrupt status flag; causes blocking methods to throw `InterruptedException`. |
| **Synchronized Method**| `synchronized void inc()`| `public synchronized void add() { ... }`| Monitor lock | Acquires intrinsic lock for `this` instance during method execution. |

---

## 4. Modern Idiomatic Java Code Implementation

```java
// Comprehensive demonstration of thread coordination, volatile visibility, and synchronized monitors
package devtype.engine.concurrency;

public final class ThreadBasicsLab {

    public static class ThreadSafeCounter {
        private int count = 0;
        private volatile boolean active = true;

        public synchronized void increment() {
            count++; // Thread-safe atomic update protected by monitor
        }

        public synchronized int getCount() {
            return count;
        }

        public void stop() {
            active = false; // Immediately visible across all CPU cores
        }

        public boolean isActive() {
            return active;
        }
    }
}
```

---

## 5. Common Traps, Anti-Patterns & Best Practices

1. **Invoking `run()` Instead of `start()`:**
   - *Trap:* Calling `thread.run()` executes the task synchronously on the current thread, creating no new thread.
   - *Remedy:* Always invoke `thread.start()`.

# Module 22: Regular Expressions I — NFA Engine, Character Classes & Quantifiers (ReDoS) > **Source Track:** Oracle Java Tutorials — *Essential Java Classes* > **Source Lessons:** `regex/index.html`, `intro.html`, `char_classes.html`, `pre_char_classes.html`, `quant.html`, `pse.html` > **Scope:** NFA Backtracking Engine, Character Classes (Unions, Intersections, Subtractions), Predefined Classes, Greedy vs Reluctant vs Possessive Quantifiers, Catastrophic Backtracking (ReDoS). --- ## 1. Architectural Overview & The Three Quantifier Engines Java regex (`java.util.regex`) uses a **Nondeterministic Finite Automaton (NFA)** engine. Quantifiers govern how many times an element may repeat: ```mermaid flowchart TD Q["Quantifier Operational Modes"] Q --> Greedy["1. GREEDY (X*, X+, X{n,})
Reads entire input first.
Backtracks one char at a time."] Q --> Reluctant["2. RELUCTANT / LAZY (X*?, X+?, X{n,}?)
Reads one char at a time.
Expands forward upon failure."] Q --> Possessive["3. POSSESSIVE (X*+, X++, X{n,}+)
Reads entire input like greedy.
NEVER BACKTRACKS! (No ReDoS)"] ``` ### Catastrophic Backtracking & ReDoS Prevention When nested greedy quantifiers (e.g. `(a+)+$`) encounter a non-matching string like `"aaaaaaaaaaaaab"`, the NFA explores $2^N$ combinatorial paths, pegging CPU at 100% indefinitely (**Regular Expression Denial of Service**). - *Solution:* Use **Possessive Quantifiers (`X++`, `X*+`)** to completely disable backtracking. --- ## 2. Exhaustive Member Function & Character Class Reference | Category | Syntax / Pattern (Example) | Use Case (Code Snippet) | Complexity | Description & Behavioral Invariant | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | **Character Class** | `[a-z]` | `Pattern.compile("[0-9a-fA-F]");` | O(1) table check | Matches any character within range. | | **Intersection** | `[a-z&&[def]]` | `Pattern.compile("[a-z&&[^aeiou]]");`| O(1) bitwise | Matches characters belonging to both sets (e.g. consonants). | | **Predefined Class**| `\d`, `\w`, `\s` | `Pattern.compile("\\w+@\\w+\\.\\w+");` | O(1) lookup | Shorthand for digits, word characters, and whitespace. | | **Possessive Quant**| `X++` | `Pattern.compile("\\d++");` | O(N) zero backtrack | Matches greedily without backtracking; eliminates ReDoS vulnerabilities. | --- ## 3. Modern Idiomatic Java Code Implementation ```java // Comprehensive demonstration of possessive quantifiers and character class filtering package devtype.engine.regex; import java.util.regex.*; public final class RegexBasicsLab { // Possessive quantifier prevents catastrophic backtracking private static final Pattern HEX_PATTERN = Pattern.compile("^[0-9a-fA-F]++$"); public static boolean isValidHex(String text) { if (text == null) return false; return HEX_PATTERN.matcher(text).matches(); } } ``` --- ## 4. Common Traps, Anti-Patterns & Best Practices 1. **Recompiling `Pattern.compile()` in Loops:** - *Trap:* Compiling regex strings repeatedly inside loops incurs massive CPU overhead reconstructing the NFA graph. - *Remedy:* Compile once as `private static final Pattern`.

title: ArrayList<E>: Resizable Contiguous Object Reference Array
coreConcept: Dynamically resizing Object[] reference array with 1.5x growth factor and O(1) random index access

theory:
#### Container Specification & Hierarchy (java.util.ArrayList)
`ArrayList<E>` is the standard resizable-array implementation of the `List<E>` interface.
* Implements: `List<E>`, `RandomAccess`, `Cloneable`, `java.io.Serializable`.
* Allows all elements, including `null`.
* Roughly equivalent to `Vector`, except that it is unsynchronized and substantially faster.

#### JVM Memory Model & 1.5x Growth Formula
In Java, an `ArrayList<E>` does not hold primitive values or objects inline; it stores an array of **32-bit or 64-bit object references** (`transient Object[] elementData`):
* **Initial Capacity**: Default is 10 elements when the first item is added.
* **1.5x Growth**: When `size == elementData.length`, capacity expands using bit-shifting:
$$\text{newCapacity} = \text{oldCapacity} + (\text{oldCapacity} \gg 1) = 1.5 \times \text{oldCapacity}$$
* It uses `Arrays.copyOf()` which delegates to the native `System.arraycopy()` for high-throughput memory relocation.

```text
JVM Heap Layout (Compressed OOPs, 64-bit JVM):
ArrayList Object Header (12B) + size (4B) + elementData ref (4B) + padding (4B) = 24 Bytes
        |
        +---> Object[] elementData (Heap Buffer):
              +----------+----------+----------+--------------------+
              | ref[0]   | ref[1]   | ref[2]   | null (unallocated) |
              +----+-----+----+-----+----+-----+--------------------+
                   |          |          |
                   v          v          v
              [Item 0]   [Item 1]   [Item 2]
```

#### Exhaustive Member Method Reference Table
| Category | Function (Example) | Use Case (Code Snippet) | Time Complexity | Description & Behavior |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Element Access** | `list.get(0)` | `String item = list.get(i);` | $O(1)$ | Returns reference at index without bounds scanning. |

#### Container Specification & Hierarchy (java.util.LinkedList)

* Implements: `List<E>`, `Deque<E>`, `Cloneable`, `java.io.Serializable`.

```text
+-----+-----+-----+     +-----+-----+-----+     +-----+-----+-----+
| null| "A" |  * -+---->|  *  | "B" |  * -+---->|  *  | "C" | null|
```

theory:
#### Container Specification & Hierarchy (java.util.concurrent)
`CopyOnWriteArrayList<E>` is a thread-safe list designed specifically for scenarios where **read operations vastly outnumber write operations** (e.g. event listener registries, routing tables, cached state).
* Package: `java.util.concurrent`.
* Implements: `List<E>`, `RandomAccess`, `Cloneable`, `java.io.Serializable`.

#### The Copy-on-Write Memory Synchronization Protocol
All mutative operations (`add`, `set`, `remove`) acquire an internal `ReentrantLock`, make a fresh copy of the entire underlying array, modify the copy, and publish it via a **`volatile Object[] array`** pointer swap:
$$\text{Write Overhead} = O(N) \text{ memory allocation and arraycopy}$$

```text
Thread 1 (Reader): Traversing Snapshot Array A [ 10 | 20 | 30 ] (Lock-free!)
                                                ^
Thread 2 (Writer): Clones Array A -> Array B [ 10 | 20 | 30 | 40 ]
                   Updates volatile pointer: array = Array B
```

theory:
#### Container Specification & Hierarchy (java.util.ArrayDeque)
`ArrayDeque<E>` is the recommended general-purpose implementation of both the `Queue<E>` and `Deque<E>` interfaces.
* Implements: `Deque<E>`, `Queue<E>`, `Cloneable`, `java.io.Serializable`.
* Prohibits `null` elements (calling `add(null)` throws `NullPointerException`).
* Recommended Replacement: Replaces legacy synchronized `java.util.Stack` and allocation-heavy `LinkedList`.

#### Circular Buffer & Power-of-Two Bitmask Pointer Wraps
Backing capacity is always constrained to a **power of two** ($2^K$). This eliminates expensive modulo division (`%`), wrapping indices via ultra-fast bitwise AND:
$$\text{head} = (\text{head} - 1) \mathbin{\&} (\text{elements.length} - 1)$$
$$\text{tail} = (\text{tail} + 1) \mathbin{\&} (\text{elements.length} - 1)$$

```text
Circular Array Buffer: capacity = 8 (mask = 7 -> 0b111)
[ Slot 0 | Slot 1 | Slot 2 | Slot 3 | Slot 4 | Slot 5 | Slot 6 | Slot 7 ]
             ^                                   ^
            head (tail wraps around)            tail
```

title: HashMap<K, V>: Bucket Table with Red-Black Treeification

theory:
#### Container Specification & Hierarchy (java.util.HashMap)
`HashMap<K, V>` is a hash-table based implementation of the `Map<K, V>` interface.
* Implements: `Map<K, V>`, `Cloneable`, `java.io.Serializable`.
* Permits one `null` key and multiple `null` values.
* Unsynchronized (use `ConcurrentHashMap` for concurrent threads).

#### The Java 8 Treeification Architecture
In Java 8+, `HashMap` solves the denial-of-service hash collision vulnerability:
1. **Buckets**: `Node<K, V>[] table` array sized to a power of two ($2^K$).
2. **Singly-Linked Chain**: Collisions begin as a forward-linked list.
3. **Treeify Threshold (8)**: When collisions in a single bucket reach **8** elements AND total capacity $\ge 64$, the bucket is converted into a **Red-Black `TreeNode<K, V>`**!
4. **Untreeify Threshold (6)**: When tree size shrinks to 6 during resizing, it converts back to a linked list.
This guarantees worst-case lookups degrade to **$O(\log N)$** instead of $O(N)$!

```text
Buckets:
[ Bucket 0 ] ----> Node {"A", 1} ----> Node {"B", 2}  (Linked Chain < 8)
[ Bucket 1 ] ----> null
[ Bucket 2 ] ----> TreeNode {"X", 10}  (Treeified Red-Black Tree >= 8 elements!)
                   /              \
         TreeNode {"M", 5}     TreeNode {"Z", 20}
```

By overriding the protected method `removeEldestEntry(Map.Entry<K, V> eldest)`, `LinkedHashMap` transforms into an automated, bounded **LRU Cache**:
```java

}
```

* BitSet's `bs.or(other)` processes 64 elements per clock cycle:

title: Stack Modification: Minimum Stack in O(1)
coreConcept: Augmenting stack frames with prefix minima pairs
timeComplexity: O(1) Push, O(1) Pop, O(1) Top, O(1) getMin
spaceComplexity: O(N) Auxiliary Space
theory:
#### Problem Definition & Motivation
A standard stack is a Last-In, First-Out (LIFO) container supporting two primary operations:
* `push(x)`: Appends an element to the top of the stack.
* `pop()`: Removes the most recently added element from the top of the stack.

In many algorithmic contexts, we also need to continuously query the smallest element currently residing anywhere inside the stack:
$$\min_{0 \le j \le \text{size}-1} \text{stack}[j]$$
In an unmodified stack, computing this value requires either iterating through all $N$ elements (costing $O(N)$ time per query) or maintaining an external sorted container like a balanced binary search tree or priority queue (which degrades push and pop times to $O(\log N)$).

Our goal is to modify the stack data structure in such a way that finding the smallest element in the stack takes strictly $O(1)$ constant time, while preserving $O(1)$ push and pop operations without any logarithmic overhead.

#### Mathematical Invariant & Pair Decomposition
On a stack, elements are added and removed only at one end (the top). Because of this strict LIFO discipline, the set of elements located underneath any element $x$ remains completely static throughout the entire lifespan of $x$ in the stack.

Therefore, for every element added to the stack at height $i$, we do not merely store the raw element itself. Instead, we store a pair:
$$\text{st}[i] = \langle \text{element}_i, \ \mu_i \rangle$$
where $\mu_i$ represents the minimum value among all elements from the bottom of the stack up to index $i$:
$$\mu_i = \min_{0 \le j \le i} \text{element}_j$$

* **Base Case (Empty Stack)**:
  When pushing onto an empty stack, the new element $x$ is trivially the minimum of the stack:
  $$\mu_0 = x$$
* **Inductive Step (Non-Empty Stack)**:
  When pushing a new element $x$ onto a non-empty stack with top minimum $\mu_{\text{top}}$, the new running minimum is:
  $$\mu_{\text{new}} = \min(x, \mu_{\text{top}})$$
* **Constant Time Retrieval**:
  To obtain the minimum of the entire stack at any given moment, we simply read the second component of the pair located at the top of the stack:
  $$\text{minimum} = \text{st.top().second}$$
* **Pop Invariance**:
  When removing an element via `pop()`, the top pair is discarded. The new top pair already contains the precalculated minimum of all remaining elements below it. Hence, the previous state is automatically restored in $O(1)$ time without requiring recalculation.

#### ASCII Architecture & State Transitions
```text
State 1: push(5)              State 2: push(2)                  State 3: push(7)
+-----------------------+     +-----------------------+         +-----------------------+
| (5, min(5)=5)   [TOP] |     | (2, min(2,5)=2) [TOP] |         | (7, min(7,2)=2) [TOP] |
+-----------------------+     +-----------------------+         +-----------------------+
                              | (5, 5)                |         | (2, 2)                |
                              +-----------------------+         +-----------------------+
                                                                | (5, 5)                |
                                                                +-----------------------+
getMin() -> 5                 getMin() -> 2                     getMin() -> 2

State 4: pop() -> removes (7, 2)
+-----------------------+
| (2, 2)          [TOP] |  --> getMin() immediately inspects top.second = 2 in O(1)!
+-----------------------+
| (5, 5)                |
+-----------------------+
```

#### Complexity & Memory Analysis
* **Time Complexity**:
  * `push(x)`: $O(1)$ — Performs at most one `min()` comparison and one push.
  * `pop()`: $O(1)$ — Discards the top pair in constant time.
  * `top()`: $O(1)$ — Inspects `st.top().first`.
  * `getMin()`: $O(1)$ — Inspects `st.top().second`.
* **Space Complexity**:
  * $O(N)$ auxiliary memory — Each frame stores an integer value and an integer minimum.
description: Augmenting stack frames with prefix minima pairs (LIFO with Running Extremum State) — Time: O(1) Push, O(1) Pop, O(1) Top, O(1) getMin.

title: Queue Modification (Method 2): Monotonic Deque with Index Counters
paradigm: Monotonic Extremum Elimination with Lazy Expiration
coreConcept: Maintaining non-decreasing deque with global sequence counters
timeComplexity: O(1) Amortized Push, O(1) Strict Pop, O(1) Strict getMin
spaceComplexity: O(K) Auxiliary Space where K <= N is active queue size
theory:
#### Problem Definition & Motivation
We now want to achieve constant-time minimum retrieval for a First-In, First-Out (FIFO) queue, where elements are added at the tail and removed from the head. 

In cp-algorithms Method 1, we maintained a deque in non-decreasing order by cutting trailing elements larger than the incoming one, but pop required the caller to know the value of the removed element in advance. In **Method 2**, we eliminate this restriction completely: we want to pop elements in standard FIFO order without needing to supply their values.

#### The Monotonicity Invariant
The foundational insight is that we only need to store elements that can potentially serve as the minimum in the current or any future state of the queue:
* Suppose the queue currently holds an element $X$, and a new element $Y$ arrives such that $Y \le X$.
* Because $Y$ was inserted after $X$, $Y$ will remain inside the queue strictly longer than $X$.
* Therefore, as long as $Y$ is present in the queue, $X$ can **never** be the minimum of the queue.
* Consequently, $X$ becomes completely redundant and can be immediately discarded.

By purging all elements from the back of the queue that are strictly greater than or equal to $Y$, the elements remaining in the deque are always maintained in strictly non-decreasing order:
$$\text{deque}[0] \le \text{deque}[1] \le \text{deque}[2] \le \dots$$
Thus, the smallest element of the queue is always located at the very front of the deque:
$$\text{minimum} = \text{q.front().first}$$

#### Index Counters & Lazy Eviction Mechanics
Because redundant elements are purged during push operations, an element requested to be popped may have already been purged. To know whether the front of the deque should actually be popped, we record the logical insertion index of each element using two counters:
* `cnt_added`: Tracks the total number of elements pushed since initialization.
* `cnt_removed`: Tracks the total number of elements popped since initialization.

When inserting `new_elem`:
1. Pop all elements from the back of the deque while `q.back().first >= new_elem`.
2. Push the pair `{new_elem, cnt_added}` to the back.
3. Increment `cnt_added++`.

When removing an element:
1. Check if the element currently at the front of the deque was inserted at logical index `cnt_removed`:
   $$\text{if } (!q.\text{empty}() \text{ and } q.\text{front}().\text{second} == \text{cnt\_removed}) \implies q.\text{pop\_front}()$$
2. Increment `cnt_removed++`.
3. If the element was already purged previously during a cut, the front of the deque does not match `cnt_removed`, so we do nothing.

#### ASCII Architecture & State Transitions
```text
Push sequence: 4, then 6, then 2

1. push(4): Deque = [(val:4, idx:0)]                | cnt_added = 1
2. push(6): 6 >= 4 -> Deque = [(4, 0), (6, 1)]      | cnt_added = 2
3. push(2): 6 >= 2 -> pop 6!
            4 >= 2 -> pop 4!
            Deque = [(2, 2)]                         | cnt_added = 3

Query: getMin() -> q.front().first = 2

Pop operation (removing logical index 0):
cnt_removed is 0. Front index is 2 != 0.
Element 0 was already purged by the arrival of 2!
Deque remains [(2, 2)]. cnt_removed becomes 1.
```

#### Amortized Analysis Proof
Every element is pushed to the back of the deque at most once. Inside the `push` operation, the `while` loop pops elements from the back. Since an element cannot be popped more than once from the back, $N$ push operations can perform at most $N$ back-pops in total across the entire lifetime of the structure.
$$\text{Amortized Cost per Push} = \frac{N \text{ pushes} + N \text{ pops}}{N} = O(1)$$
Both `pop()` and `getMin()` perform $O(1)$ operations in the worst case.
description: Maintaining non-decreasing deque with global sequence counters (Monotonic Extremum Elimination with Lazy Expiration) — Time: O(1) Amortized Push, O(1) Strict Pop, O(1) Strict getMin.

title: Queue Modification (Method 3): Minimum Queue via Two Stacks
paradigm: FIFO Simulation via Reversible LIFO Minimum Stacks
coreConcept: Two-stack amortized transfer with partitioned extremum tracking
timeComplexity: O(1) Strict Push, O(1) Amortized Pop, O(1) Strict getMin
spaceComplexity: O(N) Auxiliary Space (Stores all elements without loss)
theory:
#### Problem Definition & Motivation
While Method 2 provides an elegant monotonic queue, it fundamentally discards elements that are not minimum candidates. In scenarios where:
1. All elements must be physically retained in the queue,
2. Arbitrary associative operations (such as GCD or matrix multiplication) must be supported without monotonicity assumptions,
Method 3 reduces the minimum queue problem to the already-solved **minimum stack** problem.

#### Two-Stack Simulation Mechanics
We instantiate two minimum stacks, $s_1$ and $s_2$:
* **Stack $s_1$ (Enqueue Stack)**: Receives all newly arrived elements.
* **Stack $s_2$ (Dequeue Stack)**: Delivers elements in correct FIFO order.

Both $s_1$ and $s_2$ are modified stacks storing pairs of `(element, running_min)`.

* **Adding an Element (`push`)**:
  Always push into stack $s_1$:
  $$\mu_{\text{new}} = s_1.\text{empty}() \ ? \ x : \min(x, s_1.\text{top}().\text{second})$$
  $$s_1.\text{push}(\{x, \mu_{\text{new}}\})$$
* **Removing an Element (`pop`)**:
  * If $s_2$ is not empty: simply pop the top element from $s_2$.
  * If $s_2$ is empty: transfer all elements from $s_1$ to $s_2$.
    * Popping from $s_1$ and pushing into $s_2$ reverses the sequence of elements.
    * This reversal transforms the LIFO order of $s_1$ into the correct FIFO order in $s_2$.
    * While pushing each element into $s_2$, $s_2$ recalculates its own running minimum from the bottom up!
    * Once the transfer finishes, the oldest element is at the top of $s_2$ and is popped.

#### Mathematical Invariant for Queue Minimum
Because the elements currently in the queue are partitioned across $s_1$ (tail elements) and $s_2$ (head elements), the minimum of the entire queue is:
$$\text{minimum} = \begin{cases} 
s_1\text{.top().second}, & \text{if } s_2\text{ is empty} \\ 
s_2\text{.top().second}, & \text{if } s_1\text{ is empty} \\ 
\min(s_1\text{.top().second}, \ s_2\text{.top().second}), & \text{otherwise} 
\end{cases}$$
Retrieving the minimum is strictly $O(1)$ at all times.

#### Rigorous Amortized Cost Proof
Let $k$ elements be processed through the queue:
* Each element is pushed onto $s_1$ exactly once ($1$ op).
* When a transfer occurs, each element in $s_1$ is popped from $s_1$ and pushed onto $s_2$ exactly once ($2$ ops).
* Each element is finally popped from $s_2$ exactly once ($1$ op).
$$\text{Total elementary operations for } N \text{ elements} = 4N$$
$$\text{Amortized time per operation} = \frac{4N}{2N} = O(1)$$
description: Two-stack amortized transfer with partitioned extremum tracking (FIFO Simulation via Reversible LIFO Minimum Stacks) — Time: O(1) Strict Push, O(1) Amortized Pop, O(1) Strict getMin.

title: Sliding Window Minimum in O(N): Monotonic Deque
paradigm: Sliding Window with Monotonic Extremum Maintenance
coreConcept: Index-based sliding window eviction and monotonic purging
timeComplexity: O(N) Total Time (Linear across the entire array)
spaceComplexity: O(K) Auxiliary Memory for window of size K
theory:
#### Problem Definition
Suppose we are given an array $A$ of length $N$ and a window size $K \le N$. We need to compute the minimum of each contiguous subarray of length $K$:
$$\min_{0 \le i \le K-1} A[i], \quad \min_{1 \le i \le K} A[i], \quad \min_{2 \le i \le K+1} A[i], \quad \dots, \quad \min_{N-K \le i \le N-1} A[i]$$
There are $N - K + 1$ such windows. We must solve this in optimal $O(N)$ total time.

#### Analysis of Approaches
* **Naive Iteration**: Scanning every window of size $K$ takes $O(K)$ time per window $\implies O(N \cdot K)$ total time. For $N, K \approx 10^5$, this requires $10^{10}$ operations, resulting in Time Limit Exceeded (TLE).
* **Self-Balancing BST / Heap**: Maintaining a `std::multiset` takes $O(\log K)$ per slide $\implies O(N \log K)$ total time.
* **Monotonic Deque ($O(N)$)**: By maintaining a double-ended queue storing array indices in strictly increasing order of their corresponding values, we achieve optimal $O(N)$ linear time.

#### Algorithmic Invariant & 4-Step Process
Let `dq` be a `std::deque<int>` holding array indices. For each index $i$ from $0$ to $N - 1$:

1. **Evict Out-of-Window Indices**:
   The current window spans $[i - K + 1, \ i]$. If the index at the front of the deque has expired:
   $$\text{if } (!dq.\text{empty}() \text{ and } dq.\text{front}() \le i - K) \implies dq.\text{pop\_front}()$$
2. **Purge Non-Optimal Candidates**:
   Before adding $A[i]$, we inspect the back of the deque. Any index $j$ currently in the deque has $j < i$. If $A[j] \ge A[i]$, then $A[j]$ is both older and larger than $A[i]$. It can never be the minimum in any window that includes $A[i]$. Thus, we pop it:
   $$\text{while } (!dq.\text{empty}() \text{ and } A[dq.\text{back}()] \ge A[i]) \implies dq.\text{pop\_back}()$$
3. **Insert Current Index**:
   Push index $i$ to the back of the deque: $dq.\text{push\_back}(i)$.
4. **Emit Window Minimum**:
   Once $i \ge K - 1$, the first complete window has formed. The minimum element of the current window is guaranteed to be at the front:
   $$\text{window\_minimum} = A[dq.\text{front}()]$$

#### Proof of Linear Complexity $O(N)$
Although the inner `while` loop can pop multiple elements in a single step, **each index from $0$ to $N - 1$ is pushed into the deque exactly once and popped at most once**. Therefore, the total number of deque operations across the entire loop is bounded by $2N$.
$$\text{Total Time} = O(N)$$
description: Index-based sliding window eviction and monotonic purging (Sliding Window with Monotonic Extremum Maintenance) — Time: O(N) Total Time (Linear across the entire array).

title: Disjoint Set Union (DSU): Path Compression & Union by Rank
coreConcept: Rooted tree sets with tree flattening and shallow-depth merging
timeComplexity: O(alpha(N)) Amortized per operation (Virtually O(1))
spaceComplexity: O(N) Auxiliary Space
theory:
#### Capabilities of Disjoint Set Union
Disjoint Set Union (DSU), also known as Union-Find, maintains a partition of a universe of elements into disjoint equivalence classes. It supports three primary operations:
1. `make_set(v)`: Initializes a new set containing the single element $v$.
2. `find_set(v)`: Returns the designated representative (leader) of the set containing element $v$. Two elements $a$ and $b$ belong to the same set if and only if:
   $$\text{find\_set}(a) == \text{find\_set}(b)$$
3. `union_sets(a, b)`: Merges the set containing $a$ with the set containing $b$.

#### Tree Representation
We represent each set as a directed rooted tree:
* Each vertex stores a reference to its immediate ancestor: `parent[v]`.
* The root of the tree is its own ancestor: `parent[root] == root`.
* The root serves as the unique identifier and representative of the set.

#### Naive Implementation & Degeneration
In an unoptimized implementation:
* `find_set(v)` traverses parent pointers from $v$ to the root.
* `union_sets(a, b)` simply attaches root $b$ under root $a$: `parent[b] = a`.
If we merge sets linearly ($1 \cup 2$, then $2 \cup 3$, then $3 \cup 4$), the tree degenerates into a linear chain of depth $N$. In that degenerate state, every `find_set` takes $O(N)$ time, causing $M$ queries to take $O(N \cdot M)$.

To prevent tree degeneration, we apply two complementary optimizations:

#### Optimization 1: Path Compression
When executing `find_set(v)`, we traverse from $v$ up to the root $p$. Path compression rewires the `parent` pointer of every node visited along that path directly to the root $p$:
$$\text{parent}[v] = \text{find\_set}(\text{parent}[v])$$
When the recursion unwinds, all nodes along the search path are flattened into direct children of the root. A subsequent call to `find_set` on any of these nodes takes $O(1)$ time! Path compression alone guarantees an average time complexity of $O(\log N)$ per call.

```text
Before Path Compression: find_set(4)      After Path Compression:
        1 (root)                                   1 (root)
       /                                         / | \
      2                                         2  3  4
     /
    3
   /
  4
```

#### Optimization 2: Union by Rank (Depth Bounding)
When executing `union_sets(a, b)`, we avoid arbitrary parent assignments. Instead, we maintain an auxiliary array `rank[v]`, which represents an upper bound on the tree depth rooted at $v$.
* When combining two trees with roots $a$ and $b$:
  * If $\text{rank}[a] < \text{rank}[b]$: Attach $a$ as a child of $b$. The maximum depth does not increase!
  * If $\text{rank}[a] > \text{rank}[b]$: Attach $b$ as a child of $a$.
  * If $\text{rank}[a] == \text{rank}[b]$: Attach $b$ under $a$, and increment $\text{rank}[a]++$.
Union by rank alone guarantees that a tree of size $K$ has depth at most $O(\log K)$.

#### Combined Complexity: The Inverse Ackermann Function
When Path Compression and Union by Rank are used simultaneously, Robert Tarjan proved that the amortized time per operation is:
$$O(\alpha(N))$$
where $\alpha(N)$ is the **Inverse Ackermann Function**. The Ackermann function $A(m, n)$ grows at a super-exponential rate:
$$A(4, 2) = 2^{65536} - 3 \gg 10^{80} \text{ (total atoms in the observable universe)}$$
For any input size $N$ that can physically exist in computation ($N \le 10^{600}$), $\alpha(N) \le 4$. Thus, DSU operations run in **practical constant time $O(1)$**.
description: Rooted tree sets with tree flattening and shallow-depth merging (Equivalence Partitioning & Disjoint Forest Management) — Time: O(alpha(N)) Amortized per operation (Virtually O(1)).

title: Fenwick Tree (Binary Indexed Tree): Point Updates & Range Sums
paradigm: Binary Decomposition of Prefix Ranges via Two's Complement
coreConcept: Implicit binary tree indexed by Least Significant Bits (LSB)
timeComplexity: O(log N) Point Update, O(log N) Prefix/Range Sum Query
spaceComplexity: O(N) Auxiliary Space (Strict 1x array memory)
theory:
#### Problem Definition & The Update-Query Tradeoff
Given an array $A$ of length $N$, we want to dynamically support:
1. **Point Update**: Add $\delta$ to element $A[i]$.
2. **Range Sum Query**: Compute $\sum_{j=l}^r A[j]$.

| Data Structure | Point Update | Range Sum Query | Memory |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Simple Array | $O(1)$ | $O(N)$ | $O(N)$ |
| Prefix Sum Array | $O(N)$ | $O(1)$ | $O(N)$ |
| **Fenwick Tree (BIT)** | **$O(\log N)$** | **$O(\log N)$** | **$O(N)$** |

The Fenwick tree (proposed by Peter M. Fenwick in 1994) provides an optimal trade-off with negligible constant factors and zero pointer overhead.

#### Mathematical Foundation & Interval Coverage
A Fenwick tree stores partial prefix sums in an array `bit[1 ... N]`. Each index $i$ stores the sum of elements over the contiguous interval $[g(i), \ i]$, defined by:
$$g(i) = i - (i \ \& \ (-i)) + 1$$
where $i \ \& \ (-i)$ isolates the **Least Significant Bit (LSB)** of $i$ in two's complement representation.

#### The Magic of Two's Complement Arithmetic
In computer systems, negative integers are represented using two's complement:
$$-i = (\sim i) + 1$$
Inverting the bits and adding 1 flips all bits up to the lowest set bit, leaving only the lowest set bit identical in both $i$ and $-i$:
$$\text{LSB}(i) = i \ \& \ (-i)$$

* Example $i = 12 = (1100)_2$:
  $$-12 = (0011)_2 + 1 = (0100)_2 \implies 12 \ \& \ (-12) = 4 = (0100)_2$$
  Interval covered: $[12 - 4 + 1, \ 12] = [9, 12]$.
* Example $i = 8 = (1000)_2$:
  $$\text{LSB}(8) = 8 \implies \text{Interval covered: } [8 - 8 + 1, \ 8] = [1, 8]$$
  Index 8 stores the sum of the first 8 elements!

#### Query Mechanics (Downward Traversal)
To compute the prefix sum from $1$ to `idx`:
1. Add `bit[idx]` to the running sum.
2. Jump to the next responsible sub-interval by stripping the lowest set bit:
   $$\text{idx} \gets \text{idx} - (\text{idx} \ \& \ (-\text{idx}))$$
3. Repeat until $\text{idx} == 0$.
Because each step removes at least one set bit, the loop executes at most $\lfloor \log_2(\text{idx}) \rfloor + 1$ times $\implies O(\log N)$.

#### Update Mechanics (Upward Traversal)
When an element at index `idx` is increased by $\delta$, all tree positions whose coverage intervals include `idx` must be updated:
1. Add $\delta$ to `bit[idx]`.
2. Move up to the next enclosing parent interval by adding the lowest set bit:
   $$\text{idx} \gets \text{idx} + (\text{idx} \ \& \ (-\text{idx}))$$
3. Repeat while $\text{idx} \le N$.
This traversal visits at most $O(\log N)$ nodes.

#### Range Sum via Prefix Subtraction
$$\sum_{j=l}^r A[j] = \text{query}(r) - \text{query}(l - 1)$$
description: Implicit binary tree indexed by Least Significant Bits (LSB) (Binary Decomposition of Prefix Ranges via Two's Complement) — Time: O(log N) Point Update, O(log N) Prefix/Range Sum Query.

title: Segment Tree: Point Updates and Range Sum Queries in O(log N)
coreConcept: Implicit flat array representation with associative interval merging
timeComplexity: O(N) Construction, O(log N) Point Update, O(log N) Range Query
spaceComplexity: O(N) Total Space (Strictly bounded by 4N vertices)
theory:
#### Problem Definition & Motivation
Given an array $a[0 \dots n-1]$, we must dynamically process two operations:
1. **Range Query**: Compute the associative combination (e.g. sum $\sum_{i=l}^r a[i]$, min, max) of elements between arbitrary boundaries $l$ and $r$.
2. **Point Modification**: Update an element $a[\text{pos}] = \text{new\_val}$.

A naive array updates in $O(1)$ but takes $O(N)$ per query. A prefix sum array queries in $O(1)$ but takes $O(N)$ per update. The Segment Tree processes **both** operations in guaranteed $O(\log N)$ time.

#### Structure of the Segment Tree
The Segment Tree organizes array segments into a binary tree:
* The root node represents the entire array segment $a[0 \dots n-1]$.
* Any non-leaf node covering $a[tl \dots tr]$ is divided into two halves at midpoint $tm = \lfloor (tl + tr) / 2 \rfloor$:
  * Left child covers: $a[tl \dots tm]$
  * Right child covers: $a[tm + 1 \dots tr]$
* Leaf nodes cover segments of length 1 ($tl == tr$), storing the raw array elements.
* The height of the tree is strictly bounded by $\lceil \log_2 n \rceil + 1 = O(\log n)$.

#### Visual Diagram of Segment Tree Decomposition
```text
Root covers [0...4]:
                     [0...4] (sum)
                   /               \
            [0...2]                 [3...4]
           /       \               /       \
        [0...1]     [2...2]     [3...3]     [4...4]
       /       \
    [0...0]   [1...1]
```

#### Mathematical Proof: Why 4N Memory is Sufficient
In competitive programming, the tree is stored implicitly in a 1D array `t[]` where vertex $v$'s left child is at index $2v$ and right child is at $2v + 1$.
* Level 0 contains 1 node.
* Level 1 contains 2 nodes.
* Level $k$ contains $2^k$ nodes.
For an array of size $n$, the leaf nodes are placed at depth $h = \lceil \log_2 n \rceil$. The total number of nodes across all levels up to depth $h$ is:
$$\sum_{k=0}^{\lceil \log_2 n \rceil} 2^k = 2^{\lceil \log_2 n \rceil + 1} - 1 < 2 \cdot 2^{\log_2 n + 1} = 4n$$
Thus, allocating an array of size $4n$ is mathematically guaranteed to prevent array out-of-bounds errors, even when $n$ is not a power of two.

#### Range Query Mechanics & Proof of $O(\log n)$ Complexity
When answering a query on interval $[l, r]$ starting from root vertex $v$ covering $[tl, tr]$:
1. **Complete Overlap**: If $l \le tl$ and $tr \le r$, the segment is entirely contained in the query. Return `t[v]` immediately.
2. **Disjoint Segment**: If $l > tr$ or $r < tl$, the segment has no intersection. Return identity element ($0$ for sum).
3. **Partial Overlap**: Recursively query both left and right children, then combine results:
   $$\text{sum}(2v, tl, tm, l, \min(r, tm)) + \text{sum}(2v + 1, tm + 1, tr, \max(l, tm + 1), r)$$

**Why does this take at most $O(\log n)$ time?**
At each level of the tree, the algorithm visits at most **4 vertices**:
* In the worst case, the query range $[l, r]$ intersects the current level.
* The vertices whose segments are strictly interior to $[l, r]$ return immediately (Case 1) and do not make recursive child calls.
* Only the boundary vertices (the leftmost vertex intersecting $l$ and the rightmost vertex intersecting $r$) make recursive calls into the next level.
* Each boundary vertex generates at most 2 child calls, bounding the active vertices at the next level to at most $2 \times 2 = 4$.
* Since tree height is $O(\log n)$, the total time is strictly $4 \times O(\log n) = O(\log n)$.

#### Point Update Mechanics
To update $a[\text{pos}] = \text{new\_val}$:
1. Traverse down the tree to the leaf node where $tl == tr == \text{pos}$.
2. Update the leaf value: `t[v] = new_val`.
3. As the recursion unwinds back to the root, recalculate each ancestor's sum as the sum of its two children:
   $$\text{t}[v] = \text{t}[2v] + \text{t}[2v + 1]$$
Since only one path from the root to a leaf is traversed, this takes strictly $O(\log n)$ time.
description: Implicit flat array representation with associative interval merging (Divide-and-Conquer Binary Interval Tree) — Time: O(N) Construction, O(log N) Point Update, O(log N) Range Query.

title: Sparse Table: Range Minimum Query (RMQ) in O(1)
paradigm: Binary Interval Decomposition with Idempotent Querying
coreConcept: Precomputing power-of-two intervals for O(1) overlapping coverage
timeComplexity: O(N log N) Precomputation, O(1) Static RMQ Query
spaceComplexity: O(N log N) Memory
theory:
#### Problem Definition & Scope
Given an **immutable** array $A$ of length $N$, we need to answer Range Minimum Queries (RMQ):
$$\text{RMQ}(L, R) = \min_{L \le j \le R} A[j]$$
Because the underlying array never changes between queries, we can invest $O(N \log N)$ preprocessing time to build a Sparse Table that answers any subsequent range query in **strict $O(1)$ constant time**.

#### Power-of-Two Interval Decomposition
Any non-negative integer can be uniquely represented as a sum of decreasing powers of two (its standard binary representation). For example:
$$13 = (1101)_2 = 8 + 4 + 1$$
Similarly, any continuous interval can be represented as a union of intervals whose lengths are powers of two. For example:
$$[2, 14] = [2, 9] \cup [10, 13] \cup [14, 14]$$
where the sub-intervals have lengths $8, 4,$ and $1$ respectively.

We precompute answers for all intervals whose length is a power of two. We store these answers in a 2D table `st[K + 1][N]`, where:
$$\text{st}[i][j] = \min(A[j \dots j + 2^i - 1])$$
$\text{st}[i][j]$ stores the minimum of the range of length $2^i$ starting at index $j$.

#### Dynamic Programming Precomputation in $O(N \log N)$
An interval of length $2^i$ starting at index $j$ splits cleanly into two contiguous halves of length $2^{i-1}$:
1. First half: $[j, \ j + 2^{i-1} - 1]$
2. Second half: $[j + 2^{i-1}, \ j + 2^i - 1]$

Using this dynamic programming transition:
$$\text{st}[i][j] = \min\Big(\text{st}[i-1][j], \ \text{st}[i-1][j + 2^{i-1}]\Big)$$
* **Base Level ($i = 0$)**: An interval of length $2^0 = 1$ is just the array element itself:
  $$\text{st}[0][j] = A[j]$$
* **Table Dimensions**: For arrays up to $N \le 10^7$, choosing $K = 25$ ($2^{25} \approx 3.3 \times 10^7$) is sufficient.

#### Why Query Takes Strict $O(1)$ (The Idempotent Property)
For non-idempotent operations like summation ($+$), sub-intervals must be strictly disjoint to avoid double-counting. 
However, the minimum function $\min(x, y)$ is **idempotent**:
$$\min(x, x) = x$$
Processing an element twice does not alter the result in any way!

Given any query range $[L, R]$ of length $\text{len} = R - L + 1$:
1. Compute the largest power of two $k$ such that $2^k \le \text{len}$:
   $$k = \lfloor \log_2(R - L + 1) \rfloor$$
2. The entire interval $[L, R]$ is completely covered by two overlapping intervals of length $2^k$:
   * Left subsegment: $[L, \ L + 2^k - 1] \implies \text{st}[k][L]$
   * Right subsegment: $[R - 2^k + 1, \ R] \implies \text{st}[k][R - 2^k + 1]$
3. The minimum of the entire range is computed with a single evaluation:
   $$\min(A[L \dots R]) = \min\Big(\text{st}[k][L], \ \text{st}[k][R - 2^k + 1]\Big)$$
Because this involves only two table lookups and one `min()` call, **the query runs in absolute $O(1)$ time**.

#### Logarithm Precomputation & Cache-Friendly Memory Layout
Computing $\log_2$ on the fly using floating-point `log2()` is slow. We precompute an integer logarithm lookup table `lg[]` in $O(N)$ time:
```cpp
lg[1] = 0;
for (int i = 2; i <= n; i++) lg[i] = lg[i / 2] + 1;
```
Notice also that in `st[K + 1][n]`, the power-of-two level $K$ is the **first dimension** and array index $n$ is the **second dimension**. This layout ensures consecutive memory access along cache lines during level-wise precomputation and queries.
description: Precomputing power-of-two intervals for O(1) overlapping coverage (Binary Interval Decomposition with Idempotent Querying) — Time: O(N log N) Precomputation, O(1) Static RMQ Query.

title: Dijkstra on Sparse Graphs: Min-Heap Priority Queue in O((V + E) log V)
paradigm: Greedy Edge Relaxation with Priority Queue Extrema
coreConcept: Single-Source Shortest Paths (SSSP) on non-negative weighted graphs
timeComplexity: O((V + E) log V)
spaceComplexity: O(V + E) Adjacency Representation & Distance Arrays
theory:
#### Problem Definition & Limitations
Given a directed or undirected graph $G = (V, E)$ with non-negative edge weights $w(u, v) \ge 0$ and a source vertex $s$, we want to find the length of the shortest path from $s$ to all other vertices $v \in V$.

* **Why Dijkstra Requires Non-Negative Weights**: Dijkstra's algorithm relies on the **Greedy-Choice Property**: once a vertex with the minimum tentational distance is extracted from the frontier, its distance is finalized and will never decrease. Negative edges violate this monotonic non-decreasing distance invariant.

#### Algorithm Derivation: Dense vs. Sparse Graphs
The classical Dijkstra algorithm performs two primitive operations:
1. Finding the unmarked vertex with the smallest distance $d[v]$ ($V$ times).
2. Edge relaxation: updating $d[\text{to}] = \min(d[\text{to}], \ d[v] + w)$ ($E$ times).

* In a **dense graph** ($E \approx V^2$), an array scan finds the minimum in $O(V)$, yielding $O(V^2 + E) = O(V^2)$, which is asymptotically optimal.
* In a **sparse graph** ($E \ll V^2$), finding the minimum via array scanning is the bottleneck. We must use an auxiliary priority data structure to extract the minimum in $O(\log V)$.

#### Priority Queue Workaround (Simulating Decrease-Key)
A Fibonacci Heap achieves the theoretical lower bound $O(V \log V + E)$, but suffers from massive constant-factor overhead. Standard C++ `std::priority_queue` does not support an explicit `decrease_key` operation. 

Instead, we use a simple and fast CP technique:
1. When relaxing an edge to vertex `to`, we simply push a new pair $\{d[\text{to}], \text{to}\}$ into the priority queue.
2. When extracting a pair $\{d_v, v\}$ from the top, we inspect if $d_v > d[v]$. If it is greater, this entry is **stale** (a leftover duplicate superseded by a later, shorter path) and is discarded immediately:
   $$\text{if } (d_v \ne d[v]) \implies \text{continue}$$
3. Because at most $E$ edges are relaxed, there are at most $E$ pairs in the queue. Each operation takes $O(\log E) = O(\log V^2) = O(2 \log V) = O(\log V)$.

#### ASCII Architecture & Relaxation Walkthrough
```text
Source: Node 0, Initial: d[0] = 0, all other d[v] = INF

Pop (dist:0, node:0)
  Relax edge 0 -> 1 (w:4): d[1] = 4, push (4, 1)
  Relax edge 0 -> 2 (w:2): d[2] = 2, push (2, 2)
Queue: [(2, 2), (4, 1)]

Pop (dist:2, node:2)
  Relax edge 2 -> 1 (w:1): d[1] = 2 + 1 = 3 < 4!
  Update d[1] = 3, push (3, 1)
Queue: [(3, 1), (4, 1)]

Pop (dist:3, node:1):
  Valid! Finalize node 1 at distance 3.

Pop (dist:4, node:1):
  Stale check: d_v (4) != d[1] (3) -> Discarded immediately in O(1)!
```
description: Single-Source Shortest Paths (SSSP) on non-negative weighted graphs (Greedy Edge Relaxation with Priority Queue Extrema) — Time: O((V + E) log V).

title: Topological Sorting: Kahn's In-Degree BFS & DFS Post-Order in O(V + E)
paradigm: Dependency Resolution & Directed Acyclic Graph Linearization
coreConcept: Ordering vertices such that for every directed edge u -> v, u precedes v
timeComplexity: O(V + E) Strict Linear Time
spaceComplexity: O(V + E) Auxiliary Space
theory:
#### Problem Definition & Existence Condition
Given a directed graph $G = (V, E)$ with $V$ vertices and $E$ edges, a **topological sort** is a linear permutation of the vertices such that for every directed edge $(u, v) \in E$, vertex $u$ appears strictly before vertex $v$ in the ordering.

* **Condition of Existence**: A topological ordering exists **if and only if the directed graph contains no directed cycles** (i.e. it is a Directed Acyclic Graph, or **DAG**). If a cycle exists involving $a$ and $b$, $a$ must precede $b$ (since $b$ is reachable from $a$) and $b$ must precede $a$ (since $a$ is reachable from $b$), creating an impossible contradiction.
* **Non-Uniqueness**: A DAG may possess multiple valid topological orderings whenever vertices are mutually independent.

#### Method 1: Kahn's Algorithm (In-Degree BFS)
Kahn's algorithm simulates dependency resolution by processing vertices whose dependencies are completely satisfied:
1. Compute the **in-degree** ($\text{indegree}[v]$) for every vertex (number of incoming edges).
2. Push all vertices with $\text{indegree}[v] == 0$ into a standard BFS queue. These vertices have zero dependencies and can safely be placed first.
3. While the queue is not empty:
   * Pop vertex $u$ and append it to the topological order.
   * For each neighbor $v$ of $u$, simulate the removal of edge $(u, v)$ by decrementing $\text{indegree}[v]--$.
   * If $\text{indegree}[v]$ drops to $0$, all of $v$'s prerequisites have been resolved; push $v$ into the queue.
4. **Cycle Detection**: If the number of processed vertices in the topological order is strictly less than $V$, the graph contains at least one directed cycle!

#### Method 2: DFS with Exit Times (Post-Order Reversal)
Let's consider Depth-First Search on a DAG:
* When `dfs(v)` completes, all vertices reachable from $v$ have already been completely explored.
* Therefore, in a post-order traversal, if we record vertex $v$ upon exiting `dfs(v)`, every vertex reachable from $v$ appears **before** $v$ in this list.
* Reversing this exit-order list yields a valid topological order: vertices are arranged in descending order of their DFS exit times ($\text{tout}[v]$).
description: Ordering vertices such that for every directed edge u -> v, u precedes v (Dependency Resolution & Directed Acyclic Graph Linearization) — Time: O(V + E) Strict Linear Time.

title: 0-1 Breadth-First Search: Shortest Paths in O(V + E) using Deque
paradigm: Dial's Bucket Reduction with Double-Ended Queue
coreConcept: Optimal SSSP when edge weights are restricted to {0, 1}
timeComplexity: O(V + E) Strict Linear Time (Faster than Dijkstra's O((V+E)logV))
spaceComplexity: O(V + E) Auxiliary Memory
theory:
#### Problem Definition & Limitations
Given a directed or undirected graph where **every edge weight is either $0$ or $1$**, compute the shortest path from a starting source vertex $s$ to all other vertices.
* Running standard Dijkstra takes $O(E \log V)$ time.
* Running unweighted BFS fails because $0$-weight edges do not advance traversal level.
* **0-1 BFS** achieves optimal **$O(V + E)$ linear time** using a `std::deque`.

#### The Bounded Distance Property
Consider Dijkstra's priority queue $Q$ when edge weights are restricted to $\{0, 1\}$.
Suppose we extract vertex $v$ with distance $d[v]$. When relaxing an outgoing edge $(v, u, w)$ with $w \in \{0, 1\}$:
$$d[u] = d[v] + w \in \{d[v], \ d[v] + 1\}$$
Consequently, at any moment in time, the frontier of vertices under exploration can differ by **at most 1**:
$$\forall u \in Q, \quad d[v] \le d[u] \le d[v] + 1$$
The queue structure is simply:
$$Q = \underbrace{x_1, x_2, \dots, x_k}_{\text{distance } d[v]}, \quad \underbrace{y_1, y_2, \dots, y_m}_{\text{distance } d[v] + 1}$$

#### Deque Operational Invariant
Because there are only two consecutive distance levels present at any time, we do not need a heap!
* When an edge has weight $w = 0$: the destination vertex $u$ is at distance $d[v] + 0 = d[v]$. It belongs to the current distance level, so we insert it at the **front** of the deque: `dq.push_front(u)`.
* When an edge has weight $w = 1$: the destination vertex $u$ is at distance $d[v] + 1$. It belongs to the next distance level, so we insert it at the **back** of the deque: `dq.push_back(u)`.

Because elements are popped from the front and smaller distance elements ($w=0$) are immediately re-injected at the front, vertices are extracted in **strictly non-decreasing order of distance**. This preserves Dijkstra's greedy invariant without logarithmic overhead.
description: Optimal SSSP when edge weights are restricted to {0, 1} (Dial's Bucket Reduction with Double-Ended Queue) — Time: O(V + E) Strict Linear Time (Faster than Dijkstra's O((V+E)logV)).

title: Cycle Detection & Extraction in O(V + E) using 3-Color DFS
paradigm: Depth-First Search State Classification & Ancestor Back-Edge Tracking
coreConcept: 3-Coloring (White/Gray/Black) for directed; parent tracking for undirected
timeComplexity: O(V + E) Linear Time
spaceComplexity: O(V + E) Auxiliary Space
theory:
#### Problem Definition
Given a graph $G = (V, E)$, check whether it is acyclic. If a cycle exists, extract the exact sequence of vertices that form the cycle.

#### Directed Graphs: The 3-Color DFS Algorithm
In directed graphs, an edge to an already-visited vertex does not necessarily imply a cycle (it could be a forward-edge or cross-edge). We categorize vertices into three states:
* **Color 0 (White)**: Unvisited vertex.
* **Color 1 (Gray)**: Currently inside the active DFS recursion call stack (an active ancestor).
* **Color 2 (Black)**: Fully visited vertex; its entire subtree has been explored and exited.

**The Cycle Invariant**:
A directed cycle exists **if and only if DFS encounters an edge $(u, v)$ where vertex $v$ is Gray (Color 1)**. 
Because $v$ is Gray, $v$ is an active ancestor of $u$ in the DFS tree. The edge $(u, v)$ is a **back-edge**, completing a directed cycle from $v \rightsquigarrow u \to v$.

#### Cycle Reconstruction
When a back-edge from $u$ to gray node $v$ is found:
1. Mark `cycle_start = v` and `cycle_end = u`.
2. Terminate the DFS search.
3. Trace backwards using the `parent` array from `cycle_end` up to `cycle_start`:
   $$u, \ \text{parent}[u], \ \text{parent}[\text{parent}[u]], \ \dots, \ v$$
4. Reverse the list to output the cycle in forward traversal order.

#### Undirected Graphs: Direct Parent Exclusion
In undirected graphs, an edge connects bidirectionally. When exploring from $u$ to $v$, we must ignore the trivial edge leading back to the immediate parent $p$. If we encounter any visited vertex $v \ne p$, a cycle is confirmed.
description: 3-Coloring (White/Gray/Black) for directed; parent tracking for undirected (Depth-First Search State Classification & Ancestor Back-Edge Tracking) — Time: O(V + E) Linear Time.

title: Bipartite Graph Verification: 2-Coloring via BFS in O(V + E)
coreConcept: A graph is bipartite if and only if it contains no odd cycles
timeComplexity: O(V + E) Linear Time
spaceComplexity: O(V) Partition Color Array
theory:
#### Problem Definition & Theorem
A graph is **bipartite** if its vertex set $V$ can be partitioned into two disjoint subsets $L$ and $R$ such that every edge connects a vertex in $L$ to a vertex in $R$. No edge may exist between vertices in the same set.

* **Fundamental Theorem**: An undirected graph is bipartite **if and only if it contains no cycles of odd length**.
* **Equivalent Formulation (2-Colorability)**: A graph is bipartite if and only if it can be colored using two colors ($\{0, 1\}$) such that no two adjacent vertices share the same color.

#### Breadth-First Search 2-Coloring Algorithm
We test 2-colorability using BFS across all connected components:
1. Initialize an array `color` of size $V$ with $-1$ (unvisited).
2. For every unvisited vertex $i \in [0, V-1]$:
   * Assign `color[i] = 0` and push $i$ into a BFS queue.
   * While the queue is not empty:
     * Pop vertex $v$.
     * For each neighbor $u$ of $v$:
       * If $u$ is uncolored (`color[u] == -1`):
         Assign $u$ the complementary color:
         $$\text{color}[u] = \text{color}[v] \oplus 1$$
         Push $u$ into the queue.
       * If $u$ is already colored and $\text{color}[u] == \text{color}[v]$:
         **A monochromatic edge exists!** This confirms an odd cycle, meaning the graph is **not bipartite**.
description: A graph is bipartite if and only if it contains no odd cycles (Parity Partitioning & Odd-Cycle Detection) — Time: O(V + E) Linear Time.

title: Lowest Common Ancestor (LCA): Binary Lifting in O(log N)
paradigm: Binary Exponentiation on Tree Hierarchies & Euler Tour Invariance
coreConcept: Precomputing 2^k ancestors with DFS entry/exit time ancestor tests
timeComplexity: O(N log N) Preprocessing, O(log N) per LCA Query
spaceComplexity: O(N log N) Precomputed Binary Table
theory:
#### Problem Definition
Given a rooted tree with $N$ vertices, the **Lowest Common Ancestor (LCA)** of two vertices $u$ and $v$ is the deepest node $w$ that is an ancestor of both $u$ and $v$.

#### Binary Lifting Concept
Instead of climbing parent pointers one step at a time (taking $O(N)$ worst-case time), binary lifting precomputes ancestors at powers-of-two depths ($2^0, 2^1, 2^2, \dots, 2^{\lfloor \log_2 N \rfloor}$).
Let `up[v][k]` denote the $2^k$-th ancestor of vertex $v$:
* Base Case ($k = 0$): $\text{up}[v][0] = \text{parent}[v]$.
* Inductive Step ($k > 0$):
  $$\text{up}[v][k] = \text{up}\big[\text{up}[v][k-1]\big][k-1]$$
  To jump $2^k$ steps above $v$, jump $2^{k-1}$ steps to node $x$, then jump $2^{k-1}$ steps from $x$.

#### Fast $O(1)$ Ancestor Test via Euler Tour Times
During the initial DFS, we record two timestamps:
* `tin[v]`: Time of entry into node $v$.
* `tout[v]`: Time of exit from node $v$ after exploring all descendants.

A node $u$ is an ancestor of node $v$ **if and only if** the exploration interval of $v$ is entirely nested within the exploration interval of $u$:
$$\text{is\_ancestor}(u, v) \iff \text{tin}[u] \le \text{tin}[v] \quad \text{and} \quad \text{tout}[u] \ge \text{tout}[v]$$
This test executes in strictly $O(1)$ constant time!

#### Answering an LCA Query in $O(\log N)$
Given query $(u, v)$:
1. If $\text{is\_ancestor}(u, v)$ is true, $u$ is the LCA.
2. If $\text{is\_ancestor}(v, u)$ is true, $v$ is the LCA.
3. Otherwise, we iterate $k$ downwards from $L = \lceil \log_2 N \rceil$ to $0$:
   * If $\text{up}[u][k]$ is **not** an ancestor of $v$, we can safely jump: $u = \text{up}[u][k]$.
   * If $\text{up}[u][k]$ is an ancestor of $v$, we do not jump (a jump might overshoot past the LCA).
4. After testing all powers of two, $u$ is positioned just below the LCA. Therefore:
   $$\text{LCA}(u, v) = \text{up}[u][0]$$
description: Precomputing 2^k ancestors with DFS entry/exit time ancestor tests (Binary Exponentiation on Tree Hierarchies & Euler Tour Invariance) — Time: O(N log N) Preprocessing, O(log N) per LCA Query.

title: Bridges & Articulation Points: Tarjan's Single-Pass DFS in O(V + E)
paradigm: DFS Tree Low-Link Values & Discovery Time Invariants
coreConcept: Identifying critical edges and vertices whose removal disconnects the graph
timeComplexity: O(V + E) Single-Pass DFS
spaceComplexity: O(V + E) Adjacency & Discovery Arrays
theory:
#### Definitions
In an undirected connected graph:
* **Bridge**: An edge whose removal strictly increases the number of connected components.
* **Articulation Point (Cutpoint)**: A vertex whose removal (along with its incident edges) strictly increases the number of connected components.

#### Low-Link Invariant ($\text{low}[v]$)
Run DFS from an arbitrary root. DFS partitions edges into two categories:
* **Tree Edges**: Edges leading to unvisited vertices during DFS traversal.
* **Back Edges**: Edges connecting a vertex to one of its ancestors in the DFS tree. (No cross edges exist in undirected graphs!).

Let $\text{tin}[v]$ be the discovery time of vertex $v$. We define $\text{low}[v]$ as the earliest discovery time reachable from $v$ or its subtree via at most one back-edge:
$$\text{low}[v] = \min \begin{cases}
\text{tin}[v] \\
\text{tin}[p], & \text{for all back-edges } (v, p) \\
\text{low}[\text{to}], & \text{for all tree-edges } (v, \text{to})
\end{cases}$$

#### Bridge Condition
A tree-edge $(v, \text{to})$ is a bridge **if and only if**:
$$\text{low}[\text{to}] > \text{tin}[v]$$
* **Intuition**: If $\text{low}[\text{to}] \le \text{tin}[v]$, there exists a back-edge from the subtree of $\text{to}$ to $v$ or an ancestor of $v$. Thus, there is an alternate path, and removing $(v, \text{to})$ will not disconnect the graph.
* If $\text{low}[\text{to}] > \text{tin}[v]$, no alternative path exists back to $v$ or above; hence $(v, \text{to})$ is a bridge.

#### Articulation Point Conditions
A vertex $v$ is an articulation point if:
1. **Non-Root Vertex**: $v$ has a child $\text{to}$ in the DFS tree such that:
   $$\text{low}[\text{to}] \ge \text{tin}[v]$$
   (Descendants of $\text{to}$ cannot bypass $v$ to reach ancestors of $v$).
2. **Root Vertex**: The root of the DFS tree is an articulation point **if and only if it has $> 1$ children in the DFS tree**.
description: Identifying critical edges and vertices whose removal disconnects the graph (DFS Tree Low-Link Values & Discovery Time Invariants) — Time: O(V + E) Single-Pass DFS.

title: Minimum Spanning Tree (MST): Kruskal with DSU in O(E log E)
paradigm: Greedy Edge Selection with Disjoint Set Equivalence
coreConcept: Optimal subtree merging using path-compressed Union-Find
timeComplexity: O(E log E) Edge Sorting + O(E alpha(V)) DSU Operations
spaceComplexity: O(V + E) Edge List & DSU Disjoint Forest
theory:
#### Problem Definition
Given a connected, undirected, weighted graph $G = (V, E)$, a **Spanning Tree** is a subgraph that is a tree and connects all $V$ vertices using exactly $V - 1$ edges. The **Minimum Spanning Tree (MST)** is the spanning tree that minimizes the total sum of edge weights:
$$\min \sum_{e \in T} w(e)$$

#### The Cut Property
For any cut in the graph (a partition of $V$ into two sets $S$ and $V \setminus S$), if an edge $e$ crossing the cut has the strictly minimal weight among all crossing edges, then this edge **must belong to the Minimum Spanning Tree**.

#### Kruskal's Greedy Algorithm
Kruskal's algorithm applies the cut property globally by sorting all edges by weight:
1. Sort all $E$ edges in non-decreasing order of weight: $w(e_1) \le w(e_2) \le \dots \le w(e_m)$.
2. Initialize a Disjoint Set Union (DSU) structure where each vertex $v \in V$ is in its own independent set (`make_set(v)`).
3. Iterate through each edge $e = (u, v, w)$ in sorted order:
   * Test if $u$ and $v$ belong to different sets using `find_set(u) != find_set(v)`.
   * If they belong to different sets: adding this edge will **not create a cycle**. Add $e$ to the MST and merge their components using `union_sets(u, v)`.
   * If they belong to the same set: adding this edge would create a redundant cycle; discard it.
4. Stop when $V - 1$ edges have been added (or after scanning all edges).

#### Complexity Analysis
* Sorting $E$ edges takes $O(E \log E)$ time.
* For each edge, DSU operations `find_set` and `union_sets` take nearly constant $O(\alpha(V))$ amortized time.
* Total Time: $O(E \log E + E \alpha(V)) = O(E \log E)$. Since $E \le V^2$, $\log E = O(\log V)$.
description: Optimal subtree merging using path-compressed Union-Find (Greedy Edge Selection with Disjoint Set Equivalence) — Time: O(E log E) Edge Sorting + O(E alpha(V)) DSU Operations.

title: Bellman-Ford & Negative Cycle Extraction in O(V * E)
paradigm: Iterative Dynamic Edge Relaxation & Negative Cycle Discovery
coreConcept: Single-source shortest path with negative edges and cycle recovery
timeComplexity: O(V * E)
spaceComplexity: O(V + E) Flat Edge List
theory:
#### Problem Definition
Given a directed weighted graph $G = (V, E)$ which may contain **negative weight edges**, find shortest paths from source $s$, or detect and extract a **negative weight cycle** (a cycle whose total sum of edge weights is strictly $< 0$).

#### Why V - 1 Phases Suffice
In any graph without negative weight cycles, any simple shortest path visits each vertex at most once, and therefore contains at most $V - 1$ edges.
* Phase 1 calculates shortest paths using at most 1 edge.
* Phase 2 calculates shortest paths using at most 2 edges.
* Phase $k$ calculates shortest paths using at most $k$ edges.
After $V - 1$ phases, all shortest paths must be completely finalized!

#### Detecting Negative Cycles
If we run a $V$-th phase and **any edge $(u, v)$ can still be relaxed**:
$$d[u] + w < d[v]$$
then a negative weight cycle exists! A negative cycle allows unbounded relaxation towards $-\infty$.

#### Extracting the Negative Cycle
To recover the actual sequence of vertices forming the cycle:
1. When a vertex $x$ is relaxed on the $V$-th pass, $x$ is either inside a negative cycle or reachable from one.
2. To ensure we are inside the cycle, pass to predecessors $V$ times:
   $$\text{for } i \in [0, V-1]: \quad x = \text{parent}[x]$$
   Because a cycle length is at most $V$, stepping back $V$ times is guaranteed to place $x$ strictly inside the cycle!
3. Collect vertices by stepping backwards from $x$ through `parent` until returning to $x$.
4. Reverse the list to output the cycle in forward directed order.
description: Single-source shortest path with negative edges and cycle recovery (Iterative Dynamic Edge Relaxation & Negative Cycle Discovery) — Time: O(V * E).

title: Floyd-Warshall: All-Pairs Shortest Paths (APSP) in O(V^3)
paradigm: Dynamic Programming over Intermediate Vertex Sets
coreConcept: Optimal pairwise distance matrix updating and path reconstruction
timeComplexity: O(V^3) Strictly Nested Triple Loop
spaceComplexity: O(V^2) Distance & Predecessor Matrices
theory:
#### Problem Definition
Given a weighted directed or undirected graph with $V$ vertices, compute the length of the shortest path between **every pair of vertices** $(i, j)$. The graph may contain negative weight edges, but no negative cycles.

#### Dynamic Programming Formulation
Let $d^{(k)}[i][j]$ denote the length of the shortest path from vertex $i$ to vertex $j$ such that all intermediate vertices in the path belong strictly to the prefix set $\{0, 1, \dots, k-1\}$.

* **Base Case ($k = 0$)**:
  No intermediate vertices are permitted.
  $$d^{(0)}[i][j] = \begin{cases} 
  0, & \text{if } i = j \\ 
  w(i, j), & \text{if edge } (i, j) \in E \\ 
  \infty, & \text{otherwise} 
  \end{cases}$$
* **Transition Step ($k \to k + 1$)**:
  When allowing vertex $k$ to serve as an intermediate vertex, the shortest path between $i$ and $j$ either:
  1. Does not pass through $k$ (length is $d^{(k-1)}[i][j]$).
  2. Passes through $k$ (decomposed into path $i \rightsquigarrow k$ and $k \rightsquigarrow j$, both using intermediate vertices from $\{0, \dots, k-1\}$).
