  $$d^{(k)}[i][j] = \min\Big(d^{(k-1)}[i][j], \ d^{(k-1)}[i][k] + d^{(k-1)}[k][j]\Big)$$

#### Memory Compression & Negative Cycle Check
Because $d^{(k)}[i][k] = d^{(k-1)}[i][k]$ and $d^{(k)}[k][j] = d^{(k-1)}[k][j]$, the DP transitions can be performed **completely in-place** on a single 2D matrix $d[i][j]$ without storing historical copies.

* **Negative Cycle Detection**: A negative cycle exists if and only if any vertex has a negative distance to itself after execution:
  $$\exists v \in V \text{ such that } d[v][v] < 0$$
description: Optimal pairwise distance matrix updating and path reconstruction (Dynamic Programming over Intermediate Vertex Sets) — Time: O(V^3) Strictly Nested Triple Loop.

title: 0-1 Knapsack: 1D Space Optimization & Reconstruction in O(N * W)
coreConcept: Optimal substructure with backward 1D array state rolling
timeComplexity: O(N * W) Time
spaceComplexity: O(W) Auxiliary Space for 1D Rolling Array; O(N * W) for Reconstruction
theory:
#### Problem Definition & Motivation
We are given $N$ distinct items and a knapsack with a maximum capacity $W$. Each item $i$ ($1 \le i \le N$) has two positive integer attributes:
* Weight: $w_i$
* Value: $v_i$

Each item can either be **taken (1)** or **not taken (0)**. We must select a subset of items such that the total weight does not exceed the capacity $W$, while maximizing the total accumulated value:
$$\max \sum_{i=1}^N v_i \cdot x_i \quad \text{subject to} \quad \sum_{i=1}^N w_i \cdot x_i \le W, \quad x_i \in \{0, 1\}$$

#### 2D Dynamic Programming Formulation
Let $f(i, j)$ denote the maximum value obtainable using a subset of the first $i$ items with a knapsack capacity of exactly $j$:
1. **Item $i$ is NOT taken**: The capacity remains $j$ and the value is inherited from the first $i - 1$ items:
   $$f(i - 1, j)$$
2. **Item $i$ IS taken** (valid only if $j \ge w_i$): The remaining capacity decreases to $j - w_i$, and the value increases by $v_i$:
   $$f(i - 1, j - w_i) + v_i$$

Combining both choices gives Bellman's principle of optimality:
$$f(i, j) = \max\Big(f(i - 1, j), \ f(i - 1, j - w_i) + v_i\Big)$$
* **Base Case**: $f(0, j) = 0$ for all $0 \le j \le W$.
* Evaluating this 2D table directly takes $O(N \cdot W)$ time and $O(N \cdot W)$ memory.

#### 1D Space Compression: The Crucial Backward Iteration Invariant
Notice that $f(i, j)$ depends solely on the previous row $f(i - 1, \star)$. Therefore, we can compress the 2D table into a single 1D array $dp[j]$ of size $W + 1$.

However, to ensure that each item is used **at most once**, the inner capacity loop $j$ **MUST iterate in strictly decreasing order** from $W$ down to $w_i$:
$$dp[j] \gets \max\big(dp[j], \ dp[j - w_i] + v_i\big)$$

**Why Decreasing Order?**
* When computing $dp[j]$ for a given $j$, $dp[j - w_i]$ has **not yet been updated** in the current iteration $i$.
* Therefore, $dp[j - w_i]$ still holds the value from the previous step ($i - 1$).
* If we iterated forward in increasing order ($j = w_i \dots W$), $dp[j - w_i]$ would have already incorporated item $i$, allowing item $i$ to be picked multiple times!

#### Item Reconstruction Mechanics
To output the exact subset of items that yielded the maximum value:
* Maintain the full 2D decision matrix or parent pointers.
* Trace backwards from state $(N, W)$:
  $$\text{If } f(i, W) \ne f(i - 1, W) \implies \text{Item } i \text{ was selected! Decrement } W \gets W - w_i$$
  $$\text{If } f(i, W) == f(i - 1, W) \implies \text{Item } i \text{ was bypassed.}$$
description: Optimal substructure with backward 1D array state rolling (Subset Selection with Capacity Constraints) — Time: O(N * W) Time.

title: Unbounded (Complete) Knapsack: Forward 1D DP in O(N * W)
coreConcept: Optimal substructure with forward 1D array reuse
timeComplexity: O(N * W)
spaceComplexity: O(W) 1D Auxiliary Array
theory:
#### Problem Definition
The **Unbounded (or Complete) Knapsack** problem has identical inputs to 0-1 Knapsack ($N$ items, weights $w_i$, values $v_i$, and capacity $W$). However, each item may be selected an **unlimited number of times**:
$$\max \sum_{i=1}^N v_i \cdot k_i \quad \text{subject to} \quad \sum_{i=1}^N w_i \cdot k_i \le W, \quad k_i \in \{0, 1, 2, \dots\}$$

#### Naive Multiplicity Enumeration ($O(N \cdot W^2)$)
A naive approach enumerates $k$ copies of item $i$:
$$f(i, j) = \max_{0 \le k \le \lfloor j / w_i \rfloor} \Big(f(i - 1, \ j - k \cdot w_i) + k \cdot v_i\Big)$$
This introduces an extra loop over $k$, degrading the time complexity to $O(N \cdot W^2)$.

#### The Forward 1D Optimization ($O(N \cdot W)$)
Notice the structural relationship between selecting $k$ items and selecting $k - 1$ items:
$$f(i, j) = \max\Big(f(i - 1, j), \ f(i, j - w_i) + v_i\Big)$$
Notice the second term references $f(i, \dots)$ rather than $f(i - 1, \dots)$!
* In 0-1 Knapsack: adding item $i$ transitions from the $(i - 1)$-th step.
* In Unbounded Knapsack: adding item $i$ transitions from the **$i$-th step itself**, allowing the same item $i$ to be picked repeatedly!

Therefore, we can use the **exact same 1D array** as 0-1 Knapsack, with one critical change:
The capacity loop $j$ **MUST iterate in forward, increasing order** from $w_i$ up to $W$:
$$dp[j] \gets \max\big(dp[j], \ dp[j - w_i] + v_i\big)$$

Because $j$ increases, $dp[j - w_i]$ reflects updates made in the current step $i$, naturally compounding multiple copies of item $i$ without any extra loop!

#### Visual Comparison: 0-1 vs. Unbounded Knapsack Loop Direction
```text
0-1 Knapsack (Each item <= 1 time):
j: W ------> w_i (Decreasing)
dp[j - w_i] is from step (i - 1). Item i cannot be duplicated.

Unbounded Knapsack (Each item infinite times):
j: w_i ------> W (Increasing)
dp[j - w_i] is from step i. Item i can be reused arbitrarily many times!
```
description: Optimal substructure with forward 1D array reuse (Unbounded Item Multiplicity Selection) — Time: O(N * W).

title: Longest Increasing Subsequence (LIS): Patience Sorting in O(N log N)
paradigm: Monotonic Frontier Maintenance with Binary Search (Patience Sorting)
coreConcept: Tracking minimal tail values for each subsequence length
timeComplexity: O(N log N) Strict Time
spaceComplexity: O(N) Auxiliary Space
theory:
#### Problem Definition
Given an array $A$ of $N$ numbers $a[0 \dots N - 1]$, find the length and elements of the longest strictly increasing subsequence:
$$i_1 < i_2 < \dots < i_k \quad \text{such that} \quad a[i_1] < a[i_2] < \dots < a[i_k]$$

#### Classical $O(N^2)$ Dynamic Programming
Let $d[i]$ be the length of the longest increasing subsequence ending at element $a[i]$:
$$d[i] = 1 + \max_{\substack{j < i \\ a[j] < a[i]}} d[j]$$
Evaluating this requires scanning all $j < i$, taking $O(N^2)$ time. For $N \ge 10^5$, $N^2 = 10^{10}$, causing Time Limit Exceeded (TLE).

#### The $O(N \log N)$ Patience Sorting State Formulation
To break the quadratic barrier, we redefine our dynamic programming state:
Let $tails[l]$ denote the **smallest tail element** of any valid increasing subsequence of length $l$ found so far.

**Key Invariant**:
The array $tails$ is **strictly increasing**:
$$tails[1] < tails[2] < tails[3] < \dots < tails[k]$$
* **Proof by Contradiction**: If $tails[l] \ge tails[l + 1]$, then an increasing subsequence of length $l + 1$ ends with a value smaller than or equal to $tails[l]$. Dropping the last element from that subsequence produces an increasing subsequence of length $l$ whose tail is strictly smaller than $tails[l]$, contradicting the minimality of $tails[l]$.

#### Binary Search Progression (`std::lower_bound`)
For each element $x$ in the array $A$:
1. We want to find the largest length $l$ such that $tails[l] < x$.
2. This means $x$ can extend this subsequence to length $l + 1$.
3. Since $tails$ is sorted, we can locate the first element in $tails$ that is $\ge x$ using binary search (`std::lower_bound`):
   $$\text{idx} = \text{lower\_bound}(tails, \ x)$$
4. If $\text{idx}$ is at the end of $tails$: $x$ is strictly greater than all current tails, so we append $x$: $tails.\text{push\_back}(x)$.
5. If $\text{idx}$ is within $tails$: $x$ can replace $tails[\text{idx}]$, establishing a smaller, more optimal tail for subsequences of length $\text{idx} + 1$.

#### Full Subsequence Reconstruction in $O(N \log N)$
To reconstruct the actual subsequence:
* Maintain `parent[i]`: index of the previous element in the optimal subsequence ending at index $i$.
* Maintain `tails_indices[l]`: array index of the current tail for length $l$.
* Whenever $x = a[i]$ updates or extends length $l$, set:
  $$\text{parent}[i] = \text{tails\_indices}[l - 1]$$
  $$\text{tails\_indices}[l] = i$$
* After the pass, trace backwards from $\text{tails\_indices}[\text{LIS\_length}]$ using `parent` pointers.
description: Tracking minimal tail values for each subsequence length (Monotonic Frontier Maintenance with Binary Search (Patience Sorting)) — Time: O(N log N) Strict Time.

title: Largest Zero/One Submatrix: Dynamic Histogram & Monotonic Stack in O(N * M)
paradigm: 2D Grid Column Heights with Monotonic Stack Histogram Reduction
coreConcept: Converting 2D binary grid rows into contiguous maximal rectangles
timeComplexity: O(N * M) Strict Linear Time
spaceComplexity: O(M) Auxiliary Space
theory:
#### Problem Definition
Given a 2D binary matrix $A$ of dimensions $N \times M$ containing only $0$s and $1$s, find the maximum area of a rectangular submatrix consisting entirely of $0$s (or entirely of $1$s).

#### Reduction to 1D Histogram Problem
A naive search checks all $O(N^2 \cdot M^2)$ submatrices. 
We can reduce the 2D problem to $N$ independent **Largest Rectangle in Histogram** subproblems:
1. Process the matrix row by row from top to bottom ($i = 0 \dots N - 1$).
2. For each column $j$, maintain an auxiliary array $h[j]$ representing the height of contiguous zeros ending at cell $(i, j)$:
   $$h[j] = \begin{cases} h[j] + 1, & \text{if } A[i][j] == 0 \\ 0, & \text{if } A[i][j] == 1 \end{cases}$$
3. For row $i$, the array $h[0 \dots M - 1]$ defines a histogram of bar heights! The largest zero submatrix with its bottom edge on row $i$ is exactly the largest rectangle under this histogram.

#### Monotonic Stack Solution in $O(M)$ per Row
To find the largest rectangle in histogram $h$ in $O(M)$ time:
For each bar $j$ with height $h[j]$:
* We want to find the nearest column to the left $L[j]$ such that $h[L[j]] < h[j]$.
* We want to find the nearest column to the right $R[j]$ such that $h[R[j]] < h[j]$.
* The rectangle with height $h[j]$ spans from column $L[j] + 1$ to $R[j] - 1$:
  $$\text{width} = R[j] - L[j] - 1$$
  $$\text{area} = h[j] \times (R[j] - L[j] - 1)$$

We can determine $L[j]$ and $R[j]$ for all $j$ in a single linear pass using a **Monotonic Increasing Stack**:
* Push column indices onto the stack such that heights remain non-decreasing.
* When popping an index $k$ because the current height $h[j] < h[k]$:
  * The right boundary for bar $k$ is the current index $j$: $R[k] = j$.
  * The left boundary for bar $k$ is the index directly below it on the stack!
  * Compute area immediately: $h[k] \times (j - \text{st.top}() - 1)$.

Because each column index is pushed and popped at most once per row, processing row $i$ takes strictly $O(M)$ time.
$$\text{Total Time} = N \times O(M) = O(N \cdot M)$$
description: Converting 2D binary grid rows into contiguous maximal rectangles (2D Grid Column Heights with Monotonic Stack Histogram Reduction) — Time: O(N * M) Strict Linear Time.

title: Divide and Conquer DP Optimization in O(M * N log N)
coreConcept: Speeding up 2D DP from O(M * N^2) to O(M * N log N) via Quadrangle Inequality
timeComplexity: O(M * N log N)
spaceComplexity: O(N) Rolling Array State
theory:
#### Problem Preconditions & Recurrence Form
Consider dynamic programming recurrences of the standard partitioning form:
$$dp(i, j) = \min_{0 \le k \le j} \Big(dp(i - 1, k - 1) + C(k, j)\Big)$$
where:
* $i$ represents the number of partitions / stages ($1 \le i \le M$).
* $j$ represents the prefix boundary of elements ($1 \le j \le N$).
* $C(k, j)$ is a cost function evaluated in $O(1)$ time.

**Naive Complexity**:
There are $M \times N$ states. Each state iterates $k$ from $0$ to $j$, taking $O(N)$ transitions $\implies O(M \cdot N^2)$ total time. For $N = 10^5$, $N^2 = 10^{10}$, which is far too slow!

#### The Monotonicity Condition & The Quadrangle Inequality
Let $opt(i, j)$ be the optimal splitting point $k$ that minimizes the recurrence for state $(i, j)$:
$$opt(i, j) = \arg\min_{0 \le k \le j} \Big(dp(i - 1, k - 1) + C(k, j)\Big)$$

If the cost function $C(k, j)$ satisfies the **Quadrangle Inequality (QI)**:
$$\forall a \le b \le c \le d, \quad C(a, c) + C(b, d) \le C(a, d) + C(b, c)$$
then the optimal splitting points satisfy the **Monotonicity Condition**:
$$opt(i, j) \le opt(i, j + 1)$$
This means as the prefix $j$ increases, the optimal transition point $opt(i, j)$ **never moves backwards**!

#### Divide and Conquer Recursive Acceleration
Instead of computing states sequentially, we compute a whole row of states $dp(i, \star)$ using divide and conquer:
1. To compute the answers for $j \in [L, R]$ with search range for optimal $k \in [opt_L, opt_R]$:
2. Pick the midpoint $mid = \lfloor (L + R) / 2 \rfloor$.
3. Compute $dp(i, mid)$ by testing all $k \in [opt_L, \min(mid, opt_R)]$, recording the optimal point $opt_{mid}$.
4. Because of monotonicity:
   * For all $j < mid$, its optimal splitting point must lie in $[opt_L, opt_{mid}]$.
   * For all $j > mid$, its optimal splitting point must lie in $[opt_{mid}, opt_R]$.
5. Recursively solve for the left half $[L, mid - 1]$ and right half $[mid + 1, R]$!

#### Complexity Proof ($O(M \cdot N \log N)$)
* At each recursion level of the divide and conquer, the search intervals $[opt_L, opt_R]$ partition the range $[0, N]$. Across all nodes at depth $d$, the total number of tested candidates $k$ is bounded by $O(N)$.
* The recursion tree has depth $\lceil \log_2 N \rceil$.
* Thus, computing one full partition row $i$ takes $O(N \log N)$ time.
* Across all $M$ partitions, the total runtime is strictly:
$$\text{Total Time} = O(M \cdot N \log N)$$
description: Speeding up 2D DP from O(M * N^2) to O(M * N log N) via Quadrangle Inequality (Optimal Splitting Point Monotonicity Speedup) — Time: O(M * N log N).

title: Knuth's Optimization: Knuth-Yao Range DP Speedup in O(N^2)
paradigm: Range Dynamic Programming Splitting Bound Narrowing
coreConcept: Reducing interval DP from O(N^3) to O(N^2) via dual optimal point bounding
timeComplexity: O(N^2) Strictly Quadratic Time (Linear Factor Speedup over O(N^3))
spaceComplexity: O(N^2) Matrix Space
theory:
#### Problem Definition & Range DP Form
Knuth's Optimization (also known as the **Knuth-Yao Speedup**) applies to Range Dynamic Programming problems with interval transitions of the form:
$$dp(i, j) = \min_{i \le k < j} \Big(dp(i, k) + dp(k + 1, j) + C(i, j)\Big)$$
where $dp(i, j)$ is the optimal cost for the interval $[i, j]$ and $C(i, j)$ is an interval cost function.
* **Standard Evaluation**: There are $O(N^2)$ intervals $[i, j]$. For each interval, $k$ ranges from $i$ to $j - 1$ ($O(N)$ candidates) $\implies O(N^3)$ total time.

#### Preconditions for Knuth's Optimization
Let $opt(i, j)$ denote the optimal splitting index $k$ that minimizes the transition for interval $[i, j]$.
Knuth's optimization applies if the cost function $C(i, j)$ satisfies two conditions for all $a \le b \le c \le d$:
1. **Monotonicity**: $C(b, c) \le C(a, d)$ (smaller sub-intervals have smaller costs).
2. **Quadrangle Inequality (QI)**:
   $$C(a, c) + C(b, d) \le C(a, d) + C(b, c)$$

When these hold, Donald Knuth and Andrew Yao proved the fundamental **Splitting Point Bounding Inequality**:
$$opt(i, \ j - 1) \le opt(i, j) \le opt(i + 1, \ j)$$

#### The $O(N^2)$ Speedup Algorithm
Instead of searching all $k \in [i, j - 1]$, we restrict our search **strictly between the optimal splitting point of the one-smaller subsegment to the left and the one-smaller subsegment to the right**:
$$k \in \big[opt(i, \ j - 1), \ opt(i + 1, \ j)\big]$$

#### Telescoping Sum Complexity Proof ($O(N^2)$)
To compute all intervals of length $L = j - i + 1$:
The work done for all $i$ is proportional to:
$$\sum_{i=0}^{N - L} \Big(opt(i + 1, \ i + L - 1) - opt(i, \ i + L - 2) + 1\Big)$$
Notice that this sum **telescopes**!
All intermediate terms cancel out:
$$\big(opt(N - L + 1, \ N) - opt(0, \ L - 2)\big) + (N - L) \le N + N = O(N)$$
Thus, processing all intervals of a fixed length $L$ takes only $O(N)$ work in total!
Summing across all $N$ lengths gives:
$$\text{Total Time} = \sum_{L=1}^N O(N) = O(N^2)$$
This eliminates an entire factor of $N$, speeding up execution from $O(N^3)$ to $O(N^2)$!
description: Reducing interval DP from O(N^3) to O(N^2) via dual optimal point bounding (Range Dynamic Programming Splitting Bound Narrowing) — Time: O(N^2) Strictly Quadratic Time (Linear Factor Speedup over O(N^3)).

title: Prefix Function & Knuth-Morris-Pratt (KMP): Linear String Matching in O(N + M)
paradigm: Automaton-Like State Fallback via Proper Prefix-Suffix Boundaries
coreConcept: Linear pi-array precomputation avoiding redundant character comparisons
timeComplexity: O(N + M) Total Time (Strict Linear Bound)
spaceComplexity: O(N) Auxiliary Memory for pi-array
theory:
#### Problem Definition & Motivation
Given a text $T$ of length $M$ and a pattern $P$ of length $N$, find all index positions where $P$ occurs as a contiguous substring in $T$.

* **Naive Approach**: Scanning from each position in $T$ takes $O(N \cdot M)$ worst-case time (e.g., matching $P = \text{"aaaab"}$ in $T = \text{"aaaaaaaaaaaaa"}$).
* **KMP Goal**: Avoid ever backtracking the text pointer. When a mismatch occurs after matching $j$ characters, shift the pattern forward to the longest proper prefix of the matched segment that is also a suffix of it.

#### Definition of the Prefix Function ($\pi$)
Given a string $S$ of length $N$, the **prefix function** is an array $\pi$ of length $N$, where $\pi[i]$ is defined as the length of the longest **proper prefix** of the substring $S[0 \dots i]$ that is also a suffix of $S[0 \dots i]$:
$$\pi[i] = \max_{0 \le k \le i} \big\{ k : S[0 \dots k - 1] == S[i - k + 1 \dots i] \big\}$$
By definition, $\pi[0] = 0$ (a proper prefix must be strictly shorter than the whole string).

* **Example**: For $S = \text{"aabaaab"}$:
  * $i = 0$ ("a"): $\pi[0] = 0$
  * $i = 1$ ("aa"): prefix "a" == suffix "a" $\implies \pi[1] = 1$
  * $i = 2$ ("aab"): no proper prefix-suffix match $\implies \pi[2] = 0$
  * $i = 3$ ("aaba"): "a" == "a" $\implies \pi[3] = 1$
  * $i = 4$ ("aabaa"): "aa" == "aa" $\implies \pi[4] = 2$
  * $i = 5$ ("aabaaa"): "aa" == "aa" $\implies \pi[5] = 2$
  * $i = 6$ ("aabaaab"): "aab" == "aab" $\implies \pi[6] = 3$
  $$\pi = [0, 1, 0, 1, 2, 2, 3]$$

#### Efficient $O(N)$ Construction of $\pi$
1. **Bounded Growth Property**: Notice that $\pi[i] \le \pi[i - 1] + 1$. The value can increase by at most $1$ in each step, because appending one character cannot extend the matching boundary by more than $1$.
2. **Transition Rule**: To compute $\pi[i]$, let candidate length $j = \pi[i - 1]$.
   * If $S[i] == S[j]$: The match extends cleanly: $\pi[i] = j + 1$.
   * If $S[i] \ne S[j]$: We must find the next longest prefix of $S[0 \dots j - 1]$ that is also its suffix.
     By definition, that sub-boundary is given by:
     $$j \gets \pi[j - 1]$$
   * Repeat this jump until either $S[i] == S[j]$ (in which case $\pi[i] = j + 1$) or $j = 0$ (in which case $\pi[i] = (S[i] == S[0] ? 1 : 0)$).

#### Amortized Linear Complexity Proof
Although the inner `while` loop can perform multiple jumps in a single step:
* Variable $j$ increases by at most $1$ per loop iteration ($N$ times total).
* Variable $j$ decreases only inside the `while` loop ($j \gets \pi[j - 1]$), and each jump decreases $j$ by at least $1$.
* Since $j \ge 0$ always, $j$ cannot decrease more times than it increases.
* Thus, the inner loop executes at most $N$ times across the entire algorithm.
$$\text{Total Time} = O(N)$$

#### Pattern Matching via Sentinel Delimiter
To find all occurrences of pattern $P$ in text $T$:
1. Form the composite string:
   $$S = P + \text{'\#'} + T$$
   where $\text{'\#'}$ is a unique sentinel delimiter character not present in $P$ or $T$.
2. Compute the prefix function array $\pi$ for $S$.
3. Since $\text{'\#'}$ never matches any character, $\pi[i] \le |P|$ always.
4. Whenever $\pi[i] == |P|$ for an index in the text part ($i > |P|$):
   A complete match of $P$ has occurred! The 0-based start index in $T$ is:
   $$\text{start\_index} = i - 2 \cdot |P|$$
description: Linear pi-array precomputation avoiding redundant character comparisons (Automaton-Like State Fallback via Proper Prefix-Suffix Boundaries) — Time: O(N + M) Total Time (Strict Linear Bound).

title: Z-Function & Z-Algorithm: Longest Common Prefix Array in O(N + M)
coreConcept: Reusing previous LCP computations to achieve linear pattern discovery
timeComplexity: O(N + M) Strict Linear Time
spaceComplexity: O(N) Auxiliary Space
theory:
#### Problem Definition
Given a string $S$ of length $N$, the **Z-function** produces an array $Z$ of length $N$, where $Z[i]$ is the length of the longest substring starting at position $i$ that matches a prefix of $S$:
$$Z[i] = \max \big\{ k : S[i \dots i + k - 1] == S[0 \dots k - 1] \big\}$$
In other words, $Z[i]$ is the **Longest Common Prefix (LCP)** between the entire string $S$ and the suffix of $S$ starting at index $i$.
* By convention, $Z[0] = 0$.

* **Example**:
  * $S = \text{"aaaaa"} \implies Z = [0, 4, 3, 2, 1]$
  * $S = \text{"aaabaab"} \implies Z = [0, 2, 1, 0, 2, 1, 0]$
  * $S = \text{"abacaba"} \implies Z = [0, 0, 1, 0, 3, 0, 1]$

#### The Rightmost Segment Match Window $[l, r)$
To achieve $O(N)$ linear time without re-comparing characters, we maintain an active window $[l, r)$ representing the **rightmost segment match** detected so far:
* $S[l \dots r - 1] == S[0 \dots r - l - 1]$
* Index $r$ is the furthest boundary scanned by the algorithm.

When calculating $Z[i]$ for the current index $i$:
1. **Case 1 ($i \ge r$)**: Index $i$ falls outside the scanned window. We must compute $Z[i]$ from scratch using character-by-character comparisons (the trivial scan).
   * Once finished, if $i + Z[i] > r$, we update the window: $l = i, \ r = i + Z[i]$.
2. **Case 2 ($i < r$)**: Index $i$ lies inside the active segment match $[l, r)$.
   * By the segment match invariant, the substring $S[l \dots r - 1]$ matches prefix $S[0 \dots r - l - 1]$.
   * Therefore, the character at index $i$ corresponds to the character at index $i - l$ in the prefix!
   * We can safely initialize $Z[i]$ using the already-computed value $Z[i - l]$:
     $$Z_0[i] = \min(r - i, \ Z[i - l])$$
   * **Why the $\min$ bound?** We only know that characters match up to the right boundary $r$. Characters beyond $r$ have not yet been inspected.
   * After initializing with $Z_0[i]$, we continue character comparisons starting from $r$ onwards, expanding $r$ further if possible.

#### Proof of Linear Time $O(N)$
* In each step, if $i < r$ and $i + Z[i - l] < r$, $Z[i]$ is determined in strictly $O(1)$ without any character comparison.
* If comparisons are performed, each successful comparison increments the right boundary $r$.
* Because $r$ only ever increases and is strictly bounded by $N$, at most $N$ character comparisons can succeed across the entire execution of the algorithm!
$$\text{Total Time} = O(N)$$
description: Reusing previous LCP computations to achieve linear pattern discovery (Rightmost Segment Matching Window (Z-Box Expansion)) — Time: O(N + M) Strict Linear Time.

title: Polynomial Double String Hashing & Rabin-Karp: O(1) Substring Equality
paradigm: Algebraic Rolling Fingerprint with Modulo Pair Invariance
coreConcept: Comparing arbitrary substrings in O(1) time with near-zero collision probability
timeComplexity: O(N) Precomputation, O(1) per Substring Hash Query
spaceComplexity: O(N) Prefix Hash & Base Power Arrays
theory:
#### Problem Definition & Motivation
We want to compare whether two substrings $S[i \dots j]$ and $S[k \dots l]$ are identical in strictly $O(1)$ constant time.
A standard string comparison takes $O(L)$ time where $L$ is the substring length. By converting substrings into deterministic integer fingerprints (hashes), equality tests reduce to single integer comparisons in $O(1)$.

#### Polynomial Rolling Hash Definition
For a string $S$ of length $N$, its polynomial rolling hash modulo $M$ with prime base $P$ is:
$$\text{hash}(S) = \sum_{k=0}^{N-1} S[k] \cdot P^k \pmod M$$
* **Base $P$**: Should be a prime roughly equal to or greater than the alphabet size. For lowercase English letters ($a \dots z$), $P = 31$ or $P = 53$ is standard.
* **Modulo $M$**: Must be a large prime (e.g., $10^9 + 7$ or $10^9 + 9$).
* **Warning against $M = 2^{64}$**: Choosing $2^{64}$ (relying on unsigned 64-bit integer overflow) is vulnerable to anti-hash test cases generated using Thue-Morse sequences, which force systematic collisions.

#### Why Double Hashing is Mandatory
The probability of two random distinct strings colliding under a single hash modulo $M \approx 10^9$ is $1 / M \approx 10^{-9}$. Under the **Birthday Paradox**, after testing $\sqrt{M} \approx 3 \times 10^4$ distinct substrings, the probability of a collision exceeds $50\%$!

By employing **Double Hashing** with two independent large prime moduli:
$$(P_1 = 31, \ M_1 = 10^9 + 7) \quad \text{and} \quad (P_2 = 37, \ M_2 = 10^9 + 9)$$
The composite collision probability becomes:
$$\frac{1}{M_1 \cdot M_2} \approx \frac{1}{10^{18}}$$
This is small enough to guarantee correctness across all conceivable contest and real-world inputs.

#### $O(1)$ Substring Hash Retrieval
Let $H[k]$ be the precomputed prefix hash for $S[0 \dots k - 1]$:
$$H[k] = \sum_{x=0}^{k-1} S[x] \cdot P^x \pmod M$$
The hash of substring $S[i \dots j]$ multiplied by $P^i$ is given by simple prefix subtraction:
$$\text{hash}(S[i \dots j]) \cdot P^i \equiv H[j + 1] - H[i] \pmod M$$

To compare two substrings $S[i_1 \dots j_1]$ and $S[i_2 \dots j_2]$ of equal length $L$:
Multiply each hash difference by $P^{\max(i_1, i_2) - i}$ to align powers of $P$ without needing modular division!
description: Comparing arbitrary substrings in O(1) time with near-zero collision probability (Algebraic Rolling Fingerprint with Modulo Pair Invariance) — Time: O(N) Precomputation, O(1) per Substring Hash Query.

title: Manacher's Algorithm: Longest Palindromic Substrings in O(N)
paradigm: Palindrome Mirror Symmetry with Active Boundary Expansion
coreConcept: Reusing mirror palindrome radii to eliminate quadratic center expansion
timeComplexity: O(N) Strict Linear Time
spaceComplexity: O(N) Transformed String & Radii Arrays
theory:
#### Problem Definition
A string is a **palindrome** if it reads the same forwards and backwards ($T = T_{\text{rev}}$).
Given a string $S$ of length $N$, find all palindromic substrings, their lengths, and the maximum length palindromic substring.
* A string of length $N$ can contain up to $O(N^2)$ palindromic substrings.
* A naive expansion around every center takes $O(N^2)$ time.
* **Glenn Manacher (1975)** discovered an algorithm that computes the radii of all palindromes in **strictly $O(N)$ linear time**.

#### String Interleaving Transformation (Unifying Odd & Even)
Palindromes can be:
* **Odd length**: Centered at a character (e.g., $\text{"aba"}$).
* **Even length**: Centered between two characters (e.g., $\text{"abba"}$).

To eliminate separate code branches for odd and even lengths, we interleave the string with dummy delimiter characters `#'` and surround it with boundary guards `^'` and `$'`:
$$S = \text{"aba"} \implies T = \text{"^\#a\#b\#a\#\$"}$$
* Every palindrome in $S$ (odd or even) maps to an **odd-length palindrome centered on a character** in $T$!
* Guard characters `^` and `$` prevent out-of-bounds checks without branching.

#### Mirror Symmetry Invariant
Let $P[i]$ be the palindromic radius centered at index $i$ in the transformed string $T$.
We maintain:
* $C$: Center of the rightmost palindrome found so far.
* $R$: The exclusive right boundary of this palindrome ($R = C + P[C]$).

When processing center $i$:
1. If $i < R$, index $i$ lies inside the active palindrome centered at $C$.
2. The **mirror position** of $i$ with respect to center $C$ is:
   $$i_{\text{mirror}} = 2C - i$$
3. By palindrome symmetry, the radius at $i$ can be initialized directly from its mirror:
   $$P[i] = \min(R - i, \ P[i_{\text{mirror}}])$$
4. After initialization, we attempt to expand $P[i]$ further beyond $R$ by comparing $T[i - P[i] - 1]$ and $T[i + P[i] + 1]$.
5. If $i + P[i] > R$, we update the new rightmost palindrome: $C = i, \ R = i + P[i]$.

#### Proof of Linear Time $O(N)$
* The `while` loop for character expansion only executes when the expansion reaches beyond boundary $R$.
* Every successful character comparison strictly increases $R$.
* Since $R$ starts at $0$ and cannot exceed the length of $T$ ($2N + 3$), the total number of character comparisons is bounded by $2N$.
$$\text{Total Time} = O(N)$$
description: Reusing mirror palindrome radii to eliminate quadratic center expansion (Palindrome Mirror Symmetry with Active Boundary Expansion) — Time: O(N) Strict Linear Time.

title: Aho-Corasick Automaton: Multi-Pattern Dictionary Matching in O(N + sum|P|)
paradigm: Trie-Based Deterministic Finite Automaton with Suffix Failure Links
coreConcept: Simultaneous discovery of all dictionary pattern occurrences in text
timeComplexity: O(sum|P| * Sigma) Construction, O(N + Total Matches) Text Scanning
spaceComplexity: O(sum|P| * Sigma) Automaton Transitions
theory:
#### Problem Definition & Motivation
Given a text $T$ of length $N$ and a set of $K$ patterns (dictionary) $P_1, P_2, \dots, P_K$ with total length $\sum |P_i| = M$:
Find all occurrences of all dictionary patterns in the text $T$.
* Running KMP for each pattern separately takes $O(K \cdot N + M)$ time.
* **Alfred Aho and Margaret Corasick (1975)** constructed an automaton that processes the text $T$ in a **single linear pass** of $O(N + \text{matches})$, completely independent of the number of patterns $K$!

#### Automaton Architecture
The automaton consists of a **Trie** augmented with two types of links:
1. **Trie Edges (`next[v][c]`)**: Standard tree transitions corresponding to pattern characters.
2. **Suffix Links (`link[v]`)**: Similar to the prefix function in KMP. For a vertex $v$ representing string $S$, its suffix link points to the vertex representing the **longest proper suffix of $S$ that exists in the trie**.
3. **Exit Links / Output Lists**: Direct shortcuts to pattern-ending states within the suffix-link ancestor chain.

#### Construction via Breadth-First Search (BFS)
Suffix links are built level by level using BFS:
1. The root (state $0$) has $\text{link}[0] = 0$.
2. All direct children of the root have $\text{link}[v] = 0$.
3. For a vertex $u$ reached from parent $p$ via character $c$:
   We follow the suffix link of the parent ($\text{link}[p]$) until we find a vertex that has an edge labeled $c$:
   $$\text{link}[u] = \text{go}(\text{link}[p], \ c)$$
4. By caching transitions into a direct transition matrix $\text{go}[v][c]$, moving between states is an $O(1)$ table lookup.

#### Text Processing Mechanics
To search a text $T$:
* Start at root state $u = 0$.
* For each character $c$ in $T$:
  * Transition to next state: $u = \text{go}[u][c]$.
  * All patterns ending at $u$, or reachable from $u$ via suffix links, match at the current position!
description: Simultaneous discovery of all dictionary pattern occurrences in text (Trie-Based Deterministic Finite Automaton with Suffix Failure Links) — Time: O(sum|P| * Sigma) Construction, O(N + Total Matches) Text Scanning.

title: Binary Exponentiation & Modular Inverse: Fast Power in O(log N)
paradigm: Binary Decomposition of Exponents (Divide & Conquer Multiplicative Squaring)
coreConcept: Evaluating a^b mod m using repeated squaring based on binary bits
timeComplexity: O(log b) Multiplications
spaceComplexity: O(1) Auxiliary Memory
theory:
#### Problem Definition & Motivation
Given integers $a$, $b$, and modulo $m$, calculate:
$$a^b \pmod m$$
* **Naive Multiplication**: Multiplying $a$ by itself $b$ times requires $O(b)$ operations. When $b \approx 10^{18}$ (common in competitive programming and cryptography), this requires $10^{18}$ multiplications, resulting in Time Limit Exceeded (TLE).
* **Binary Exponentiation**: Exploits the binary representation of the exponent $b$ to solve the problem in strictly $O(\log b)$ operations (at most $64$ multiplications for 64-bit integers).

#### Binary Decomposition Principle
Any integer $b \ge 0$ can be written uniquely in base 2:
$$b = \sum_{i=0}^{\lfloor \log_2 b \rfloor} b_i \cdot 2^i, \quad b_i \in \{0, 1\}$$
Using exponent multiplication rules:
$$a^b = a^{\sum b_i 2^i} = \prod_{b_i = 1} a^{2^i}$$

* **Example**: Consider $3^{13}$:
  $$13 = (1101)_2 = 8 + 4 + 1 = 2^3 + 2^2 + 2^0$$
  $$3^{13} = 3^8 \cdot 3^4 \cdot 3^1$$
Instead of computing $3^{13}$ from scratch, we compute the powers of two:
$$\begin{aligned}
3^1 &= 3 \\
3^2 &= (3^1)^2 = 9 \\
3^4 &= (3^2)^2 = 81 \\
3^8 &= (3^4)^2 = 6561
\end{aligned}$$
Each term is simply the **square of the previous term**!
Multiplying the terms corresponding to the set bits ($b_i = 1$) yields:
$$3^{13} = 6561 \cdot 81 \cdot 3 = 1594323$$

#### Iterative Bitwise Algorithm
We iterate through the bits of $b$ from lowest to highest:
1. If the current lowest bit of $b$ is set (`b & 1`):
   Multiply the accumulated answer by the current base $a$:
   $$\text{res} = (\text{res} \cdot a) \pmod m$$
2. Square the base for the next power of two:
   $$a = (a \cdot a) \pmod m$$
3. Shift $b$ right by one bit: `b >>= 1`.
4. Repeat until $b == 0$.

#### Modular Multiplicative Inverse (Fermat's Little Theorem)
If $m$ is a prime number and $\gcd(a, m) = 1$, Fermat's Little Theorem states:
$$a^{m - 1} \equiv 1 \pmod m \implies a \cdot a^{m - 2} \equiv 1 \pmod m$$
Therefore, the modular multiplicative inverse $a^{-1} \pmod m$ is simply:
$$a^{-1} \equiv a^{m - 2} \pmod m$$
We can compute $a^{-1}$ in strictly $O(\log m)$ time using binary exponentiation with exponent $m - 2$!
description: Evaluating a^b mod m using repeated squaring based on binary bits (Binary Decomposition of Exponents (Divide & Conquer Multiplicative Squaring)) — Time: O(log b) Multiplications.

title: Euclidean Algorithm & Extended GCD: Bézout's Identity in O(log min(a, b))
paradigm: Division Algorithm & Recursive Linear Combination Reconstruction
coreConcept: Computing greatest common divisors and solving a*x + b*y = gcd(a, b)
timeComplexity: O(log(min(a, b))) (Lamé's Theorem Bound)
spaceComplexity: O(log(min(a, b))) Recursion Stack
theory:
#### Problem Definition
Given two non-negative integers $a$ and $b$:
1. Compute their **Greatest Common Divisor** ($\gcd(a, b)$).
2. Find integer coefficients $x$ and $y$ satisfying **Bézout's Identity**:
   $$a \cdot x + b \cdot y = \gcd(a, b)$$

#### The Classical Euclidean Algorithm
The Euclidean algorithm relies on the fundamental division theorem:
$$\gcd(a, b) = \gcd(b, \ a \bmod b)$$
* **Base Case**: $\gcd(a, 0) = a$.
* **Lamé's Theorem**: The number of division steps in Euclid's algorithm never exceeds $5$ times the number of decimal digits of the smaller number.
  $$\text{Steps} \le 5 \log_{10}(\min(a, b)) = O(\log(\min(a, b)))$$
The worst-case input consists of consecutive Fibonacci numbers ($F_{n+1}, F_n$), where each modulo step reduces the value by the golden ratio $\phi \approx 1.618$.

#### Derivation of the Extended Euclidean Algorithm
Bézout's identity guarantees that integers $x$ and $y$ always exist such that:
$$a \cdot x + b \cdot y = g \quad \text{where } g = \gcd(a, b)$$

Suppose by recursion we have already solved the smaller subproblem:
$$b \cdot x_1 + (a \bmod b) \cdot y_1 = g$$
Using integer division, rewrite $a \bmod b$:
$$a \bmod b = a - \left\lfloor \frac{a}{b} \right\rfloor \cdot b$$
Substitute this into the recursive equation:
$$b \cdot x_1 + \left(a - \left\lfloor \frac{a}{b} \right\rfloor \cdot b\right) \cdot y_1 = g$$
Rearranging terms by grouping coefficients of $a$ and $b$:
$$a \cdot y_1 + b \cdot \left(x_1 - \left\lfloor \frac{a}{b} \right\rfloor \cdot y_1\right) = g$$

Comparing this with $a \cdot x + b \cdot y = g$, we deduce the exact inductive transition:
$$\begin{aligned}
x &= y_1 \\
y &= x_1 - \left\lfloor \frac{a}{b} \right\rfloor \cdot y_1
\end{aligned}$$
* **Base Case ($b = 0$)**:
  $$a \cdot 1 + 0 \cdot 0 = a \implies x = 1, \ y = 0$$

#### Application: Solving Linear Diophantine Equations
Given $a \cdot x + b \cdot y = c$:
* A solution exists **if and only if** $c$ is divisible by $g = \gcd(a, b)$.
* If divisible, one particular solution is:
  $$x_0 = x \cdot \frac{c}{g}, \quad y_0 = y \cdot \frac{c}{g}$$
* All general integer solutions are given by parameterizing with $k \in \mathbb{Z}$:
  $$x = x_0 + k \cdot \frac{b}{g}, \quad y = y_0 - k \cdot \frac{a}{g}$$
description: Computing greatest common divisors and solving a*x + b*y = gcd(a, b) (Division Algorithm & Recursive Linear Combination Reconstruction) — Time: O(log(min(a, b))) (Lamé's Theorem Bound).

title: Linear Sieve (Euler's Sieve) & Smallest Prime Factor (SPF) in O(N)
coreConcept: Generating primes and factoring integers in O(log X) using linear precomputation
timeComplexity: O(N) Strict Linear Precomputation, O(log X) per Factorization
spaceComplexity: O(N) Precomputed SPF & Prime Arrays
theory:
#### Classical Sieve vs. Linear Sieve
The standard **Sieve of Eratosthenes** runs in $O(N \log \log N)$ time. While very fast, it has a theoretical redundancy: composite numbers are marked multiple times by different prime factors.
* Example: $12$ is marked when iterating over $2$, and marked again when iterating over $3$.
* For $N = 10^7$, redundant operations waste millions of memory accesses.

**Euler's Linear Sieve** eliminates all redundant operations by enforcing a strict invariant:
$$\text{Every composite number is marked exactly once by its Smallest Prime Factor (SPF)!}$$
This guarantees strictly **$O(N)$ linear time**.

#### The Linear Sieve Invariant
Let $\text{spf}[i]$ be the Smallest Prime Factor of integer $i$.
We maintain:
* An array `spf` of size $N + 1$.
* A list `primes` containing all discovered prime numbers in ascending order.

For each integer $i$ from $2$ to $N$:
1. If $\text{spf}[i] == 0$: $i$ has no divisors smaller than itself, so $i$ is prime!
   Set $\text{spf}[i] = i$ and append $i$ to `primes`.
2. For every known prime $p \in \text{primes}$:
   * If $p > \text{spf}[i]$ or $i \cdot p > N$: **BREAK immediately!**
   * Mark the composite number: $\text{spf}[i \cdot p] = p$.

**Why Break When $p > \text{spf}[i]$?**
* Suppose $\text{spf}[i] = 2$, and we continued to $p = 3$.
* The composite number would be $x = i \cdot 3$.
* But since $i$ is divisible by $2$, $x = i \cdot 3$ is also divisible by $2$!
* Therefore, the smallest prime factor of $x$ is $2$, NOT $3$.
* If we marked $x$ with $3$, $x$ would be visited again later by $2$, violating the linear invariant!
* Breaking at $p == \text{spf}[i]$ ensures that every composite number is marked **strictly once by its smallest prime factor**.

#### Instant $O(\log X)$ Prime Factorization
Once the `spf` array is computed up to $N$:
To factorize any integer $X \le N$:
1. Query $p = \text{spf}[X]$.
2. Divide $X \gets X / p$.
3. Repeat until $X == 1$.
Because each step divides $X$ by at least $2$, the factorization completes in at most $\lfloor \log_2 X \rfloor$ steps: **$O(\log X)$ query time!**
description: Generating primes and factoring integers in O(log X) using linear precomputation (Unique Minimal Prime Factorization Sieve) — Time: O(N) Strict Linear Precomputation, O(log X) per Factorization.

title: Submask Enumeration & Bit Tricks: Iterating All Submasks in O(3^N)
paradigm: Bitwise Arithmetic Decrementation & In-Place Bit Twiddling
coreConcept: Iterating over all submasks s of a mask using s = (s - 1) & mask
timeComplexity: O(2^k) per Mask with k Set Bits; O(3^N) across All Masks of Size N
spaceComplexity: O(1) Auxiliary Space
theory:
#### Problem Definition
Given a bitmask `mask` representing a set of elements:
A bitmask $s$ is a **submask** of `mask` if every bit set in $s$ is also set in `mask`:
$$(s \ \& \ \text{mask}) == s$$
We want to iterate through all valid submasks of a given mask efficiently, and across all submasks of all masks of size $N$.

#### The Decrement-and-AND Trick: `s = (s - 1) & mask`
A naive approach loops through all integers from $0$ to $2^N - 1$ and checks if $(s \ \& \ \text{mask}) == s$. For a mask with $k$ set bits, this takes $O(2^N)$ rather than $O(2^k)$.

We can iterate **only through the valid submasks in strictly decreasing order** using bit arithmetic:
```cpp
for (int s = mask; s > 0; s = (s - 1) & mask) {
    // Process submask s
}
// Optionally process s = 0 (the empty submask)
```

**Why Does `s = (s - 1) & mask` Work?**
1. Subtracting 1 ($s - 1$) clears the lowest set bit of $s$, and sets all bits below it to $1$.
2. Performing bitwise AND with `mask` (`(s - 1) & mask`) clears all extraneous bits that were not present in the original `mask`.
3. Thus, $(s - 1) \ \& \ \text{mask}$ produces the largest valid submask strictly smaller than $s$.
4. It never visits any invalid number, running in strictly **$O(2^k)$ steps** for a mask with $k$ set bits!

#### Mathematical Proof: Why Total Work Across All Masks is $O(3^N)$
Suppose we iterate through all submasks for every mask from $0$ to $2^N - 1$:
```cpp
for (int mask = 0; mask < (1 << n); mask++) {
    for (int s = mask; s > 0; s = (s - 1) & mask) { ... }
}
```
A mask with $k$ set bits has exactly $2^k$ submasks.
The number of masks with exactly $k$ set bits is given by the binomial coefficient $\binom{N}{k}$.
Therefore, the total number of inner loop executions across all masks is:
$$\text{Total Operations} = \sum_{k=0}^N \binom{N}{k} \cdot 2^k$$
By Newton's **Binomial Theorem**:
$$(1 + x)^N = \sum_{k=0}^N \binom{N}{k} \cdot x^k$$
Setting $x = 2$:
$$(1 + 2)^N = 3^N$$
* **Complexity**: Total operations is strictly **$O(3^N)$**, which is exponentially faster than the naive $O(2^N \cdot 2^N) = O(4^N)$!
  * For $N = 15$: $3^{15} \approx 1.4 \times 10^7$ (runs in $< 0.05$ seconds in C++).
description: Iterating over all submasks s of a mask using s = (s - 1) & mask (Bitwise Arithmetic Decrementation & In-Place Bit Twiddling) — Time: O(2^k) per Mask with k Set Bits; O(3^N) across All Masks of Size N.

title: Floyd's Tortoise & Hare: Cycle Detection & Entrance Recovery in O(N)
paradigm: Two-Pointer Speed Differential (Pointers at Different Velocities)
coreConcept: Detecting functional/linked cycles and locating entrance in O(1) space
timeComplexity: O(N) Linear Time
spaceComplexity: O(1) Strictly Constant Memory
theory:
#### Problem Definition
Given a sequence or functional graph defined by $x_{i+1} = f(x_i)$ (or a singly-linked list with a `next` pointer), determine whether a cycle exists. If a cycle exists, find:
1. The **entrance of the cycle** (first node $\mu$ where the loop begins).
2. The **length of the cycle** ($\lambda$).
We must do this using **$O(1)$ constant memory**, without maintaining hash sets or visited arrays.

#### Phase 1: Detecting Cycle Presence (The Speed Differential)
We maintain two pointers initialized at the starting element $x_0$:
* **Tortoise (Slow Pointer)**: Advances $1$ step at a time: $\text{slow} = f(\text{slow})$.
* **Hare (Fast Pointer)**: Advances $2$ steps at a time: $\text{fast} = f(f(\text{fast}))$.

If the structure is acyclic, `fast` reaches the terminal end (`nullptr` / out-of-bounds).
If a cycle exists, `fast` will enter the cycle first and loop indefinitely. Once `slow` enters the cycle, the relative distance between `fast` and `slow` decreases by $1$ in each iteration until **they are guaranteed to collide**:
$$\text{slow} == \text{fast}$$

#### Phase 2: Mathematical Proof of Cycle Entrance Recovery
Let:
* $\mu$: Distance from the start node to the cycle entrance.
* $\lambda$: Length of the cycle.
* $k$: Number of steps taken until `slow` and `fast` collide.

When `slow` and `fast` meet at step $k$:
* The distance traveled by `slow` is $k$.
* The distance traveled by `fast` is $2k$.
* Since they occupy the exact same node inside the cycle:
  $$2k - k = k \equiv 0 \pmod \lambda \implies k = m \cdot \lambda \quad (\text{a multiple of the cycle length})$$

Now, express $k$ in terms of $\mu$:
$$k = \mu + (\text{distance within the cycle from entrance to meeting point})$$
$$\text{distance within cycle} = k - \mu = m \cdot \lambda - \mu \equiv -\mu \pmod \lambda$$

**The Master Stroke**:
1. Reset the `slow` pointer back to the start node $x_0$.
2. Keep the `fast` pointer at the meeting point $M$.
3. Advance **both pointers at the same speed ($1$ step per turn)**.
* After taking $\mu$ steps:
  * `slow` moves from $x_0$ to the cycle entrance (distance $\mu$).
  * `fast` moves from $M$ forward by $\mu$ steps:
    $$\text{position} = (m \cdot \lambda - \mu) + \mu = m \cdot \lambda \equiv 0 \pmod \lambda$$
    which is **the exact cycle entrance**!
They collide at the exact cycle entrance node!
description: Detecting functional/linked cycles and locating entrance in O(1) space (Two-Pointer Speed Differential (Pointers at Different Velocities)) — Time: O(N) Linear Time.

title: Quickselect: K-th Order Statistic in Average O(N)
paradigm: Divide and Conquer In-Place Partitioning (Hoare's Selection)
coreConcept: Finding the k-th smallest element without sorting the entire array
timeComplexity: Average O(N), Worst-Case O(N^2)
spaceComplexity: O(1) In-Place Partitioning (O(log N) Recursion Stack)
theory:
#### Problem Definition
Given an unsorted array $A$ of $N$ elements and an integer $K$ ($0 \le K < N$), find the element that would appear at index $K$ if the array were completely sorted.
* Sorting the whole array with QuickSort/MergeSort takes $O(N \log N)$ time.
* **Quickselect (Hoare, 1961)** achieves **average $O(N)$ linear time** by only recursing into the single partition containing $K$.

#### Partitioning Invariant
Choose a pivot element $P$ and partition the array into three contiguous zones:
$$[\text{elements } < P], \quad [\text{elements } == P], \quad [\text{elements } > P]$$
Let the pivot end up at index $M$:
1. If $K == M$: The pivot itself is the $K$-th order statistic! Return $A[M]$.
2. If $K < M$: The target element lies in the left subarray. Discard the right half and recurse only into $[L, M - 1]$.
3. If $K > M$: The target element lies in the right subarray. Discard the left half and recurse only into $[M + 1, R]$.

#### Proof of Average $O(N)$ Complexity
In standard QuickSort, both halves are recursively sorted:
$$T(N) = 2T(N / 2) + O(N) = O(N \log N)$$
In Quickselect, **only one half** is searched:
$$T(N) = T(N / 2) + O(N)$$
Expanding the geometric series:
$$T(N) = N + \frac{N}{2} + \frac{N}{4} + \frac{N}{8} + \dots = N \left(1 + \frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{4} + \dots\right) = 2N = O(N)$$
Thus, the expected runtime is strictly **linear $O(N)$**!

#### Pivot Selection & Worst-Case Protection
To protect against adversarial inputs (already-sorted arrays that degrade deterministic quickselect to $O(N^2)$), we select a **randomized pivot** or use median-of-three before partitioning.
description: Finding the k-th smallest element without sorting the entire array (Divide and Conquer In-Place Partitioning (Hoare's Selection)) — Time: Average O(N), Worst-Case O(N^2).

title: Kadane's Algorithm: Maximum Subsegment Sum & Range Extraction in O(N)
coreConcept: Optimal contiguous subarray sum tracking in strictly linear time
timeComplexity: O(N) Strict Single-Pass Time
spaceComplexity: O(1) Constant Auxiliary Memory
theory:
#### Problem Definition
Given an array $A$ of $N$ integers (which may include negative numbers), find the maximum possible sum of a non-empty contiguous subarray:
$$\max_{0 \le l \le r < N} \sum_{i=l}^r A[i]$$
and recover the starting and ending indices $(l, r)$ of this optimal subsegment.

#### Dynamic Programming Formulation
Let $\text{current\_sum}[i]$ denote the maximum sum of a contiguous subarray ending at index $i$:
At step $i$, there are only two choices:
1. Extend the previous subarray: $\text{current\_sum}[i - 1] + A[i]$
2. Start a completely fresh subarray at index $i$: $A[i]$

Thus:
$$\text{current\_sum}[i] = \max\Big(A[i], \ \text{current\_sum}[i - 1] + A[i]\Big)$$
* If $\text{current\_sum}[i - 1] < 0$, it is always detrimental to extend it; we restart the subarray at index $i$.

The global maximum subsegment sum across the entire array is simply:
$$\text{max\_sum} = \max_{0 \le i < N} \text{current\_sum}[i]$$

#### Space Compression to $O(1)$
Because $\text{current\_sum}[i]$ depends only on $\text{current\_sum}[i - 1]$, we do not need an array! We maintain a single running scalar `cur_sum` and update `max_sum` in real time.

#### Subsegment Boundary Reconstruction
To extract the exact indices $(l, r)$:
* Keep a running candidate start pointer `cur_start`.
* When `cur_sum < 0`, reset `cur_sum = 0` and advance `cur_start = i + 1`.
* Whenever `cur_sum > max_sum`, update `best_l = cur_start` and `best_r = i`.
description: Optimal contiguous subarray sum tracking in strictly linear time (Dynamic Programming Running Prefix Reset) — Time: O(N) Strict Single-Pass Time.
